L01.subgoal: Identify the core concepts and objectives of the XR course

key_points.text: The field commonly uses terms such as Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), Extended Reality (XR), and Mixed Reality (MR).
A primary objective of the course is to clarify the meanings and differences between these multiple terms.
The course aims to help students find answers to questions regarding the significance of these technologies in their future prospects.
Finding answers to the questions about XR, AR, VR, and MR is one of the main objectives of this course.

key_terms.definition: Extended reality (XR) is a broad term used to encompass several related immersive experiences. It refers to the umbrella concept that includes various forms of reality blending.
Virtual reality (VR) is a specific type of immersive experience mentioned in the course title. It involves creating a simulated environment that users can interact with.
Augmented reality (AR) is another specific type of immersive experience mentioned in the course title. It involves overlaying digital information onto the real world.
Mixed reality (MR) is a distinct term that is currently being heard in the field. It represents a specific type of reality blending.

L01.subgoal: Distinguish between common public perceptions and technical applications of XR technologies

key_points.text: The terms AR, VR, MR, and XR are often immediately associated with fantastic, imaginary, or magical environments (47).
A common perception of Virtual Reality (VR) is that a user wears a headset to be transported into a virtual world (58, 59).
Augmented Reality (AR) is often perceived as seeing virtual objects overlaid onto the real world through a screen (61, 62).
XR technologies can also be used for specialized viewing, such as seeing internal skeletal or vein structures (70, 71).

L01.subgoal: Define Extended Reality (XR) and differentiate it from specific immersive technologies

key_points.text: XR (Extended Reality) is an umbrella term that encapsulates all immersive technologies, including AR, VR, and MR.
The term 'immersive' describes an environment where the sensory experience is indistinguishable from the real environment.
XR refers to all present or future immersive technologies, where 'X' represents the specific technology (e.g., A for Augmented, V for Virtual).

key_terms.definition: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term that encompasses all immersive technologies, including Augmented Reality, Virtual Reality, and Mixed Reality. XR refers to all present or future immersive technologies.

Immersive technology is a type of technology where the user experiences an environment through sensory organs in such a way that they fail to distinguish it from the real environment. This perceived experience leads the user to assume the environment is real.

L01.subgoal: Define the reality-virtuality continuum and its components

key_points.text: The reality-virtuality continuum is a scale ranging from a purely real environment to a purely virtual environment.
Augmented Reality (AR) involves augmenting the real world with digital or virtual content.
Augmented Virtuality (AV) involves augmenting a virtual world with real-world content.
Mixed Reality (MR) is the broad term for the entire space between the purely real and purely virtual environments.

key_terms.definition: Reality-virtuality continuum is a scale used to visualize the spectrum between a completely real environment and a completely virtual environment.
Virtual environment is one extreme of the scale where there is nothing real present, meaning the environment is completely virtual.
Augmented reality is a state where the real world is enhanced by adding digital or virtual content.
Augmented virtuality is the opposite of augmented reality, where a virtual world is enhanced by incorporating real-world content.
Mixed reality is the broad space between the completely real and completely virtual environments, encompassing various degrees of augmentation.

L01.subgoal: Justify the growing commercial and technological importance of XR

key_points.text: XR technologies are being applied across diverse industries, including video games, healthcare, and engineering.
The global XR market is projected to grow exponentially, reaching around 860 billion dollars by 2030.
The Metaverse represents a shift toward reimagining human interaction in a fully immersive 3D digital world.
The rapid growth of XR necessitates a highly knowledgeable and skilled workforce, making it a major emerging field.

key_terms.definition: The Metaverse is not merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology. The Metaverse is a broad concept that involves reimagining how humans interact with the digital world in an all-around 3D environment.
Human-computer interaction is a different way of looking at how humans interact with digital content. This interaction occurs within a 3D environment using a natural way of interaction.

L01.subgoal: Outline the objectives, structure, and learning focus of the XR course

key_points.text: The broad objective is to master the field of AR/VR and gain a comprehensive idea of developing and deploying these systems. (course)
The course structure focuses on basic understanding, theoretical background, and practical knowledge. (course)
Basic understanding includes defining systems, distinguishing between technologies, and understanding how senses influence technology use. (course)
Theoretical background covers understanding software components, hardware technologies, and designing interactions in XR environments. (course)
Learning will be facilitated through a case study focused on a digital heritage preservation project. (course)

key_terms.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is a type of system within the field of virtual and augmented reality that students will learn to develop and deploy. This field includes allied concepts that are necessary to master the subject.

Augmented reality (AR) is a type of system within the field of virtual and augmented reality that students will learn to develop and deploy. This field includes allied concepts that are necessary to master the subject.
Cognitive side refers to the understanding of the human mind that is necessary to grasp how our senses influence the desired experience when using technology or a system.
Psychological side refers to the understanding of the human mind that is necessary to grasp how our senses influence the desired experience when using technology or a system.
Interactions refers to the process of designing and implementing how users engage with the environment within VR or AR systems.

L01.subgoal: Outline the course scope and the importance of XR technologies

key_points.text: XR (Extended Reality) refers to extending reality, which can range from augmenting reality to replacing perception (211, 212).
The course will use a virtual reality system related to a digital heritage preservation project as its primary example (220, 221).
Learning XR concepts is important because the field is a major emerging technology requiring skilled manpower (216, 217).
The reality-virtuality continuum was referenced from the 1994 paper by Paul Milgram and Fumio Kishino (222, 223).

key_terms.definition: Extended reality (XR) refers to extending reality by some means. Systematically, it involves using systems to either augment our reality or replace our perception of reality.

The reality-virtuality continuum is a concept that illustrates the spectrum between two extremes. One end represents the complete replacement of reality with virtual reality systems, while the other end is the complete replacement of virtuality with the entirely real world.
Virtual reality (VR) is one end of the reality-virtuality continuum where reality is completely replaced by virtual reality systems.

Augmented reality (AR) is an extended reality concept that exists between the extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum. It is one of the concepts that falls under the broader category of extended reality.

Mixed reality (MR) is a broad term used to refer to the extended reality or augmented reality concepts. These concepts are situated between the complete replacement of reality and the entirely real world.

L02.subgoal: Identify key application domains and market potential of extended reality technologies

key_points.text: This lecture will cover application areas and system categories related to virtual and augmented reality.
Extended reality technologies show huge potential across various application areas.
Key application domains include video games, healthcare, engineering, and military.
Even small percentage forecasts for technology adoption can translate into a significant financial value.

key_terms.definition: Extended reality is the overarching field that encompasses both virtual reality and augmented reality technologies. This field covers various application areas where these technologies are utilized.
Virtual reality is one of the primary technologies under extended reality that is being covered in the course. It is discussed alongside augmented reality as a key component of the field.
Augmented reality is the other primary technology under extended reality that is being covered in the course. It is discussed alongside virtual reality as a key component of the field.

L02.subgoal: Identify and describe the major application domains of virtual and augmented reality systems

key_points.text: Gaming and entertainment is a prominent application domain where immersive technologies are increasingly relied upon to enhance user experience.
Healthcare and education utilize immersive technologies for training, such as medical education and improving learner engagement.
Travel and tourism uses virtual tours to allow users to explore places and aids in the preservation of digital heritage.
Defense applications involve simulating military training, combat environments, and specialized personnel training.

key_terms.definition: Immersive technologies are a type of technology where a user's senses are blocked, transporting them into a virtual world. These technologies are used across various application domains.
Virtual tours are experiences that allow a user to visit a place remotely, even if they cannot physically go there. This method saves both money and physical effort for the user.

Heritage tourism involves allowing users to explore a heritage place virtually, even if physical visits are restricted. This enables users to explore every part of the heritage space without having to travel there.

Preservation of digital heritage is the process of digitally saving a heritage space, often in the form of virtual tours. This digital preservation can increase the lifespan and potential for the space to be visited by many users.

L02.subgoal: Differentiate between non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive VR systems

key_points.text: VR systems are broadly categorized into three types: non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive.
Non-immersive VR provides a virtual experience through a computer where the environment is not directly interacting with the user.
Semi-immersive systems offer partial immersion by blocking only some sensory organs, such as when using a VR headset for virtual tours.
Fully immersive systems completely block the user's ability to sense the real world, replacing reality with virtual realism.

key_terms.definition: Non-immersive refers to a virtual experience obtained through a computer where the user controls activities within the software, but the environment does not directly interact with the user. This type of system relies on psychological engagement, allowing the user to remain physically attached to, a

L03.subgoal: Identify and describe diverse application domains of Augmented Reality systems

key_points.text: Unlike VR, AR focuses on augmenting real-world content with digital content, rather than emphasizing immersive experience.
AR is widely used in commerce and e-commerce to enhance customer experience, allowing users to virtually test products like furniture or cosmetics before purchasing.
In healthcare, AR applications support diagnosis, surgery, and treatment plans, such as using devices to visualize internal vein networks.
AR applications are utilized across various fields, including archaeology for reconstructing lost structures, and industrial manufacturing for troubleshooting.

key_terms.definition: Augmentation is the process of enhancing the real world by overlaying digital content onto it. This focus is distinct from Virtual Reality, which emphasizes a fully simulated environment.

Immersive experience is a concept emphasized in Virtual Reality (VR) where the user is fully enveloped in a simulated environment. This level of immersion is not a mandatory requirement for Augmented Reality (AR).
Telemedicine is an application that enables medical professionals to interact with patients remotely. It is one of the many interesting applications developed using Augmented Reality.
Virtual tape measure is an augmented reality application that allows users to measure heights or lengths of objects. This tool eliminates the need for carrying a physical tape measure.

L03.subgoal: Differentiate between marker-based and markerless AR applications and their subcategories

key_points.text: Marker-based AR applications use physical markers, such as QR codes, to trigger augmented experiences.
Markerless AR applications are more versatile and utilize computer vision techniques, eliminating the need for physical markers.
Markerless AR is categorized into four subcategories: location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based.
Location-based AR relies on sensors, such as GPS, to augment digital content based on the user's specific location.

key_terms.definition: Markerless AR application is a versatile type of AR that does not require placing any markers in the physical world. These applications function based on computer vision techniques, allowing users to decide where virtual objects are placed.

L03.subgoal: Compare and contrast the system categories and application focuses of VR and AR

key_points.text: VR systems are categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive types based on psychological experience.
AR systems are broadly categorized by technology into marker-based and markerless systems.
Markerless techniques, used in AR, primarily rely on computer vision and may use sensors like GPS.
The next lecture will provide precise definitions for concepts such as VR, AR, and immersion.

key_terms.definition: Marker-based systems are easier to create and rely on simple algorithms. However, these systems require a very sanitized environment to maintain the markers, as they are prone to damage in outdoor settings.

Markerless techniques are used to overcome the maintenance difficulties of markers. These techniques primarily rely on computer vision and may utilize other sensors, such as GPS sensors, for location-based applications.
Fully immersive is one of the three categories of Virtual Reality (VR) systems. This category is defined by the importance of the psychological aspect and the overall experience provided to the user.
Superimposition-based is a type of computer vision-based application. This application involves placing digital content over the real-world view.
Holographic projection is an example of a projection-based technique. This technique can be utilized in the development of Augmented Reality (AR) applications.

L04.subgoal: Identify and explain the three defining characteristics of a Virtual Reality system

key_points.text: A virtual reality (VR) is defined as an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, where user actions partially determine the environment's outcome.
The first characteristic of a VR system is that it must have an artificial or synthetic environment, which is a computer-generated representation of a real or imaginary world.
The second characteristic requires the VR system to provide computer-generated stimuli, allowing the user to experience the environment immersively through sensory organs.
The third characteristic is interaction, meaning the VR system must be dynamic and change based on the user's actions or inputs.

key_terms.definition: Virtual reality is an artificial environment that is experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, where the user's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

Artificial environment is a computer-generated setting that is not real, which must be populated with artificial objects. This environment can be a graphical representation of either a real world or an imaginary world.

Sensory stimuli are computer-generated inputs that a VR system provides to the user. These stimuli allow the user to experience the artificial or synthetic environment through their sensory organs, such as their eyes and ears.

Interactivity is the characteristic of a VR system where dynamic changes in the virtual environment occur based on the user's actions or inputs. This allows the user to interact with the elements present in the environment, similar to how they interact with objects in the real world.

L04.subgoal: Apply the three characteristics (Virtual Environment, Immersive Experience, Interaction) to classify systems

key_points.text: A system is classified as Virtual Reality (VR) only if it satisfies three characteristics: virtual environment, immersive experience, and interactivity.
If even one of the three required characteristics is not supported, the system cannot be called a VR system.
A CAD system is not considered a VR system because it lacks an immersive experience.
Video conferencing is not a VR system because it lacks a virtual environment and immersive experience.
The next lecture segment will cover Augmented Reality (AR), its definition, and the differences between AR and VR.

key_terms.definition: Virtual reality is a classification of a system that must satisfy three specific characteristics: a virtual environment, immersive experience, and interactivity. A system is only considered VR if it supports all three of these characteristics.

Virtual environment is the presence of content that is not physically real, such as screen content, which is experienced by the user. This environment can be virtual, even if it is viewed through a screen.

Immersive experience is the generation of stimuli designed to stimulate all of the user's sensory organs. This experience can be partly immersive, as seen in 3D movies, even if it is not fully immersive.
Interaction is the ability of the user to engage with the content, causing the screen content to change based on the user's input. This characteristic requires the system to be interactive in nature.
Non-immersive VR is a screen-based experience that does not meet the criteria for a fully immersive experience. This type of experience is sometimes called regular computer screen based experience.

L05.subgoal: Define and analyze the core characteristics of Augmented Reality (AR) systems

key_points.text: Augmented reality is defined as an enhanced version of reality created by overlaying digital information onto an image of something viewed through a device.
An AR system must be real world enhanced, registered in 3D, experienced through sensory organs, and support user interaction.
For seamless mixing with the real world, digital content must be registered in 3D and appear in an appropriate, believable place.
This lecture will also cover the definition of Mixed Reality (MR) and the differences between AR and VR systems.

key_terms.definition: Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by using technology to overlay digital information onto an image being viewed through a device. This process enhances the existing reality.
Mixed reality (MR) is a concept related to augmented reality (AR) that the lecture will touch upon to examine the relationship between the two.

L05.subgoal: Compare and contrast the fundamental differences between Virtual and Augmented Reality systems

key_points.text: AR systems alter the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas VR systems completely replace the sense of reality.
AR technology requires the physical existence of the real-world environment, such as a building, to function.
VR systems do not require the physical existence of an object because they create a completely virtual environment.
AR allows for the superimposition of extra digital information over the existing physical space.

key_terms.definition: Virtual reality is a system where the sense of reality is completely replaced by a virtual environment. This means the user's perception of the real world is entirely substituted.
Superimposition is a category of AR system where extra information is placed over the building space. This allows digital content to appear on the real-world view.

L05.subgoal: Identify the course's working assumption regarding Mixed Reality and Augmented Reality

key_points.text: There is no universal agreement among practitioners regarding the precise definition of Mixed Reality (MR).
MR has been defined in various ways, including as the space between the real and virtual extremes, or as a combination of AR and VR.
The course will ignore definitional differences between AR and VR that do not affect the material.
For the purpose of this course, MR and AR will be used interchangeably, representing the same technology.

key_terms.definition: Mixed reality (MR) is a medium that combines immersive computer-generated environments with elements from both physical and virtual environments. It is also defined as existing in the space between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum.
Augmented reality (AR) is a way of viewing reality that is enhanced with digital content overlaid on the user's view, allowing for interaction.

L05.subgoal: Recap the definitions and key differences between VR, AR, and MR

key_points.text: VR systems completely replace the perception of reality, while AR systems augment or enhance it.
For simplicity, AR and MR are assumed to refer to the same technology and idea.
The systemic definition of AR is based on three key characteristics.
The next lecture will discuss the historical evolution of VR and AR technologies.

key_terms.definition: Augmented reality (AR) is a type of system that augments or enhances a person's sense of reality.
Mixed reality (MR) is a term that the instructor assumes refers to the same technology and idea as Augmented reality (AR).

L06.subgoal: Identify and describe the distinct historical phases of Virtual and Augmented Reality

key_points.text: The evolution of the field can be divided into distinct phases, though some overlap may occur.
The field has four broad phases: the Early Era (before digital computers), Formative Years (1950-1990), Modern Phase (1991-2015), and Growth Phase (2016 onwards).
The lecture will first examine the historical evolution of virtual reality, and later discuss augmented reality.

key_terms.definition: Virtual reality is a field whose historical evolution is being examined, starting with a quick look at its development.
Augmented reality is a field that will be discussed separately in the later part of the lecture, following the discussion of virtual reality.
Phases are distinct periods into which the evolution of the field can be divided, although some overlap may occur between them.

L06.subgoal: Identify key historical inventions that laid the groundwork for virtual reality

key_points.text: Sir Charles Wheatstone demonstrated a stereoscopic device in 1838, proving that the brain can process 2D images as 3D objects.
David Brewster created a compact stereoscope in 1860, which helped create the illusion of depth in viewing images.
Edwin A. Link introduced the concept of a flight simulator in 1928, which served as a precursor to modern multi-sensory VR experiences.
Immersion is achieved when 2D display images are perceived as 3D objects due to stereoscopic vision.

key_terms.definition: Virtual reality is a concept immediately associated with computer-based devices and displays. Essentially, it is difficult to conceive of virtual reality without considering the role of computers.

Immersive experience refers to a conceptual state similar to virtual reality, where the user feels deeply involved in the simulated environment. This experience is achieved when the brain processes visual information to create a sense of presence.

Stereoscopic device is a type of apparatus that allows the brain to interpret two-dimensional images as three-dimensional objects. This device established the possibility of creating a sense of depth from flat images.

Stereoscopic vision is the biological ability of the brain to perceive three-dimensional space by viewing two-dimensional images. This perception allows us to see images together as objects existing in 3D space.

Flight simulator is an early concept developed to provide an immersive experience. It utilizes multiple sensors to simulate the environment, serving as a precursor to modern multi-sensory VR experiences.

L06.subgoal: Trace the historical evolution of key VR technologies and concepts from 1950 to 1990

key_points.text: Morton Heilig's Sensorama (1962) is considered the first immersive VR system because it stimulated multiple sensory organs, including smell, wind, and vibration.
The Sword of Damocles (1967) was a revolutionary HMD because it was the first to demonstrate head tracking combined with computer-generated imagery.
VIVED (1985) was the first commercially viable stereoscopic head-tracked HMD, unlike earlier versions which were costly research prototypes.
Jaron Lanier proposed the term 'virtual reality' towards the late 1980s, which is the term used to refer to immersive technologies today.

key_terms.definition: Head-mounted display is a new kind of computer display that people began working on in the 1950s. It is a device worn by the user to display visual information.
An immersive experience is the state achieved when a device stimulates all of a user's sensory organs. This allows the user to feel vibrations, sounds, smell, and wind recorded in advance.
Haptic feedback is a method where touch sensations are provided to the user. This allows the user to feel objects on the screen while manipulating them.
Virtual reality is a system that stimulates all sensory organs to provide an immersive experience. It was first defined in modern times by devices like Sensorama in the 1960s.
Artificial reality is an early term proposed in 1973 for what is now known as virtual reality. This term eventually evolved into the modern terminology used for immersive technologies.

L06.subgoal: Trace the key hardware and software milestones of the modern VR phase (1990–2015)

key_points.text: The CAVE system, which provided an immersive experience, was invented in 1992 at the University of Illinois, Chicago.
VRML, a virtual reality modeling language, was presented in 1994, initiating the development of many other VR modeling languages.
HMDs evolved from quite bulky appearances to becoming more portable and usable over time.
The creation of the inexpensive Oculus Rift headset in 2012 significantly spurred interest in the field of VR.

key_terms.definition: CAVE system is a type of immersive environment that used a single computer to render images in a surrounding setting, giving the user the sensation of being surrounded by holograms.
Immersive experience is the sense of being surrounded by the environment, which was provided by the CAVE system.
WTK package is a software package developed in 1992 that provided higher-level tools for application development within Virtual Reality (VR).
VRML is a modeling language for virtual reality that was presented in 1994, which subsequently led to the appearance of many other modeling languages.
Field of view is a technical specification, such as the 150-degree FOV, that describes the angular extent of the visual area presented by a Head-Mounted Display (HMD).

L06.subgoal: Understand the key milestones and drivers of the current VR growth phase

key_points.text: The growth phase of VR, which is the last and continuing phase, began roughly from 2016 onwards.
The growth of the field was spurred by well-known companies releasing affordable commercial VR headsets, such as Oculus Rift, HTC Vive, and PlayStation VR.
The term Metaverse was popularized by Zuckerberg of Meta in 2021, drawing public interest to the concept.
The historical evolution of VR is divided into four developmental phases: pre-digital, formative, modern, and growth.
The next lecture will discuss the history of Augmented Reality (AR) in a similar manner, using phases and key milestones.

key_terms.definition: Growth phase is the last and continuing phase of VR evolution, which began around 2016. This phase is characterized by continuous development and acceleration of the field.
Metaverse is a term popularized by Zuckerberg in 2021, referring to a concept that had existed since the 1990s. The term gained widespread interest when people began interpreting it in various ways.
Developmental phase is one of the four evolutionary stages used to describe the history of VR. These phases track the evolution of the technology over time.

L07.subgoal: Outline the four historical phases of Augmented Reality development

key_points.text: The evolution of Augmented Reality (AR) can be broadly divided into four distinct phases, although these phases may sometimes overlap.
The initial phases included the experimental phase (before the 1980s) and the basic research phase (1980s to mid-1990s), focusing on defining concepts and enabling technologies.
The subsequent phases involved the tools or applications phase (mid-1990s to 2007) and the commercial application phase (starting from 2007 to date).

key_terms.definition: Augmented reality is the field of study that tracks how the technology has evolved over time. It is the subject of discussion that contrasts with virtual reality.

Experimental phase is the initial period of development that occurred before the 1980s. This phase was primarily related to early experimentation, which defined concepts and showed the types of technology required.

Tools or applications phase is the period spanning from the mid-1990s to 2007. During this phase, early applications and exploratory tasks were developed, focusing on interaction techniques, usability, and design theory related to AR.

Commercial application phase is the current phase, starting from 2007. This phase is characterized by widespread AR availability and the continuous emergence of newer applications in various market domains.

L07.subgoal: Trace the development of early AR and VR systems through historical examples

key_points.text: Ivan Sutherland and Bob Sproull created the first truly computer-generated AR prototype system in 1968.
The initial AR prototype used a CRT-based optical see-through HMD connected to a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system.
Tom Furness's research on the US Air Force Super Cockpit program resulted in key augmented reality technologies.
Early AR experiments led to the development of modern AR and VR displays and advancements in input and tracking technologies.

key_terms.definition: Augmented reality is the process of augmenting the real world view with digital content, allowing the user to see real objects combined with computer-generated imagery. This combination is achieved through proper 3D registering.
Head mounted display is an optical see-through device that is worn by the user. This device is used to display augmented or virtual content onto the user's view.

Computer-generated imagery is graphics created by a computer that can appear either superimposed over the real world view or as a substitute for the real world view. This imagery is used to augment or replace the user's perception.

Prototype AR system is an early functional system that combined an optical see-through head mounted display with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system and custom graphics hardware. This system was designed to register 3D content based on head movements.

L07.subgoal: Trace the foundational research and early systems that defined Augmented Reality

key_points.text: Tom Caudell coined the term 'augmented reality' in 1992 during the basic research phase.
Early research focused on developing registration tracking, interaction methods, and mobile AR systems.
The Chameleon system (1993) allowed users to view virtual content by moving an LCD display over a piece of paper.
NaviCam by Rekimoto (1995) superimposed virtual tags on real objects using handheld and head-mounted displays.

key_terms.definition: Augmented reality is a type of application that combines virtual content with the real world. These applications are precursors to the AR-type applications seen in modern times.
Registration tracking techniques were research areas carried out during the early development of the field. These techniques helped in the overall development of the field.
See-through head mounted displays were utilized in early research on AR during the period of 1995 and 1996. These displays allowed for the development of AR applications.
AR interaction methods refer to the ways in which a user can interact with the augmented digital content. Work was carried out on these methods in 1993.
Mobile AR systems were a topic of research carried out during the basic research phase. These systems were developed alongside other AR research activities.

used_concepts: Overlaying virtual cues on stereoscopic video

L07.subgoal: Trace the evolution of AR tools and applications from the mid-1990s to the early 2000s

key_points.text: The mid-1990s ushered in the 'tools or applications phase' of AR development, focusing on key enabling technologies like tracking and display.
Early AR applications included medical uses, such as visualizing laparoscopic surgery and image-guided surgery.
Wearable computing using HMDs and AR overlay on real-world markers using computer vision emerged in the late 1990s.
Viewpoint tracking was a significant challenge addressed by systems like Rekimoto's matrix system and the AR Toolkit.
The first mobile phone-based AR application was demonstrated in 2004.

key_terms.definition: Tracking is the process used to register content in 3D, which allows people to see and interact with shared augmented reality content. This technology is specifically done to register the content in three dimensions.
Viewpoint tracking is the activity of determining how to track the user's viewpoint. This is necessary so that the registration of content in 3D happens accurately.

Wearable computing refers to devices, such as headsets, where the computer hardware is carried externally, for example in a backpack. Interaction with these devices is achieved through different input devices.
AR overlay on real-world marker is a technique that uses computer vision to place augmented reality content onto physical markers in the real world.

L07.subgoal: Trace the key milestones and drivers of AR's commercial evolution

key_points.text: The commercial phase of AR began around 2007 with the release of the PlayStation 3 game, The Eye of Judgment.
The field saw a major turning point in 2009, driven by Adobe Flash-based AR tools, the rise of smartphones, and global marketing campaigns.
The real growth spark for AR came starting in 2017 with the launch of Apple's ARKit and Google's ARCore.
Future AR growth is expected due to improvements in hardware, such as wearable devices, and advancements in AI and computer vision.
The lecture categorized the evolution of AR into four distinct phases.

key_terms.definition: Commercial phase is the stage of AR evolution where AR experiences transition from niche research to becoming widely popular and available to the general public. This phase is characterized by increased commercial interest and the potential for AR applications to drive sales and popularity of goods.

AR authoring tools are software that enable the creation of Augmented Reality experiences. These tools, such as those based on Adobe Flash, made it possible to experience AR directly through web browsers, thus expanding accessibility.

ARKit SDK is a Software Development Kit launched by Apple for the purpose of developing Augmented Reality systems. This launch significantly stimulated growth in the field by allowing a large number of developers to create AR applications.

Tracking and registration in 3D is the process of accurately locating and mapping objects within a three-dimensional space. This capability is expected to become increasingly feasible on low-end devices due to advancements in AI and computer vision.

L08.subgoal: Summarize the foundational concepts, definitions, and history of VR and AR systems

key_points.text: The course initially discussed the importance of VR/AR from a commercial and market perspective.,,
Formal definitions were provided for virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality.,
Augmented reality and mixed reality are treated as synonyms and used interchangeably.,
Key characteristics help distinguish between various virtual reality and augmented reality systems.,

key_terms.definition: Augmented reality (AR) is a term that is used interchangeably with Mixed Reality (MR). This synonymy means that the two terms can be used in place of each other in all subsequent discussions.
Mixed reality (MR) is a term that is used interchangeably with Augmented Reality (AR). This synonymy means that the two terms can be used in place of each other in all subsequent discussions.

Defining characteristics are features that help distinguish between different types of systems. These characteristics allow one to differentiate between a virtual reality system and an augmented reality system, for example.

L08.subgoal: Identify the two major technological and psychological issues in virtual reality systems

key_points.text: The main objective of any VR system is to allow the user to experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer.
There are two major issues in experiencing VR: technological and psychological.
The technological issue focuses on how to generate suitable stimuli to experience the virtual environment.
The psychological issue refers to how the human factor perceives the stimuli generated by the technology.

key_terms.definition: Virtual reality system is an artificial environment that is experienced through sensory stimuli. This environment is provided by a computer and allows the user's actions to partially determine what happens within it.

Sensory stimuli are the inputs provided by a computer that allow a user to experience an artificial environment. These stimuli are perceived through the body's sensory organs, such as sight and sound.

Technological issue refers to the challenge of generating suitable stimuli for a virtual environment. This involves figuring out how to create the necessary inputs for the user to experience the virtual world.

Psychological issue refers to the challenge of how a user perceives the stimuli that have been generated. This relates to the human factor and how individual psychological characteristics affect perception.

L08.subgoal: Explain the definition and six qualitative components of immersion in VR systems

key_points.text: Immersion is the objective degree to which a VR system projects stimuli onto the user's sensory receptors.
Immersion is characterized by six qualitative terms: extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot informing.
Extensive refers to the range of sensory modalities that are presented to the user.
Matching refers to the congruence between sensory modalities, such as appropriate visual presentation corresponding to head motion.

key_terms.definition: Immersion is the objective degree to which a Virtual Reality (VR) system projects stimuli onto a user's sensory receptors in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot informing. This degree determines the qualities of the experience a user is likely to have while a

Extensive refers to the range of sensory modalities that are presented to the user. The more sensory organs that are stimulated by the stimuli provided by the computer, the more extensive the immersion is.

Matching refers to the congruence between different sensory modalities. For instance, the visual presentation must instantly correspond to head motion and the virtual representation of the user's body.
Surrounding is the extent to which the cues provided are panoramic. This refers to the scope of the field of view for visual senses or the extent of auditory perception for sound sources.

Vivid is the quality of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality. This quality relates to how much energy the computer generates to stimulate a sensory organ, which is enhanced by factors such as resolution, lighting, and audio bitrate.

L08.subgoal: Define and compare the concepts of immersion and presence in VR systems

key_points.text: Immersion is the technological issue, referring to the objective degree to which sensory qualities are imparted to the user.
Presence is a psychological state where the user fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.
Immersion is an objective and quantifiable description of what a system provides, while presence is a subjective state of consciousness.
Achieving presence means the user cannot distinguish between stimuli generated by a computer and stimuli generated from the real world.

key_terms.definition: Immersion is the objective degree to which sensory qualities are imparted to the user, referring to the technological or systemic side of the experience. Immersion is what the technology provides and can be measured or comprehended.

Presence is a psychological state or subjective perception where the individual fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in their current experience. This state occurs even when the individual's perception is generated or filtered through human-made technology.

An immersive experience is a state where the user is exposed to stimuli generated by technology, referring to the technological or systemic side of the experience. This experience is captured by the objective degree to which sensory qualities are imparted to the user.

Sensory organs are the biological mechanisms that are activated in a suitable way to receive input. Activation of one or more sensory organs is what technology can do to generate an immersive experience.

L08.subgoal: Explain how immersion relates to and influences the achievement of presence in VR systems

key_points.text: Presence is determined by both the user's subjective experience and the objective technological experience (immersion).
Immersion aids presence, but it does not guarantee it, as the user's internal state can override the technological experience.
The primary goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, making users indistinguishable from the virtual world.
To achieve a high degree of presence, the system must provide a high degree of immersion.

key_terms.definition: Presence is the subjective experience of feeling truly located within a virtual world. Presence is achieved when a user is unable to distinguish between the real world and the virtual world.
Immersion is the objective or technological experience provided by a system. Immersion aids the potential for a user to feel present in a virtual world.
Immersive experience is the initial goal of a virtual reality system. This goal is later refined to focus on creating a high degree of presence, given the understanding of both concepts.

L09.subgoal: Analyze the challenges of achieving presence in VR using fidelity concepts

key_points.text: The goal of a VR system is to achieve high presence, making users believe they are in the virtual world.
The uncanny valley effect causes feelings of unease when digital representations of humans are highly realistic but contain subtle imperfections.
VR developers must consider three types of fidelity: representational, interaction, and experiential.
Representational fidelity measures how well the VR experience matches or exploits familiarity with real-world places.

key_terms.definition: Presence is the concept referred to by psychological issues in VR. Presence is the goal of any VR system, aiming to make people believe they are in the real world while actually being in the virtual world.

Representational fidelity is the degree to which the VR experience conveys a place that is or could be on Earth. This fidelity measures how closely the VR experience matches or exploits the familiarity of a real-world place.

Experiential fidelity is the degree to which the user's personal experience matches the intended experience of the VR creator. Higher experiential fidelity is achieved when real-world constraints are incorporated into the virtual world's navigation, movement, and interaction.

L09.subgoal: Explain the requirements and pose determination phases of Augmented Reality systems

key_points.text: An AR system must combine real and virtual worlds, be interactive in 3D, and be registered in 3D.
3D registration requires determining the viewer's pose (position and orientation) relative to a real-world anchor.
Pose determination consists of two phases: the registration phase (initial pose) and the tracking phase (continuous pose update).
Tracking is necessary because the user moves, requiring continuous pose updates to ensure digital and real content mixes properly.

key_terms.definition: Pose refers to the viewer's position and orientation within the context of the system. Pose determination is necessary to register virtual content in the real world.
Registration phase determines the pose of a viewer relative to a real world anchor. This phase is performed when the user begins using the system.

Tracking phase is the process that follows registration, requiring the continuous updating of the viewer's pose relative to a previously known pose. This is necessary because the user is likely to move while using the AR application.
Real world anchor is a physical element in the environment used by the system to anchor virtual content. This allows the virtual content to appear as a seamless part of the physical environment.

L09.subgoal: Identify the major issues and concepts in VR and AR systems

key_points.text: VR issues are categorized as technological and psychological, which relate to immersion and presence, respectively.
The uncanny valley effect warns that making virtual environments too familiar can cause uneasiness or creepiness in the user.
Major issues in AR systems are technological, focusing on display technology, input mechanisms, and pose tracking.
The next lecture will cover cyber sickness, discussing its causes, measurement, and mitigation strategies.

key_terms.definition: Immersion is a concept tied to the technological issues of Virtual Reality (VR) systems. It relates to the technological aspects of the VR experience.
Presence is a concept tied to the psychological issues of Virtual Reality (VR) systems. It relates to the user's psychological experience within the VR environment.

The uncanny valley effect is a phenomenon where making environments familiar to the user can sometimes lead to feelings of uneasiness or creepiness. This occurs even when the objective is to make the environment as familiar as possible to the user's real-world experience.
Tracking is the process of pose estimation and updating, which is a major concern in Augmented Reality (AR) systems. It involves tracking the pose of the user or objects within the system.
Cyber sickness is a major concern related to VR systems that will be discussed in detail. The discussion will cover its causes, how it can be measured, and strategies to reduce or eliminate it.

L10.subgoal: Define cybersickness, identify its symptoms, and outline its study structure

key_points.text: Cybersickness (CS) is also known as Visually Induced Motion Sickness (VIMS) and is relevant to virtual reality systems.
Common symptoms of cybersickness include nausea, headache, dizziness, and fatigue.
Reducing cybersickness is vital for improving the overall user experience and acceptability of VR applications.
The discussion of cybersickness will be structured around three aspects: causes, evaluation, and mitigation strategies.

key_terms.definition: Mitigation refers to the strategies that can be adopted to overcome the challenges associated with cybersickness. Finding a feasible solution to reduce the impact of cybersickness is extremely important in the context of VR systems.
Evaluation refers to the process of measuring or assessing cybersickness. This process helps determine how to know if cybersickness has happened or is going to happen.
Causes refers to the factors that can lead to cybersickness. It is important to understand that not a single factor is responsible for this condition.

L10.subgoal: Identify and describe the internal factors contributing to cybersickness

key_points.text: Children between 2 and 12 years of age are highly sensitive to cyber sickness, while older persons are also likely to experience higher levels of CS.
Although some studies suggest women are more likely to experience severe CS, there is no conclusive relationship between gender and cyber sickness.
Individuals with high motion sickness susceptibility tend to have a higher CS risk, but this risk can be reduced by prior or repeated VR exposure.
Internal factors contributing to CS include physical conditions (like poor sleep or posture) and negative emotional states (like anxiety or stress).

key_terms.definition: Cyber sickness is a condition resulting from using virtual reality systems. This condition is characterized by symptoms such as nausea and dizziness.

Motion sickness susceptibility is an internal factor referring to an individual's tendency to experience motion sickness. This susceptibility is related to Cyber sickness because both conditions involve the brain receiving conflicting sensory signals.
Body awareness is the ability of the user to attend to and perceive bodily sensations. This awareness can be affected by factors such as poor sleep quality.
Stereoscopic vision is the visual experience achieved through Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs). This experience is determined by the distance between the user's eyes.
Inter-pupillary distance (IPD) is the distance between the user's pupils. This distance determines how stereoscopic vision is achieved through the HMDs.

L10.subgoal: Identify and explain various hardware factors that induce cybersickness

key_points.text: Higher display resolution reduces cybersickness, but this benefit plateaus after a certain point (e.g., 2K).
Cybersickness increases with latency, which is the time delay between a user's physical movement and the virtual world's response.
Latency jitter refers to the variability in the time delay between physical and virtual actions.
Users using HMD-based VR systems are likely to experience more cybersickness compared to those using conventional monitors.
External factors causing cybersickness are broadly divided into hardware and content.

key_terms.definition: Display resolution is a hardware factor that determines the clarity of the visual experience. Higher resolution generally leads to a better experience and reduced cybersickness up to a specific point.

Latency is the time gap between an action performed in the physical world and the corresponding change reflected in the virtual world. Increased latency is found to increase the likelihood of inducing sickness.

Latency jitter is the variability in the time gap between a user's action and its reflection in the virtual world. This variability causes irregularities in the timing of data delivery, leading to discomfort and disorientation.

Type of display is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness symptoms. Users utilizing Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs) tend to feel more cyber sick compared to those using conventional monitors.
Type of input refers to the various methods used in virtual reality, such as hand controllers or treadmills. The specific input device or technology used can cause cybersickness to vary.

L11.subgoal: Analyze how specific VR content factors influence the severity of cybersickness

key_points.text: Vection, or the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, indicating a positive correlation with visual motion stimulus.
Greater control over locomotion leads to a greater sense of presence, which generally results in a lower likelihood of experiencing cybersickness.
Teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to be less cyber-sickness-inducing compared to naturalistic free movement like walking or running.
Both prolonged exposure time and increased visual complexity are positively correlated with increased cybersickness symptoms.

key_terms.definition: Cyber sickness is a condition resulting from various factors, including internal, external hardware, and external content, that contributes to discomfort and disorientation in virtual reality. This discomfort is often caused by a sensory mismatch between the user's physical and virtual movements.

Visual motion stimulus is the movement experienced by the user within a virtual environment. This stimulus is considered one of the primary causes of cyber sickness, and its severity is affected by how the content moves.
Vection is the sensation of self-motion, which is the feeling of movement experienced by the user. This sensation is highest when the user perceives motion in peripheral stimuli.
Field of view is the extent to which the user's field of vision is captured by the display in a VR headset. A larger field of view generally results in greater immersion.

Means of locomotion refers to how a user is moving within the virtual world. This aspect of movement affects cyber sickness because a mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause disorientation.

L11.subgoal: Identify the four categories of input used to measure cybersickness

key_points.text: Measurement of cybersickness relies on three components: the input, the measurement technique, and the output.
There are four categories of input for measuring cybersickness: questionnaire-based, physiological/biometric, behavioral, and content-based.
Questionnaire-based input uses self-report scales, such as the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ), to rate user discomfort.
Physiological inputs, such as EEG or galvanic skin response (GSR), are objective methods used to overcome the inaccuracies of subjective questionnaires.
Content-based inputs evaluate cybersickness by analyzing features of the VR environment, such as optical flow and depth cues.

key_terms.definition: Questionnaire-based input is a method of input where users rate their discomfort or disorientation using self-report scales. These scales are typically administered before, during, or after the experience.
Physiological input is an objective method used to detect cybersickness by measuring bodily functions. Examples of these inputs include heart rate, galvanic skin response, and EEG.
Behavioral input involves detecting cybersickness using observable cues related to how a user moves. These cues include head and body movement, blink rate, and postural sway.
Content-based input measures cybersickness by analyzing features within the virtual reality environment itself. These features include optical flow and depth cues.

Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is a widely used questionnaire designed to measure cybersickness. It contains 16 items divided into subscales for oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea symptoms.

L11.subgoal: Compare manual and automated techniques used to measure cybersickness

key_points.text: CS can be measured using two broad types of techniques: manual evaluation (human intervention) or automated evaluation (ML-based).
Manual evaluation typically involves questionnaires, such as SSQ or VRSQ, requiring human intervention to collect feedback.
Automated evaluation uses objective inputs, such as psychological, physiological, or biometric data, to train models.
Transparent models are a type of automated approach that provides clear insight into the decision-making process and is easy to understand.

key_terms.definition: Manual evaluation is a measurement technique that relies on human intervention to assess cyber sickness. This process requires someone to distribute questionnaires, collect feedback, and analyze responses to determine the severity or onset of cyber sickness.

Automated evaluation is a measurement technique that uses automated algorithms to measure cyber sickness. This method processes various inputs, such as physiological or biometric data, to automatically determine the presence of cyber sickness.

Transparent models are types of models that provide clear insight into their internal workings and decision-making process. When an automated evaluation uses these models, the process is easily understood.
Stepwise regression analysis is a method utilized to measure cyber sickness using a variety of physiological signals. This technique is considered to be a transparent model.

L12.subgoal: Identify and describe the inputs, processes, and outputs used to evaluate cybersickness

key_points.text: Cybersickness evaluation is broadly organized into three aspects: the input, the process, and the output.
Inputs collected during evaluation include questionnaire-based, physiological, behavioral, and content-based data.
Evaluation processes include manual evaluation and various MLDL-based models, such as interpretable black box and hybrid models.
The course will conclude by discussing mitigation strategies for cybersickness from both developers' and users' points of view.

key_terms.definition: Cybersickness is the specific topic currently being discussed in the course, which is the focus of this lecture segment.
Questionnaire-based subjective input is a type of input collected by using questionnaires to gather subjective data.
Physiological and biometric input is a type of input that involves collecting data related to the body's functions and biological measurements.
Manual evaluation is one method of evaluation that has already been covered in the discussion.
Interpretable black box model is one of the models being discussed for evaluation, which is contrasted with other evaluation models.

L12.subgoal: Compare the characteristics and trade-offs of interpretable, black box, and hybrid ML models

key_points.text: Interpretable models provide flexibility and precise details regarding the relationship between input and output data.
Black box models are difficult to understand, as their decision-making process is shrouded in mystery.
Black box models generally achieve high prediction accuracy but require huge amounts of data and processing power.
Hybrid models combine different ML models to achieve both high accuracy and a degree of transparency.

key_terms.definition: Interpretable models are similar to transparent models and offer flexibility in how they are used. Interpretable models provide precise details regarding the relationship between the input provided and the output received.

Black box models are types of models whose decision-making process is shrouded in mystery and cannot be easily understood. The model simply takes input and produces an output, making the relationship between them difficult to discern.

Hybrid models are combinations of different Machine Learning models designed to achieve both high accuracy and transparency in their decision-making process. Combining multiple ML models results in a hybrid model.

L12.subgoal: Differentiate between cybersickness detection, prediction, and model outputs

key_points.text: Most existing research focuses on detecting cybersickness after it occurs, rather than predicting it beforehand.
Some studies employ physiological signals and machine learning to predict cybersickness.
ML-based evaluation can output classification labels (e.g., low, moderate) indicating the likelihood or severity of CS.
A sickness score, which quantifies CS severity, is typically generated using a regression model.

key_terms.definition: Prediction is the ability to anticipate upcoming Cybersickness (CS) incidents before they happen, allowing for potential mitigation measures.
Detection is the process of identifying Cybersickness (CS) after the experience has already taken place, meaning the input is generated after the experience.
Classification labels are an output from machine learning-based evaluation that indicates the likelihood or severity of Cybersickness (CS).
Sickness score is a numerical value that quantifies the severity of the Cybersickness (CS) experience.
Self-report questionnaire is a tool used to gather data for Cybersickness (CS) evaluation, providing users with rating scales to provide scores.

L12.subgoal: Analyze the challenges and perspectives of mitigating cybersickness

key_points.text: Mitigation is the third aspect of cybersickness, focusing on reducing or eliminating its impact when complete prevention is not possible.,
Mitigation strategies often create a trade-off, potentially affecting presence and the overall user experience.,
Mitigation strategies must be viewed from two perspectives: the developer's capabilities and the user's behavior.,,
Even if developers create good solutions, cyber sickness may still occur if the user does not use the system properly.,

key_terms.definition: Mitigation is the process of lessening the impact of cyber sickness when complete prevention is not possible. It involves taking measures to reduce the negative effects of the sickness.
Presence is the user's ability to perceive the virtual world. This ability can be negatively affected if mitigation strategies are implemented.
User experience is the overall experience that is impacted if the user's presence is affected. Developers aim to develop strategies without compromising this experience.
The developer's perspective is the way developers view the problem and how they can address it. This involves determining what the developers can do to solve the issue.
The user's perspective involves what users can do to prevent cyber sickness. This highlights that proper usage is necessary even if a good solution is provided.

L12.subgoal: Compare and contrast various FOV adjustment strategies for mitigating cybersickness

key_points.text: Restricting the Field of View (FOV) reduces peripheral optical flow, which helps mitigate the onset or severity of cyber sickness.
While effective, adjusting FOV can reduce the sense of presence and potentially impair performance in visual tasks.
Symmetric mask is a classical approach that occludes the periphery based on translational and/or angular velocity.
Asymmetric mask is an adaptive restrictor that obscures periphery regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion.

key_terms.definition: Symmetric mask is a classical approach that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity.
Ground visible restrictor is a technique that ensures the ground plane remains visible during movement.

L12.subgoal: Describe various techniques, such as blur, rest frames, and optical flow manipulation, to reduce cybersickness

key_points.text: Dynamic visual blur, which includes depth of field blur and peripheral blur, is a technique used to reduce the possibility of cybersickness.
Rest frames are fixed elements within the virtual environment that remain stationary relative to the real world, regardless of the user's movement.
Rest frames attached to the head reference frame are known as independent visual backgrounds.
Optical flow manipulation involves visually mixing optical flow patterns that are in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion.

key_terms.definition: Dynamic visual blur is a technique that reduces the possibility of cyber sickness by obscuring or reducing the clarity of the visual environment. This technique can be implemented using two types of blur effects.
Depth of field blur is a type of visual blur effect that utilizes well-known depth cues found in human vision. This effect is one of the two types of dynamic visual blur.
Peripheral blur is a type of visual blur effect that specifically targets the peripheral areas of the user's vision. This effect is one of the two types of dynamic visual blur.

Rest frame is a fixed element within the virtual environment that remains stationary relative to the real world, regardless of the user's movements. These frames are used as a technique to reduce cyber sickness.

Optical flow manipulation is a technique that involves visually mixing optical flow patterns in the reverse direction of the virtual visual motion. This manipulation aims to reduce the perceived optical flow.

L12.subgoal: Identify hardware and locomotion techniques to mitigate the effects of cybersickness

key_points.text: Hardware can be modified or entirely new to reduce cybersickness, including sparse peripheral displays and twin camera setups.
Haptic feedback techniques, such as phantom legs and floor vibrations, use synchronized cues to reduce cybersickness.
Locomotion techniques, such as teleportation or dynamic steering speed, can be used to reduce the duration of virtual exposure.
Modified motion platforms can reduce cybersickness by matching short bursts of rotational acceleration to visual forward acceleration.

key_terms.definition: Sparse peripheral display is a hardware addition that expands the periphery of a Head-Mounted Display (HMD) using a colorful LED matrix. This modification is used to reduce the effects of cybersickness.

Phantom legs is a technique that uses additional hardware to apply alternating haptic cues synchronized with the user's footsteps. This method was found to manage to reduce cybersickness to a great extent.
Floor vibrations is a technique that utilizes vibration-driven whole body tactile feedback. It attempts to match the vibrations that occur in the virtual environment.

Modified motion platform is a piece of hardware that can be adjusted to reduce cybersickness. Short bursts of rotational acceleration can be used to match the visual forward acceleration to achieve this effect.

Viewpoint snapping is a modification to locomotion technique that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation. This technique is used to reduce the exposure or duration of virtual exposure.

L12.subgoal: Apply strategies and countermeasures to minimize the effects of cybersickness

key_points.text: The maximum safe duration for a VR session is generally between 55 to 70 minutes for most users.
Habituation is the gradual decrease in cybersickness intensity achieved through repeated short-duration exposures followed by longer ones.
Users can adopt countermeasures such as slow diaphragmatic breathing, playing pleasant background music, or ensuring adequate external airflow.
Because cybersickness is subjective, interventions from developers alone may not be enough; users must also take countermeasures.

key_terms.definition: Habituation is a process where the intensity of cyber sickness gradually decreases after a person experiences the virtual environment repeatedly. This gradual reduction in symptoms is achieved through repeated exposure.

L12.subgoal: Summarize the causes, measurement, and mitigation strategies for cybersickness

key_points.text: Cybersickness causes are broadly categorized as internal (subjective) or external (hardware or content related).
Mitigation strategies must be considered from both the developer's system perspective and the user's proactive measures.
Due to the subjective nature of cybersickness, a one-size-fits-all mitigation approach may not work for everyone.
The next lecture will cover the hardware and software components and an overview of virtual and augmented reality technologies.

key_terms.definition: Internal causes are subjective factors that relate to a user's personal characteristics, such as age or gender. These factors are inherent to the individual experiencing the symptoms.
External causes are related to the physical components or the content being presented. These issues can stem from either the hardware or the content itself.

Evaluation strategies are methods used to measure cybersickness, involving inputs, a process (which can be manual or automated), and outputs like classes or numerical values. These strategies help quantify the severity of the sickness.

Mitigation strategies are methods, implemented by either the developer or the user, designed to reduce the negative effects of cybersickness. These strategies aim to lessen the severity of the symptoms.

L13.subgoal: Explain the holistic components and data flow of a complete VR system

key_points.text: A complete VR system is composed of three main components: the organism, VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world.
The human user (organism) is an equally important component of the VR system, not just the hardware.
VR hardware sends stimuli to the organism, which overrides the user's senses.
Tracking data flow uses sensors to monitor human motions, allowing the hardware to adjust the stimuli.

key_terms.definition: A VR system is a complete view of the experience that includes several components and the data flow between them, rather than being limited only to the hardware. This comprehensive view accounts for the hardware, the organism, and the surrounding physical world.
VR hardware refers to the physical components, such as computers, headsets, and controllers, that are used to create the VR experience. These components are part of the overall VR setup.
Stimulation is the stimuli that the hardware produces, which overrides the senses of the user. This process is referred to as the stimulation data flow.
Tracking is the process that is needed to adjust the stimulus based on the motions of the human user. This process requires sensors to monitor user movements.

L13.subgoal: Define the holistic components of a complete VR system

key_points.text: VR tracking encompasses head movement, button presses, controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.
The surrounding physical environment must be considered part of the VR system because users may respond to stimuli from the real world.
VR hardware can track objects in the surroundings, not just the user, especially if interaction with those objects is part of the experience.
The overall VR system is composed of three components: the user, the hardware, and the environment.

key_terms.definition: Head tracking is the most critical type of tracking commonly utilized in Virtual Reality (VR). It monitors the movement of the user's head.

The surrounding physical world is the real-world environment that must be considered part of the VR system. This is necessary because the user may respond to stimuli, such as light or sound, coming from this real environment.

The overall VR system is a holistic structure composed of three main components: the user, the hardware, and the environment. The hardware within this system can be used both to provide user input and to control the environment.

VR hardware is not limited to the computer, Head-Mounted Display (HMD), or controller used by the user. It includes trackers or sensors that can track objects in the surroundings or actively change the environment.

L13.subgoal: Define and categorize the three essential components of VR hardware systems

key_points.text: VR hardware is composed of three main components: displays, sensors, and computers.,
The display (output) is broadly defined as any device that stimulates the user's sensory organs, not limited to visual displays.
Sensors (input) are tracking devices that extract information from the real world, specifically focusing on tracking user movements.,
Computers (processing) are the devices responsible for processing inputs and producing outputs for the user to perceive the world.

key_terms.definition: Display or output device is any device that produces output to stimulate a user's sensory organs. This term is used broadly and does not require the device to be a visual display.
Sensor or input device refers to any tracking device that captures user input. Sensors are devices that extract information from the real world, specifically tracking user movements.
Computer or processing part is a device that processes inputs and produces outputs. This element allows the user to perceive the virtual world.

L13.subgoal: Compare and contrast the five categories of hand and non-hand VR input devices

key_points.text: Non-tracked handheld controllers lack 3D spatial tracking, which can lead to a discomfort known as 'break-in presence.'
Tracked handheld controllers (Type 3) use 6 degrees of freedom tracking to avoid break-in presence, but they restrict the user's ability to physically feel virtual objects.
Data gloves (Type 4) are categorized into bend sensing gloves, which detect hand posture, and pinch gloves, which detect fingertip contact.
Bare hand inputs (Type 5) utilize computer vision techniques, such as those in Leap Motion, to track and translate gestures without requiring the user to wear any devices.

key_terms.definition: World grounded devices are input devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move. These devices are often used to interact with grounded desktop or systems.

Non-tracked handheld controllers are devices held in the hand but are not tracked in 3D space by the system. Because they are not tracked, the system does not know the controller's exact position relative to a reference frame.

Bend sensing gloves are a type of data glove that detects hand postures and gestures because sensors are placed at all bend positions or joints. The processing unit receives continuous raw data from these sensors to detect the gesture.
Bare hand inputs are interactions where the system tracks the bare hand using computer vision techniques. This allows users to provide gestures without needing to wear or use any external device.

L13.subgoal: Analyze non-hand-based input devices, including head tracking and eye tracking, and their limitations

key_points.text: Non-hand-based input devices capture input from body parts other than the hand, such as head movement or eye gaze.
Head tracking devices use sensors in an HMD to detect yaw, roll, and pitch to infer user input and change the view.
Eye tracking devices can detect where a user is looking, but they suffer from the Midas touch problem, where accidental gazes may trigger actions.
Multimodal input is preferable to using only eye tracking-based input for interacting with a system.

key_terms.definition: Non-hand-based input device captures input from parts of the body other than the hand, such as head movement, eye gaze, or voice. These devices allow the system to capture input from various parts of the user's body.

Head tracking based input device uses the user's head motion for input, detecting movement along axes like yaw, roll, and pitch. This detection allows the device to infer the kind of input and change the view accordingly.
Eye tracker is a device, often integrated with headsets, that tracks how the user's eyes are moving. The system uses this movement to infer the user's intent and take necessary action.

Midas touch problem is a difficulty in eye tracking where the system cannot differentiate whether a user's gaze is intentional for selection or merely a natural, purposeless blank gaze. This inability can cause the system to select objects when the user did not intend to.
Multimodal input is a preferred method of interaction that utilizes multiple forms of input. This approach works better than relying solely on eye tracking-based input.

L14.subgoal: Explain the methods and mechanisms of non-hand input devices

key_points.text: Full-body tracking (FBT) tracks movement beyond the head and hands to enhance the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in virtual worlds.
One method for full-body tracking is MOCAP, which uses suits equipped with IMU sensors to capture and convert raw movement data into full body position.
Camera-based tracking uses multiple surrounding cameras to detect fiducial or reflective markers worn by an actor, allowing the system to infer overall body movement.
Non-hand input categories include head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking.

key_terms.definition: Full-body tracking is a non-hand input method that tracks movement of more than just the head and hands. This tracking adds to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in the virtual world because the user sees a fuller representation of themselves.

Motion capture suit (MOCAP) is an approach to full-body tracking that utilizes a suit containing various sensors. These sensors capture and transmit raw movement data from different parts of the body, which is then converted into full body position and movement.

Camera-based tracking is an input method that uses multiple surrounding cameras to detect movement. The system infers the overall body movement of a character by detecting the movement of fiducial markers worn by the actor.

Sound tracking is a non-hand input technique that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound. This input is captured using devices like microphones or microphone arrays for interaction within the virtual world.

Inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a type of sensor contained within motion capture suits. These sensors capture and transmit raw movement data when body movement happens, which is then combined and converted to full body position and movement.

L14.subgoal: Understand the role and components of the processing element in VR systems

key_points.text: Processing elements are chosen based on application requirements, user type, and the level of immersion needed.
The three major components of a processing element are the GPU, CPU, and RAM.
GPUs are used to speed up the rendering process due to their inherent parallel processing abilities.
GPU support is preferable for VR systems, even though modern CPUs are powerful.
A minimum of 8 GB of RAM is typically preferable for a good user experience in a VR system.

key_terms.definition: Computer is a device that processes data coming from input sensors and then activates or actuates the output devices. This processing is central to the function of the VR system.
Graphics Processing Unit is a specialized processor typically used to speed up the rendering process. This speed is achieved because of its inherent ability to perform parallel processing.
Middleware is a type of software that is required to support and render, and to develop, virtual reality experiences. It acts as a necessary layer for the VR experience.
Multicore processor is a type of processor that significantly increases computational capacity. It supports tasks much better than non-multicore or unicore processors.

L14.subgoal: Classify and describe the different types of visual displays used in VR systems

key_points.text: VR output devices are categorized into visual displays, audio output, haptics, and motion platforms.
