Head-mounted displays (HMDs) are categorized as non-see-through (VR), optical see-through (AR), and video see-through (Augmented Virtuality).
World-fixed displays render graphics onto stationary surfaces, which can range from standard monitors to large cave systems.
Regular displays, such as smartphones, are typically used for non-immersive VR and augmented reality (AR).

key_terms.definition: Visual display is a device designed to stimulate the user's visual sense, which is the sense of sight. These displays are used to render the experience in virtual and augmented reality.

Head-mounted displays (HMDs) are wearable and mobile pieces of equipment that integrate electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components. HMDs place images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens.

World-fixed displays are stationary display surfaces that render graphics onto surfaces that do not move with the user's head. These displays range from standard monitors to large screens that completely surround the user.
Regular displays are mobile or stationary devices, such as tablets or smartphones. These displays are typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality and are often used for augmented reality.
Augmented virtuality is an experience where an artificial or virtual environment is presented. Real-world images or videos appear within this environment on a real-time basis.

L14.subgoal: Classify and define various haptic rendering systems used in VR experiences

key_points.text: Haptic rendering systems activate the sense of touch and can be categorized by several criteria, including passive versus active devices.
Passive haptic devices are static physical objects, while active devices are physical feedback controlled by the computer.
Tactile haptics involve touch sensations obtained through the skin, whereas proprioceptive haptics activate forces in joints or muscles.
Self-grounded devices are worn or held by the user and move with them, while world-grounded devices are physically attached to the real world.

key_terms.definition: Haptics are outputs that explore the sense of touch perception, and they can be categorized based on various criteria. These outputs are used to provide physical feedback in virtual environments.

Passive device is a static physical object that is not controlled by the computer, allowing users to feel interaction with virtual objects. These devices match the shape of the virtual objects in the real world.

Active device is a physical object that provides feedback and is controlled by the computer to give a sense of touch when dealing with virtual objects. These devices are used to simulate touch in virtual experiences.
Tactile sensation is a type of touch obtained through the skin, where the skin itself is activated by the output device. This sensation provides the user with a sense of touch.
Proprioceptive force is a type of sensation that activates the user's joints or muscles. This force provides a sense of limb movement and muscular resistance.

L14.subgoal: Compare and classify various types of VR output devices, including motion platforms and treadmills

key_points.text: Motion platforms are hardware devices that convey a sense of physical motion, orientation, vibration, and acceleration.
Motion platforms can be active (computer-controlled) or passive (user-controlled), with passive platforms likely resulting in less motion sickness.
Treadmills are an output device that simulates walking or running while the user remains in one place.
VR hardware is broadly categorized into three types: input, computer, and output devices.

key_terms.definition: Motion platform is a hardware device that moves the entire body, resulting in a sense of physical motion and gravity, while conveying orientation, vibration, acceleration, and jerks.
Active motion platform is a type of motion platform that is controlled by computer simulation, meaning the computer controls the platform's movement.
Passive motion platform is a type of motion platform that is controlled by the user, and therefore has no direct computer control.
Treadmill is an output device that provides the sensation of walking or running while the user remains in one place by providing different sorts of input to the feet or legs.
Omnidirectional treadmill is a common type of treadmill in virtual reality systems that can be either active, meaning it is computer-controlled, or passive, meaning it is user-controlled.

L15.subgoal: Identify and categorize the different types of AR hardware devices

key_points.text: Augmented reality devices are categorized into types such as headsets, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial AR, head-up displays, and contact lenses.
Examples of AR headsets include AR HoloLens and Microsoft HoloLens, while smart glasses include Google Glass and Vuzix Blade Glasses.
AR devices have diverse applications across fields like education, healthcare, retail, and manufacturing.
This lecture segment provides an overview of AR hardware rather than focusing on minute technical details.

key_terms.definition: Augmented reality is a field of study focused on providing an AR experience using various types of hardware. This hardware allows digital information to be overlaid onto the real world.
Headsets and glasses are a category of augmented reality devices used to provide AR experiences. Examples of this category include AR HoloLens and Google Glass.
Handheld devices are a category of augmented reality hardware that includes devices such as smartphones and tablets. These devices can be used for various applications like e-commerce and tourism.

Projection-based systems are augmented reality devices that utilize methods like interactive projectors and AR sandboxes. These systems are used in fields such as industrial design and medical training.
Head-up displays are a type of AR hardware that is typically found in vehicles. These displays can be integrated into gaming experiences, medicine, and sports.

L15.subgoal: Compare and describe the components and functionality of AR headsets

key_points.text: AR headsets are generally larger and more immersive than VR headsets, combining real-world and augmented digital content.
AR headsets typically include built-in sensors, often cameras and depth sensors.
The primary function of an AR device is integrating high-definition holograms with the real-world view obtained through the glasses.
AR interaction, such as with HoloLens, is achieved through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions.

key_terms.definition: Field of view is the range of the environment that the headset allows the user to perceive. AR headsets typically provide a wider field of view compared to other types of headsets.

High-definition hologram is the digital content that is integrated with the real-world view. This content is projected onto the user's view, allowing the digital information to appear in the physical environment.
Interaction is the method by which a user engages with the augmented reality environment. Interaction in the case of HoloLens takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions.

L15.subgoal: Compare smart glasses and HMDs, detailing the features and limitations of smart glasses

key_points.text: Smart glasses are typically lighter and less immersive than AR HMDs, resembling standard eyeglasses.
Smart glasses provide simpler heads-up display overlays, unlike the full 3D holograms offered by AR headsets.
Due to their lighter nature, smart glasses are usually more comfortable to wear for extended periods than headsets.
Smart glasses are equipped with various sensors, including gyroscope, accelerometer, and ambient light sensors, alongside components like cameras and projectors.

key_terms.definition: Smart glasses are a category of AR devices that are typically lighter and resemble standard eyeglasses. They are used for AR application deployment but are less immersive than Head-Mounted Displays.
Heads-up display refers to the simpler type of AR digital content overlays provided by glasses. This display method is less complex than the full 3D holograms offered by AR headsets.
A 3D hologram is a complex visual output provided by AR headsets. This contrasts with the simpler digital content overlays found in smart glasses.

A see-through display is a component, such as the glass part of a device, that allows the user to view the real world while receiving AR content. It is one of the many components found in advanced AR glasses.

L15.subgoal: Classify AR devices based on their operational mechanisms

key_points.text: Handheld devices like smartphones and tablets augment digital content onto real-world images captured by their camera.
Marker-based AR relies on the system recognizing specific markers, such as QR codes, to augment content.
Markerless AR uses sensors like GPS or computer vision techniques to detect objects and augment content digitally.
AR devices are categorized into handheld, marker-based, markerless, and spatial augmented reality devices.

key_terms.definition: Marker-based AR is a type of augmented reality where specific markers are placed in the real world. The system recognizes these markers using image recognition to augment specific content.
Augmented content is virtual information that is overlaid onto the live streaming of the real world environment. This overlaying of virtual information happens on top of the screen.

L15.subgoal: Characterize the features, principles, and applications of Spatial AR systems

key_points.text: Spatial AR devices display digital content overlaid on physical objects, rather than just on the user's view of the real world.
A defining feature of spatial AR is that the display element is independent of the user, unlike in headsets or handheld devices.
Spatial AR systems allow multiple users to interact with the augmented digital content simultaneously.
The fundamental principle of spatial AR is augmenting the physical environment by adding virtual objects that appear to coexist with real objects.
The course will merge projection-based and spatial AR systems into a single category for discussion.

key_terms.definition: Spatial AR device is a type of augmented reality where digital content is overlaid onto specific physical objects, rather than being overlaid onto the user's view of the real world. The defining feature is that the display element is independent of the user.

Virtual object is a digital element that is added to the physical environment, appearing to coexist within the same space as the real objects. The fundamental principle of spatial AR is augmenting the physical environment by adding these virtual objects.

Room-scale AR is a specific type of augmented reality where devices typically use projectors to display graphical information directly onto physical objects. This contrasts with other AR types where content is overlaid on the user's view.
Projection-based AR system is a method of augmented reality where digital content is displayed onto physical surfaces using projectors. This category is generally similar to spatial AR systems.

Depth sensor is a component used in spatial AR systems to achieve seamless mixing of digital and physical elements. It helps the system understand the physical environment's geometry and lighting conditions.

L15.subgoal: Describe various hardware implementations of augmented reality systems

key_points.text: Interactive projectors can turn any physical surface into an interactive display by projecting a digital interface onto it.
Air sandboxes use sensors and projectors to dynamically adjust a digital map in real time based on physical changes in the sand, supporting multi-user engagement.
Projection keyboards use a projector to display a virtual keyboard on a surface, often utilizing infrared sensors to detect finger positions for interaction.
Projection mapping technology allows complex 3D objects or models to be projected and interacted with in space without requiring a physical surface, often using specialized software.

key_terms.definition: Interactive display is a surface that is converted into a display by projecting images onto it, allowing users to interact with the projected content.
Spatial AR is a type of augmented reality that serves as a prime example of multi-user engagement, allowing multiple users to interact with augmented digital content in a physical space.

L15.subgoal: Compare and contrast various AR display technologies, from HUDs to contact lenses

key_points.text: Head-up displays (HUDs) project images onto a transparent surface and are commonly used in vehicles and aircraft.
AR contact lenses are an emerging wearable technology that superimposes digital information directly onto the wearer's field of vision.
Unlike previous setups, contact lenses are very small and do not require elaborate or bulky external equipment.
The long-term effects of receiving constant digital information through contact lenses on user behavior or health are still unknown and under research.

key_terms.definition: A Head-up display is an AR display that projects images onto a transparent surface, such as a screen or a visor. The design aims for the surface to appear invisible, allowing only the projected content to be visible.

An AR contact lens is a future wearable device that superimposes digital images or information directly onto the wearer's field of vision via the lens. These lenses are very small and can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens.

L15.subgoal: Summarize the five categories of AR hardware systems covered in the lecture

key_points.text: AR hardware systems are broadly categorized into five types: wearables, handheld devices, spatial AR devices, head-up displays, and contact lenses.
Wearable AR hardware includes headsets (older technology) and glasses (state-of-the-art).
Head-Up Displays (HUDs) are commonly used in cars and aircraft.
The next lecture will provide a comprehensive discussion on tracking hardware used in both AR and VR.

key_terms.definition: Headsets are an older type of wearable AR hardware that represents an outdated concept in the field.
Glasses are a modern, state-of-the-art wearable AR device that is rapidly advancing in development.
Handheld devices are AR devices that are widely used, affordable, and ubiquitous for various AR applications.
Spatial AR systems provide an AR experience characterized by distinct features and unique functionalities.
AR contact lenses are an upcoming, state-of-the-art technology that could become very popular if affordability is achieved.

L16.subgoal: Compare the requirements and functions of tracking in Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR)

key_points.text: Tracking is an integral component of any Extended Reality (XR) system.
In VR systems, tracking translates motion from the physical world into virtual motion.
AR requires virtual content to be registered in 3D relative to a real-world anchor.
Tracking, in the context of XR, is often referred to as sensing.

key_terms.definition: Tracking is a process that is crucial to any Extended Reality (XR) system, involving the keeping track of motion in the physical world or objects.
Sensing is a term often used interchangeably with tracking, referring to the requirement of tracking in both AR and VR systems.

L16.subgoal: Categorize tracking methods based on the object or environment being tracked

key_points.text: Tracking can be categorized into three types based on what is being tracked.
One category involves tracking the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, which is often handled by head tracking in VR.
A second category tracks the user's other body parts to allow for the reproduction of representations like avatars or hand gestures.
The third category tracks the surrounding environment, which is essential for registering digital content in AR and preventing harm in VR.

key_terms.definition: Sense organ tracking involves tracking the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, whose degrees of freedom are controlled by the body. This tracking is necessary so that the position and orientation of the organ can be reflected in the virtual world.

Other body part tracking involves tracking parts of the user's body that are not sense organs, such as hands or facial features. This is required when the user needs to see a representation of their body in the virtual world, such as through avatars.

Environment tracking involves tracking physical objects in the real world that surround the user. This is crucial in augmented reality (AR) to properly register digital content in 3D, and in virtual reality (VR) to prevent physical harm.
Live capture is a method used to bring a large part of the physical world into the virtual world. This allows the virtual world to be augmented with a real-world representation.

L16.subgoal: Compare and contrast outside-in and inside-out tracking methods based on sensor location

key_points.text: Outside-in tracking uses sensors or trackers that are external to the device, such as cameras or markers in the environment.
Inside-out tracking requires cameras or sensors to be located within the device itself, such as the HMD.
Outside-in tracking is constrained to the specific area where the external sensors are placed.
Inside-out tracking does not have movement restrictions because the sensors are attached to the user.

key_terms.definition: Outside-in tracking is a method where the sensors or trackers are external to the device being used for the experience. This type of tracking is constrained to the specific area where the external sensors are placed.

Inside-out tracking is a method where the cameras or other sensors required for tracking are located within the device itself, such as the Head-Mounted Display. This allows the user to move anywhere without needing external devices to assist in the tracking.

L16.subgoal: Explain the four fundamental steps of the tracking process

key_points.text: Tracking works through four broad steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
Calibration aims to transform sensor output to match real values as closely as possible, reducing inherent sensor error.
Registration is the step used to estimate or determine the initial sensor position and orientation.
Integration involves combining sensory measurements from multiple sensors at discrete points in time.
Drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated tracking data and the actual position or orientation.

key_terms.definition: Calibration is the process where the sensor output is transformed to mimic the real-world value as closely as possible. This stage attempts to reduce the inherent error in the sensor data to the maximum extent possible.
Registration is the step used to estimate or determine the starting position and orientation of the sensor. Knowing this initial location is necessary before tracking movement can begin.

Integration is the step where sensory measurements are aggregated at specific, discrete points in time. This process combines data from multiple sensors to effectively track the target object or environment.
Drift correction is the phase that compensates for the mismatch between the estimated position and orientation and the actual values. This process aims to reduce the error in the tracking estimation.

L16.subgoal: Outline the components, methods, and stages of the tracking process

key_points.text: Tracking systems monitor three things: the user's sense organs, the user's body parts, and the surrounding environment.
Tracking methods are broadly divided into inside-out and outside-in categories.
Inside-out tracking uses sensors integrated into the user's device, while outside-in tracking uses sensors placed in the environment.
The tracking process consists of four main steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

key_terms.definition: Inside-out tracking is a method where the tracker carries the sensors that are integrated into the devices the user is wearing or using.
Outside-in tracking is a method where the trackers or sensors are part of the environment, rather than being part of the devices the user is wearing or using.
Calibration is the phase where the tracker is oriented as close to the real world as possible.
Registration is the process used to obtain the initial position and orientation of the tracker.
Drift correction means compensating for estimation error that occurs between the device trackers and the real-world values.

L17.subgoal: Identify the types of trackers and the four stages of the tracking process

key_points.text: Tracking can involve the user's sense organs, other body parts, or the external environment.
Trackers are broadly divided into two types: inside-out and outside-in.
The overall tracking process involves four stages: Calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

key_terms.definition: Tracking is the process of monitoring specific elements, which can include a user's sense organs, the user's body parts, or the external environment and its objects.
Inside-out refers to a tracker where all the necessary sensors are placed directly onto the device that the user is utilizing.
Outside-in refers to a tracker that utilizes sensors placed within the surrounding environment, rather than placing them on the user's device.

L17.subgoal: Define the Inertial Measurement Unit and explain its components' role in tracking

key_points.text: An IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) is a composite hardware containing a gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer.,
The gyroscope captures angular velocity, the accelerometer captures linear acceleration, and the magnetometer captures magnetic field strength.,,
Tracking using an IMU sensor primarily relies on the angular velocity readings from the gyroscope.
The accelerometer and magnetometer are used to detect drift errors and implement corrective measures in tracking.

key_terms.definition: Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) is a composite hardware containing three types of sensors, which is a popular group of sensors often found in modern head-mounted displays.
Gyroscope is a sensor that captures the angular velocity of movement.
Accelerometer is a sensor that captures the linear acceleration along the three axes: x, y, and z.
Magnetometer is a sensor that captures the magnetic field strength along the three axes.

L17.subgoal: Explain how sensor calibration minimizes measurement error using linear least squares

key_points.text: Measurement error exists because the measured angular velocity ($\omega_g$) from sensors is likely different from the actual angular velocity ($\omega_a$) due to sensor imperfections.
Calibration aims to minimize this measurement error by relating the measured and actual values, often by proposing a linear relationship.
The calibration process involves collecting thousands of samples from cheap, inaccurate sensors ($\omega_g$) and highly accurate benchmark sensors ($\omega_a$).
The constants required for calibration are determined by solving a classical regression problem, known as linear least squares, using the sum of squared errors.
The final calibrated value ($\omega_{cal}$) is derived by mathematically mapping the cheap sensor output to the ideal value using the determined constants.

key_terms.definition: Calibration is the process of mathematically correcting sensor readings to minimize measurement error. Calibration involves finding constants that map the output of an inaccurate sensor to a value close to the ideal, real-world measurement.
Measurement error is the difference between the measured value from a sensor and the actual, ideal value. This difference occurs because sensors are imperfect devices.

Sum of squared errors is a method used to compare data from two sensor types by computing the difference between corresponding values, squaring that difference, and then summing all the resulting squared values across all samples.
Linear least squares is a classical regression problem used to optimize a function by minimizing the square term of the difference between the predicted and actual values.

L17.subgoal: Explain how sensor data is integrated to calculate dynamic orientation over time

key_points.text: Registration establishes the initial alignment (pose and orientation) between the real and virtual worlds at time t=0.
Registration can be simplified using fiducial markers or reflectors, although computer vision techniques can perform it without them.
The current orientation at time t is computed by integrating the angular velocity samples over time and adding them to the initial orientation.
The change in orientation at each instant is determined by the calibrated angular velocity sample multiplied by the sampling interval.

key_terms.definition: Fiducial marker is a tag or reflector used to significantly aid in the registration process. These markers help the tracking system achieve accurate alignment.
Integration is the objective of computing the orientation or pose after a certain time from the initial pose. This is achieved by summing up the changes in orientation over time.
Initial orientation is the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is first turned on. This setting establishes the forward direction for the initial alignment.
Angular velocity sample is the sample of angular velocity obtained from the gyroscopic sensor at a specific instant. This sample indicates the rotation or change in orientation.

L17.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of drift correction using sensor fusion

key_points.text: Drift correction is the process of compensating for estimation errors between the real and actual value.
Drift correction generally requires the use of extra sensors, such as cameras, accelerometers, or magnetometers, in addition to primary sensors like gyroscopes.
Sensor orientations are combined using a weighted expression, where the gain parameter (alpha) is a normalized value between 0 and 1.
The process involves obtaining separate orientations from each sensor and then combining them using the blending expression: theta dk = alpha * theta gk + (1 - alpha) * theta ck.

key_terms.definition: Drift correction is the process of compensating for errors in estimation between the real and actual value. This correction is usually performed with the help of extra sensors.

The gain parameter is a normalized value between 0 and 1 used in a classical approach to blend sensor data. It is used to combine two individually computed orientations to obtain the drift-corrected orientation.

L17.subgoal: Describe the process of sensor tracking, including calibration, registration, and drift correction

key_points.text: Calibration transforms data from cheap sensors to match the values of highly accurate sensors using mathematical manipulation.
Registration involves setting the initial position and orientation of tracked body parts or objects.
Drift correction combines orientation estimates from multiple sensors to improve accuracy.
A gain parameter (normalized between 0 and 1) can be used to combine separately estimated orientations during drift correction.

key_terms.definition: Calibration is the process of transforming the values from cheap sensors to the values of highly accurate sensors using mathematical manipulation. This process requires access to a set of data samples from both the sensors being calibrated and the underlying assumption about accurate sensors.
Registration is the phase where the initial position and orientation of tracked body parts or objects are set, based on the current position and orientation of the sensor.

Drift correction is a stage that assumes access to at least two sensors and involves combining the orientation computed separately by those sensors. This combination is done in various forms to improve accuracy.

Orientation is the estimated direction of a tracked body part or object at any arbitrary instant of time. This orientation is determined by summing the sensory values, starting from the initial orientation estimated during the registration phase.
Gain parameter is a normalized value between 0 and 1 used in drift correction. This parameter is applied to combine the separately estimated orientation at a specific time instant.

L18.subgoal: Describe the structure and types of electromechanical tracking devices

key_points.text: Tracking technologies used in VR/AR are categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic, vision-based, inertial, and hybrid systems.
Electromechanical trackers are composed of a serial or parallel kinematic structure made up of links, joints, and sensors.
Electromechanical trackers are divided into two types: world-fixed or wearable.
Wearable trackers allow real human movements to be tracked and translated into avatar movements in the virtual world.

key_terms.definition: Electromechanical tracker consists of a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints and equipped with sensors. These trackers are used to capture movement data in virtual and augmented reality environments.

World-fixed electromechanical tracker is a type of electromechanical tracker that is stationary and fixed in a specific environment. This setup typically includes a display, mechanical pivoting, and tracking sensors attached to the entire structure.

Wearable tracker is a type of electromechanical tracker that is designed to be worn directly on the body of the user. These trackers capture real human movements which are then translated into virtual world movements.

Avatar is an animated representation of a real human being that is created using wearable trackers. The movements of the human wearing the tracker are tracked and translated to the avatar's movement in the virtual world.

L18.subgoal: Compare the mechanisms of electromagnetic and acoustic tracking systems

key_points.text: Electromagnetic trackers use a stationary transmitter to generate a magnetic field that determines the real-time position of a moving receiver element.
Acoustic tracking, also called ultrasonic tracking, uses ultrasonic signals produced by stationary transmitters to determine real-time position.
A key difference is that acoustic tracking requires a line of sight between the transmitter and receiver, which is not necessary for electromagnetic tracking.
Electromagnetic trackers can utilize three antennas to produce three orthogonal magnetic fields that generate electric currents in the receiver.

key_terms.definition: Electromagnetic tracker is a non-contact position measurement device that tracks movement by using a magnetic field generated by a stationary transmitter. This field determines the real-time position of a moving receiver element.
Acoustic tracking is a method of tracking that utilizes ultrasonic signals to determine the real-time position of a moving object. This technique is also referred to as ultrasonic tracking.

Line of sight is a requirement for acoustic tracking, meaning the transmitter and receiver must be within the visual range of each other. There must not be any obstacle positioned between the two devices.

L18.subgoal: Identify and explain the mechanisms of vision-based and infrared tracking systems

key_points.text: Vision-based trackers determine an object's pose (position and orientation) using optical sensors or cameras.
Optical sensors used for pose detection are categorized into infrared, visible light, and 3D structure sensors.
Infrared tracking is robust to adverse illumination effects, such as poor ambient lighting or harsh shadows.
Infrared tracking can be performed in two ways: outside looking in (external cameras track targets on the object) or inside looking out (camera is mounted with the user).

key_terms.definition: Vision-based tracker is a type of tracker that determines poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras. These trackers are currently very prevalent in the field.
Optical sensor is a device that determines poses by using optical means, such as cameras. These sensors are categorized into infrared, visible light, and 3D structure types.

Infrared tracking is a vision-based technique that utilizes targets which either emit or reflect infrared light. This method is robust to adverse illumination effects, such as poor ambient lighting or harsh shadows.

Outside looking in is a tracking method where targets are attached to the object being tracked, but the cameras are placed externally in the environment. The cameras detect the targets and use this information to determine the object's pose and position.

Inside out is a tracking method where the camera is mounted with the user, and the targets being detected are external to the user. The camera detects these external targets to estimate the user's pose.

L18.subgoal: Compare and contrast the three types of visible light tracking methods

key_points.text: Fiducial tracking uses artificial landmarks (fiducials) added to the environment to aid in registration and tracking.
Natural feature tracking uses advanced computer vision algorithms to detect unique features, such as points and corners, already present in the natural environment.
Model-based tracking, known as SLAM, simultaneously creates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it.
PTAM (Parallel Tracking and Mapping) is an optimization of SLAM specifically designed for augmented reality and is suited for smaller environments.

key_terms.definition: Visible light tracking is a method that utilizes visible light sensors or optical cameras to perform tracking. These sensors are commonly found in consumer-grade electronic devices and wearable devices.

Fiducial tracking is a method that uses artificial landmarks added to the environment to aid in registration and tracking. These artificial landmarks allow the system to track specific objects or areas within the environment.

Natural feature tracking registers camera pose in real time using features that are already present in the natural environment. This process requires advanced image processing algorithms to detect unique features such as points, corners, and line intersections.

Model-based tracking is a visible light sensing category that involves techniques for mapping and localization within a real environment. This technique is often used to simultaneously create and update a map while tracking positions.

Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it. This technique was originally developed for robot navigation and has since been adapted for augmented reality.

used_concepts: Shift or scale invariant feature transform (SIFT)

L18.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of 3D structure tracking using modern sensors

key_points.text: 3D structure tracking uses sensors to obtain information about the 3D positions of points in a scene.
The affordability of commercial sensors, such as the Microsoft Kinect, has made 3D structure detection a recent phenomenon.
3D structure sensing involves creating 3D models of the environment and using them to augment the real-world view.
Kinect Fusion is an AR system that utilizes structured light depth sensors to create high-quality 3D models.

key_terms.definition: 3D structure tracking is a technique that uses sensors to obtain information about the three-dimensional positions of points within a scene. This technique involves creating 3D models of the environment and using them for tracking.
Augmented reality (AR) is a type of system where digital models are overlaid onto the real-world view. This allows the real-world environment to be enhanced by virtual content.
A 3D model is a digital representation created from real objects or environments. These models are used for tracking the pose of devices or for augmenting the real-world view.
3D structure sensing is the process of creating 3D models of the structures present in an environment. This process is used specifically for the augmentation of the real-world view.

L18.subgoal: Compare inertial, GPS, and other tracking sensor types

key_points.text: Inertial trackers are self-contained sensors that measure changes in object orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration.
The primary sensors used in inertial tracking are gyroscopes, accelerometers, and magnetometers.
GPS is a positional tracking device useful in outdoor environments, but its accuracy may be low indoors.
RTK (Real Time Kinematic) technology can be used to improve GPS accuracy by utilizing GPS signal carrier waves.

key_terms.definition: Inertial tracker is a self-contained sensor that measures changes in an object's orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration. These trackers are typically based on microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and have no range limitations.

Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) are a type of technology typically used in inertial trackers. This technology allows the sensors to be integrated into the user's device without any range limitations.
Real Time Kinematic technology (RTK) is an enhancement to basic GPS that uses GPS signal carrier waves for measurement. This technology provides greater accuracy compared to a basic GPS system.
Gyroscope is one of the primary inertial sensors, alongside the accelerometer and magnetometer. These sensors are used to design hybrid software-level sensors that can be part of a device.

L18.subgoal: Describe the components and types of tracking used in motion capture systems

key_points.text: Motion capture is the technique of digitally recording movements of real things, typically humans.
Motion capture is often implemented using wearable suits that include facial and full-body tracking devices.
Eye-tracking systems primarily utilize optical tracking, but can also employ techniques like EOG or VOG.,
Trackers that combine multiple methods are generally referred to as hybrid trackers.

key_terms.definition: Motion capture is the technique of digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans. This technique can be based on any tracking method.
Eye-tracking system is a type of tracker that can be incorporated into other trackers. Such a system typically tracks the gaze point or area of the gaze of the user.
Optical tracking is a method that utilizes a high-resolution camera-based tracking device. This method is used to record movements.
Hybrid tracker is any other tracker that combines multiple types of tracking methods. These trackers are used to record user movements.

L18.subgoal: Define hybrid tracking and summarize the lecture's scope and future topics

key_points.text: Hybrid trackers are defined as tracking methods that utilize two or more basic tracking systems. (190)
Hybrid trackers typically perform better than tracking methods based on a single technology. (191)
The lecture covered the basic idea of tracking, how it is done, and prevalent VR/AR technologies. (196)
The next lecture will focus on covering VR software. (197)

key_terms.definition: A hybrid tracker is a tracking method that utilizes two or more basic tracking systems. This combination of systems is employed to achieve the tracking goal.

L19.subgoal: Define the unique role of software in generating VR and AR experiences

key_points.text: Previous lectures focused on VR hardware, AR hardware, and tracking hardware used to generate or enhance experiences.-
The current segment introduces the software component that is responsible for driving the hardware.-
In the context of VR or AR, the role of software is to drive the hardware to generate an experience utilizing our senses.-

key_terms.definition: VR software is the type of software used in the context of Virtual Reality (VR) or Augmented Reality (AR). VR software must drive the hardware to generate a VR experience by utilizing the user's senses.

L19.subgoal: Describe the data flow and creation activities within a VR system

key_points.text: A VR system is composed of three main components: the VR hardware, the surrounding physical world, and the user (organism).
The data flow involves the user using input devices, generating data that is processed by the VR system, and then sent to output devices to generate stimuli.
Successful VR implementation requires three design considerations: interaction design, perceptual design, and software processing.
Creating a VR experience involves three core activities: modeling the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic view, and incorporating interactions.

key_terms.definition: VR hardware is one of the three core components of a VR system, alongside the surrounding physical world and the user. It is responsible for facilitating the data movements between the user and the surrounding environment.
Input devices are utilized by the user to perform an operation that generates data. This generated data is then sent into the VR system for processing.
Output devices are responsible for generating suitable stimuli. These stimuli are intended to affect the user's sense organs.

Rendering is the process of creating the stereoscopic view, which serves as the output of the VR experience. This term is used broadly and can refer to stimulation of senses other than the visual sense.
The virtual environment is the environment that is created during the VR experience. This creation process can also be termed as modeling of the environment or object modeling.

L19.subgoal: Contrast ideal and practical approaches to VR application development

key_points.text: Ideally, developers want to provide only high-level descriptions, with the software automatically determining all low-level details.
In practice, developers may need to implement much of the functionality from scratch rather than relying on automatic conversion.
SDKs are platform-dependent tools used to handle low-level, platform-specific operations like device drivers.
While game engines can be used as middleware for VR, using non-specific engines may limit the developer's flexibility.

key_terms.definition: Middleware is a layer that can exist between the developer and the hardware, allowing developers to follow well-known patterns and avoid handling complicated micro-level details.
Software Development Kit (SDK) is a tool utilized for specific headsets that manages low-level operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output.
Platform is a broader term than headset, referring to a specific combination of hardware and operating system.
Game engine is a type of middleware specifically created or adapted for generating VR experiences, though it was originally developed for building any type of game.

L19.subgoal: Describe the function and components of the Virtual World Generator (VWG) in VR systems

key_points.text: The VR software system is conceptualized as a Virtual World Generator (VWG) abstraction.
The VWG receives input from low-level systems, such as head trackers, keyboards, and game controllers.
The key role of the VWG is to maintain an internal reality so that the experience appears real to the user.
The VWG converts input information into output information to maintain a match between the two.

key_terms.definition: Virtual world generator is an abstraction of the entire software system that converts input information into output so that the experience appears real to the user. It is responsible for maintaining the internal reality of the virtual environment.

Internal reality is the state that the Virtual world generator maintains so that the virtual experience appears real to the user. This maintained reality allows renderers to extract necessary information to calculate outputs for the displays.
Input events are data that arrive from low-level systems, such as a head tracker or game controller, and are arranged in a queue for systematic processing by the software.

L19.subgoal: Explain the different methods and requirements for creating a virtual world

key_points.text: Output devices include visual, aural, and haptic renderers that must be synced with input data.
Synthetic virtual worlds require defining triangular meshes and maintaining material properties for light and forces.,
Realistic virtual worlds can be created by capturing the real world using computer vision and SLAM techniques.
Software supporting VR must handle computer graphics operations, such as texture mapping, to create virtual worlds.,

key_terms.definition: Virtual world is a scene, which may be completely synthetic or based on a recorded physical world, that is rendered visually for the user. This world comprises the visual display.
Triangular mesh is a structure created by defining numerous triangles in a 3D space, which is required to create a synthetic scene. This mesh is the fundamental geometric representation of the scene.
Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images that are derived from synthetic models. The software used to build an application must support these computer graphics operations.
Texture mapping is an operation where camera images taken of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object within the virtual world. This is a common operation in computer graphics.

Material properties are the physical characteristics of surfaces that indicate how they interact with elements such as light, sound, and forces. These properties must be maintained alongside the geometric mesh.

L19.subgoal: Explain the challenges and requirements for maintaining motion correspondence in VR systems

key_points.text: The basic operation of a VWG is to maintain correspondence between user motions in the real and virtual worlds.
A matched zone is a region where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align, restricting physical movement.
A key challenge is the potential mismatch of obstacles between the real and virtual worlds within the matched zone.
Locomotion is the process of moving oneself in the virtual world when physical motion is not matched in the real world.

key_terms.definition: Matched motion is the correspondence between user motions in the real world and the virtual world. This ensures that the virtual environment accurately reflects the user's physical movements.

Matched zone is a specific area where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align. Within this zone, the user can move physically in the real world, and that movement is translated to the virtual world.

Locomotion is the act of moving oneself within the virtual world when the user's physical motion is not matched in the real world. This allows users to explore virtual environments without making corresponding physical movements.

Mismatch of obstacles occurs when there is a discrepancy between physical and virtual barriers in the matched zone. This happens when a user can be blocked by a virtual obstacle but not a physical one, or vice versa.

Body part tracking is the process required to monitor and record the movement of various parts of the user's body. This is necessary when the user needs to perform tasks like hand-eye coordination during the experience.

L19.subgoal: Analyze how user locomotion impacts cyber sickness and VR software design

key_points.text: Input-based locomotion in VR can lead to cyber sickness due to a mismatch between the user's physical and virtual motion.,
Supporting different types of user locomotion is necessary to address cyber sickness, and this must be part of the VR software.,
Future lectures will discuss additional VR software components, including available software packages, tools, and SDKs.

key_terms.definition: User locomotion is a concern regarding how a user moves themselves within the virtual world. Support for user locomotion is important to address potential sickness issues.
Avatar is the representation of the user in the virtual world. This avatar can perform activities like walking, running, or swimming without the user needing to move physically.
Cyber sickness is a condition that may result from a mismatch between the user's physical motion and the virtual motion. This sickness increases based on the duration of exposure and other factors.
Vehicle metaphor is an alternative way to move in the virtual world. This metaphor allows the user to operate controls to move themselves while remaining seated.
VR software is the program that must support key components and user locomotion. This software is essential for building and deploying virtual reality systems.

L20.subgoal: Identify the key components required within the virtual world generator abstraction

key_points.text: The VR software system is viewed abstractly as a virtual world generator (VWG) that stimulates sensory organs for immersion.
Synthetic virtual world generation requires support for computer graphics operations.
Realistic virtual world generation requires support for computer vision or computer graphics, such as texture synthesis.
The virtual world generator must also support matched motion and locomotion concepts.

key_terms.definition: Virtual world generator is an abstract concept that takes input from various devices and produces output designed to stimulate sensory organs, thereby providing an immersive experience.
Computer graphics operations is the required support for synthetic virtual world generation.
Computer vision is a required support for realistic virtual world generation, often used in combination with other techniques.
Texture synthesis is a method used in realistic virtual world generation that requires support from computer graphics.
Locomotion is a concept requiring specific support to ensure realistic virtual world generation.

L20.subgoal: Understand the necessity and components of physics support in virtual world generators

key_points.text: Physics support is required to ensure the virtual world behaves similarly to the real world, governing how objects move and interact.
The physics system must support basic laws of mechanics, such as objects accelerating toward the ground due to gravity.
Collision support requires both detection (determining if objects intersect) and response (defining how objects behave after intersection).
Physics support must also replicate environmental aspects, including how light propagates, interacts with surfaces, and how sound and smell travel.

key_terms.definition: Physics support is a required feature that ensures the virtual world behaves like the real world by governing how objects move and interacting with physical phenomena. This support includes replicating how light, sound, and smell propagate through the environment.

The virtual world generator is the component that usually implements physics and provides the necessary support for replicating real-world phenomena. Its capabilities depend on the specific kind of generator being used.
The collision detection algorithm is the support that determines whether two or more bodies are intersecting in the virtual world. It also dictates how those intersecting bodies should behave.
Collision response is the appropriate action needed after a collision takes place. This response determines how objects should react when they intersect with other objects.
Basic laws of mechanics are the fundamental rules that should govern how objects move in the virtual world. Support for these laws is considered sufficient for the virtual world to function.

L20.subgoal: Describe the components and interaction requirements of networked collaborative VR systems

key_points.text: A shared virtual world is maintained by a system or server, where each user has a distinct matched zone.
The VR system must manage all user interactions, including collisions, regardless of whether users are close or globally spread.
For social interaction, the VR system must support features such as eye movements, facial expressions, and body language.
The Virtual World Generator (VWG) must support these key components for networked collaborative VR.

key_terms.definition: A shared virtual world is a digital environment that is maintained and hosted by a dedicated system or server. This environment allows multiple users to interact within the same space.
A matched zone is a distinct area assigned to each user within the virtual world. These zones may either overlap in the real world or be disjoint and distributed globally.
Matched motion refers to the necessary management of movement when multiple users are interacting in a social setting. This management is required to properly handle the movement of users.

Virtual World Generator (VWG) is a component that provides the necessary support for various activities within a networked collaborative VR setting. This support includes features like eye movements, facial expressions, and body language.

L20.subgoal: Compare the two primary approaches developers use to build VR systems

key_points.text: SDKs provide basic drivers and APIs for hardware interfaces and rendering, but they do not typically handle high-level aspects like physics or networking.
Building a virtual world from scratch grants maximum control and optimization but requires the developer to handle a difficult implementation burden.
Ready-made virtual world generators, such as Unity3D, simplify development by including built-in support for physics, but they restrict the ability to create highly original experiences.

key_terms.definition: A Software Development Kit is a set of tools provided by a platform or device manufacturer that allows developers to build applications for that specific hardware. These kits typically include basic drivers and interfaces for accessing tracking data and graphical rendering libraries.

A Virtual World Generator is a tool or framework used to create a virtual environment, which can be built either from scratch or using pre-existing software. It handles the creation and management of the virtual space and its components.

Physics, in the context of a virtual world, refers to the algorithms that govern how objects behave within the environment. This includes handling movement, detecting collisions, and determining the response to those collisions.

A Game engine is a specialized software framework, such as Unity3D, that is adapted to work for virtual reality. These engines provide high-level support, including physics and collision detection, making it easier for developers to create VR experiences quickly.

A Collaborative VR experience is a virtual reality setting that supports multiple users interacting within the same environment. This requires additional support beyond basic physics and rendering, often involving network capabilities.

L20.subgoal: Understand the structure, components, and function of VR game engines

key_points.text: A game engine functions as middleware that abstracts hardware functionalities for developers creating XR applications.
Game engines are composed of multiple specialized engines, including rendering, physics, and audio engines.
A typical VR system operates using a layered architecture, ranging from hardware at the base to application software at the top.
Unity 3D and Unreal Engine are prominent examples of game engines, with Unity currently holding a large market share.

key_terms.definition: Game engine is a middleware that sits between the hardware and higher-level application software, abstracting hardware functionalities for developers of Extended Reality (XR) applications.
Rendering engine is a component designed to help generate animated 3D graphics by utilizing various methods.
Audio engine consists of algorithms related to loading, modifying, and generating sound through a speaker system.
Physics engine is a crucial component responsible for emulating the laws of physics within an application.
Rasterization is a rendering technique that is less computationally intensive when compared to the ray tracing method.

L20.subgoal: Distinguish between native and web deployment methods and their associated tools

key_points.text: Deployment can be categorized as native (requiring platform-specific SDKs) or web (allowing remote experience).
An SDK (Software Development Kit) is a collection of software development tools specific to a hardware and OS combination.
Native SDKs are categorized based on whether they support VR or AR applications, and whether they are proprietary or open source.
Web deployment tools are broadly categorized into cloud hosting/rendering support, development libraries, and complete development suites.

key_terms.definition: Native application is a type of deployment that requires the use of Software Development Kits (SDKs) specifically tailored to the platform and hardware.
Software development kit (SDK) is a collection of software development tools packaged into one installable package, which is specific to a particular hardware and operating system combination.
Head-mounted display (HMD) is the most popular type of device used for experiencing virtual reality.
Web deployment refers to the method of deploying systems so that they can be accessed and run over the web.

L20.subgoal: Review the key concepts and choices related to VR software development

key_points.text: VR software can be understood through an abstraction, a virtual world generator, which supports key components for developers.
Developers have two choices: using SDKs and developing from scratch, or using ready-made VWGs.
The discussion covered VR game engines and deployment tools available for native systems or over the web.
The next lecture will cover AR software, helping students gain a broader understanding of overall XR software.

key_terms.definition: Virtual world generator is an abstraction used to understand VR software. This generator must support key components that allow a developer to build VR applications.

L21.subgoal: Categorize AR software tools based on the required programming skill

key_points.text: The lecture aims to structure and categorize AR software tools based on the decreasing level of programming skill required by the developer.
Low-level software libraries are one extreme, requiring considerable skill in understanding functions and coding.
Simple authoring tools are the other extreme, designed for novice users who require no programming skill.
AR tools are categorized into four types: low-level software libraries/frameworks, rapid prototyping tools, plugins, and standalone AR authoring tools.

key_terms.definition: Augmented reality software is the specific set of tools and programs used for implementing augmented reality. This technology area is being discussed alongside virtual reality.

Virtual reality software is the subject of the previous lecture, which discussed various desirable components within that domain. This software includes tools and packages for building and deploying systems.
Virtual world generator is an abstraction that was discussed in the context of virtual reality software. This component helps define the elements of the virtual environment.

Low-level software libraries are tools that require considerable skill from the developer. Developers must possess skill in both understanding the library functions and in coding to call those functions.
Standalone AR authoring tools are types of software designed for novice users or developers. These tools assume that the user does not require any programming skill to operate them.

L21.subgoal: Explain how low-level libraries and scene graphs form comprehensive AR frameworks

key_points.text: AR tools can be categorized based on the required skill level, the target application platform, or the underlying technology used for tracking.
Low-level libraries provide core tracking functionality but often lack built-in support for complex rendering or interaction techniques.
To create a complete AR system, multiple libraries must be combined to form a framework, addressing the limitations of individual components.
Scene graphs represent computer graphic scenes as a node-based graph, which helps manage complexity and enable realistic interaction.

key_terms.definition: Low-level libraries provide access to the core tracking and display functionality necessary to build an Augmented Reality application. These libraries require strong programming ability from the developer.

Framework is a combination of multiple libraries created to facilitate Augmented Reality system development. This combination allows developers to overcome the limitations of single, low-level toolkits.
Scene graph represents computer graphic scenes as a node-based graph. This structure allows the entire scene to be represented as a tree, enabling selective manipulation and realistic effects.

3D registration is the process of creating and rendering a three-dimensional object at a specific position in the real world. This operation is necessary after the system has recognized a marker or feature.

Tracking is the function within AR and VR systems that monitors and recognizes various things, including objects in the environment. This function is essential for enabling the developer to perform activities within the AR application.

L21.subgoal: Understand how rapid prototyping tools simplify the development of AR experiences

key_points.text: Prototypes are beneficial for visualizing ideas and testing concepts before undertaking major coding exercises.-
The FLAR Toolkit, a version of AR toolkit ported to Flash, allows users to prototype AR systems by activating the camera, tracking markers, and overlaying virtual content with minimal code.-
The course uses skill requirement-based categorization to structure the discussion of AR software, moving from low-level libraries to authoring tools.

key_terms.definition: Rapid prototyping and development tools are software used to quickly visualize or create prototypes of an idea before committing to major coding efforts. These tools allow users to test ideas simply rather than going through the entire coding exercise.

An authoring tool is a popular software used for creating prototypes that include multimedia content for web and desktop platforms. These tools allow the creation of a variety of desktop and mobile experiences.

An AR toolkit is a version of an Augmented Reality (AR) toolkit that has been ported over to a specific platform, such as Flash. This toolkit enables users to have an AR experience directly from within their web browser.
Tracking is a function within an AR system that allows the user to look for specific AR markers within the camera view. This process is a necessary part of the AR experience.
3D registering is the process of loading and overlaying virtual content onto a tracked image. This allows the virtual content to be correctly placed in the real-world view.

L22.subgoal: Compare various rapid prototyping tools and development approaches for AR

key_points.text: Custom AR prototypes can be built using technologies like HTML or WebGL instead of relying on third-party browser plugins.
Open Frameworks is an open-source C++ middleware library that supports tracking, rendering, and interaction for AR applications.
Mobile AR applications often function as client devices, with heavy computation handled by backend servers.
The current discussion on AR software is following the skill requirement-based categorization, focusing on rapid prototyping tools.

key_terms.definition: Rapid prototyping tools are specialized tools used to quickly create an initial version of an Augmented Reality application, allowing developers to continue work on various categories of AR software.
Open Frameworks is an open-source C++ middleware library that functions as a combination of multiple libraries, designed to support interactive experiences on both desktop and mobile platforms.
Non-web-based authoring tools are specialized tools designed to create Augmented Reality experiences that run natively on mobile and desktop platforms.
Wikitude is an example of a prototyping tool that functions as an AR browser application, typically used for mobile experiences.
A client device, in the context of AR architecture, is primarily treated as a rendering device or a client that connects back to a backend server for content provision and computation.

L22.subgoal: Explain how plugins extend existing content authoring tools with AR capabilities

key_points.text: Plugins add AR-specific functionalities to existing content authoring tools that may not natively support AR development.
The use of plugins reduces the developer's learning requirement because they can rely on their existing knowledge of the original authoring tool.
Plugins are only effective if the user is already familiar with the original authoring tool; otherwise, the user must learn everything from scratch.
Plugins function by adding AR visualization and tracking functions to an existing tool, which continues to handle content authoring.

key_terms.definition: A plugin is a piece of software that is added to an existing tool to provide specific functionalities, such as Augmented Reality (AR) features. Plugins allow known tools to support AR or system development without requiring the user to learn a completely new application.
A content authoring tool is a software application that allows a user to create interactive 2D or 3D content. This tool is the base software that plugins are added to.
A software library is a collection of code that requires programming skills to understand and utilize. Users must learn or master these libraries to use them effectively.

L22.subgoal: Compare the benefits and limitations of using plugin-based AR development tools

key_points.text: Authoring tools like Unity and Vuforia offer AR plugins for creating mobile AR applications on iOS and Android.
Plugin-based tools offer an easy and quick method for developing AR applications.
Using authoring tools can limit the developer's flexibility in interaction design and interface look and feel.
Content produced with authoring tools often depends on proprietary player software, reducing flexibility.
To resolve the cons of third-party tools, developers can use low-level software development tools to build systems from scratch.

key_terms.definition: Interactive 3D graphics authoring tools are programs used to create interactive 3D applications, such as Unity or Vizard. Most of these tools include plugins specifically for AR visualization.

Plugin-based tools provide an easy and quick method for developing AR applications. However, this approach restricts the developer's flexibility in deciding on interaction methods or interface look and feel.
Marker-based tracking is a type of computer vision-based tracking that provides AR visualization support. This method is one of the options available for AR visualization.
Mobile AR applications are AR programs that function on both iOS and Android platforms. These applications can be created using plugins like Vuforia that work with Unity 3D.

Low-level software development tools are used to build a custom system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool. This method is employed to resolve the issues and cons associated with high-level authoring tools.

L22.subgoal: Understand the characteristics and utility of standalone AR authoring tools

key_points.text: Standalone authoring tools allow users to create AR experiences without needing programming experience.
Unlike plugins, standalone tools are complete packages that include content authoring and AR support, requiring no additional software.
These tools typically use drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces, making them accessible to users without coding skills.
Wikitude Studio is an example of a web-based standalone authoring tool that supports creating rich mobile AR content and 3D models.

key_terms.definition: Standalone authoring tools are complete packages that allow users to create AR experiences without needing any programming experience or additional software. These tools come as a complete package that includes both content authoring and AR support.

Plugins require a basic authoring tool to function, and AR support is provided through this add-on software. Plugins do not come as a complete package but rely on an existing basic software to provide AR functionality.

Scene construction is a function supported by authoring tools that allows developers to build the environment or setting for the AR experience. This function is one of the typical sets of capabilities provided by these tools.

Interactive behavior is a function that allows developers to add dynamic responses and actions to the elements within the AR scene. This capability can range from limited support to extensive support depending on the software package.

Graphical user interface (GUI) is a visual interface, often drag-and-drop type, that developers use to create an application or experience. This interface allows users to create an experience without requiring coding.

L22.subgoal: Summarize the AR software concepts and anticipate the next lecture's focus

key_points.text: AR software categories are based on the programming skill required, ranging from low-level libraries to standalone authoring tools.
The next lecture will cover human factors, which affect the experience in Extended Reality (AR or VR) systems.
The human factors discussion will cover interactive systems, the role of human factors in system building, and relevant factors for AR and VR experiences.

key_terms.definition: Human factors refers to the aspects of the user experience that affect how people interact with Extended reality systems. These factors are relevant during the building and deployment of both Augmented reality and Virtual reality experiences.

Low-level libraries and frameworks are tools that require the highest level of programming skill when dealing with AR software. These are situated at one extreme of the spectrum of required programming ability.

Standalone authoring tools are software that require the least amount of programming skill when working with AR software. These tools represent the opposite extreme of the programming skill requirement spectrum.
Rapid prototyping tools are a type of software that falls between the extremes of low-level libraries and standalone authoring tools. These tools are used in the development process of AR systems.
Plugins to existing systems are a category of tools that allow for integration into pre-existing systems. This category is one of the types of tools available for AR software development.

L23.subgoal: Define the core concept of 'disappearing technology' and its link to presence in XR

key_points.text: Extended reality systems belong to the broader class of interactive systems.
The lecture aims to understand interactive systems, their core concerns, and how they can improve extended reality systems.
Mark Weiser stated that the most profound technologies are those that disappear.
Presence means that the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from their perception.

key_terms.definition: Interactive systems are a broad class of systems that includes extended reality, and understanding them requires knowing their core concerns. These systems are the foundational category to which extended reality systems belong.

Presence is the state where the technological aspect surrounding the user disappears from the user's perception. This means the user should feel like they are dealing with an ordinary item rather than a specialized technological product.

L23.subgoal: Explain the evolution of computing toward invisible, interactive systems

key_points.text: The goal in computer development is to make the technology disappear from the user's point of view.
Modern computing has progressed from large, wire-based systems accessible only to experts to connected devices like wearables and mobile devices.
Current devices are examples of interactive computing systems, where interaction takes place between the system and the user.
In these systems, the user is typically a lay person who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.

key_terms.definition: Ubiquitous computing is a state where users can access multiple connected computers that communicate with each other, allowing the user to operate them without separate intervention.
Interactive systems are computing systems where interaction takes place between the user and the computer or the system.
Layman user is a person who uses a system without being a technology expert, focusing only on using the system rather than understanding its internal workings.

L23.subgoal: Explain the negative impact of technical jargon on lay users in interactive systems

key_points.text: Technical terms and codes (like hex format) are generally incomprehensible to end users who are not technology experts.
Presenting technical errors can cause users to become anxious, worried about having done something wrong, or unsure how to proceed.
Technical messages may cause users to lose motivation and refrain from using the system further.
Designers of interactive systems should avoid forcing users to learn about the underlying technology or technical terms.

key_terms.definition: A lay person is an end user who is not necessarily an expert in the technology behind the system. Designers of interactive systems should cater to these users without forcing them to learn complex technical details.

An interactive system is a computing environment designed to be used by people, particularly those who are not technology experts. The purpose of such a system is to function effectively for the user without requiring deep technical knowledge.

Technical jargon refers to specialized language or terms, such as 'security accounts manager,' that are unlikely to be understood by laypersons. Using such terms in user interfaces can confuse and potentially frustrate the user.

L23.subgoal: Define the user-centric approach and its key design characteristics

key_points.text: The user-centric approach designs computer systems by considering the users' needs and characteristics.
The user's goal is to transition from one state to another until they reach a desired goal state.
Key design elements include acceptable interface elements and layouts that meet user expectations.
Systems must help the user perceive the system state and design interactions that fulfill needs and lead to desired states.

key_terms.definition: User-centric approach is a process for designing computer systems by considering the characteristics, needs, and expectations of the users. This method ensures that the system is designed to meet the specific requirements of the people who will use it.

System state is the exact condition of the system as perceived by the user, focusing on what is happening from the user's point of view rather than technical details. This perception helps the user understand the current status of the system.

Interactions are designed elements that fulfill user needs by guiding the user from one state to another. These carefully designed interactions allow the user to transition to the desired system states.

Goal state is the final condition a user reaches after transitioning through various states to successfully complete a desired task or work. Users transition between states until they achieve this ultimate goal.
Layouts are the methods by which interface elements are organized on a screen or interface. These arrangements must meet the expectations of the user.

L23.subgoal: Define HCI and explain the necessity of incorporating human factors into system design

key_points.text: Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) is a discipline concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use.
HCI also involves the study of major phenomena surrounding interactive computing systems.
The definition of HCI was provided by ACM SIGCHI.
The core concern of HCI is incorporating humans into the design by starting with an understanding of the user.,

key_terms.definition: Human-computer interaction is a discipline focused on the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use. It also involves the study of major phenomena that surround the development of these systems.

L23.subgoal: Compare different user types to demonstrate the necessity of human factors in system design

key_points.text: Understanding user characteristics is a key concern when designing interactive systems.
Even if two users perform similar technical tasks, their expectations and required interfaces can be vastly different.
System design must be tailored to the specific user, such as a traveler or a database administrator.
Knowing the user is a necessary first step in the system design process, though it is often difficult to achieve.

key_terms.definition: Human factors is an important issue in design that focuses on how human capabilities and limitations affect the design of interactive systems. This consideration is necessary when designing for general users.
Layperson refers to the general user or layman for whom the system is being designed. Designing for a layperson requires first knowing who they are.

User characteristics refers to the specific traits and knowledge of the user that must be understood during system design. Knowledge of these characteristics is essential for building an appropriate system.

Interface is the mechanism provided to the user that allows them to input information, view outcomes, and act based on those outcomes. The required interface depends heavily on the user's technical expertise.
Querying language is a technical skill or language used by advanced users to retrieve information from a database. This language is typically known by technical experts, unlike general users.

L24.subgoal: Apply the three-class user categorization to inform interactive system design

key_points.text: Users can be categorized into three classes: novice, intermittent, and expert, to provide a starting point for understanding user behavior.
Novice users, who are using the system for the first time, find remembering hotkey combinations difficult and prefer menu options.
Expert users are defined as being experts in using the system, not necessarily technology experts.
System options should be designed to cater to different user groups, such as providing hotkeys for efficient expert use and menus for novice users.

key_terms.definition: Interactive system is a system designed for use by laypersons, meaning the users do not need to be technology experts or possess specialized knowledge of technological jargon to understand how the system functions.
Novice is the first class of users who are typically using a system for the first time and are unlikely to have prior knowledge of how the system works.
Intermittent is the second class of users who utilize a system occasionally, having used it for a limited duration or number of times.
Expert is the third class of users who have used a system regularly over a long period of time, allowing them to understand all aspects and use it very efficiently.
User categorization is a method that allows designers to gain a starting point for understanding users by classifying them into distinct groups based on their experience level.

L24.subgoal: Compare various design perspectives and explain the role of the development lifecycle

key_points.text: Knowing the user is the essential first step when starting the design process.
User-centric design is viewed differently by various stakeholders, depending on their role.
