Different design roles have distinct concerns, such as UI/UX focusing on interfaces and industrial designers focusing on form and size.
Application software developers must follow a development lifecycle to ensure the system meets user needs and expectations.

key_terms.definition: User-centric design is a concept that can be viewed differently by various stakeholders, such as designers, depending on their specific role in the product development process.
User interface designer is primarily concerned with the creative design of interface elements and layouts, which is informed by the characteristics of the user.
Industrial product designer focuses on the physical form of a product, specifically addressing its shape, size, and overall look.
Application software developer is primarily concerned with the development of software, which is the main focus when building a system.
Development lifecycle is a structured process that must be followed when building software to ensure it accounts for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations, making the system easier to use.

L24.subgoal: Define the criteria for usability based on ISO standards

key_points.text: Usability is defined by the ISO standard as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals.
A usable product must be designed for a specified group of users, not for everybody.
A usable product should focus on allowing users to perform specified tasks, rather than being feature-rich.
Usability is restricted to a specified context of use and does not need to apply to all scenarios.

key_terms.definition: Usability is a measure of how good a product is from the user's perspective. It is defined as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

Specified context of use is the particular environment or scenario in which a product is designed to be used. Usability is ideally restricted to this specific context rather than all possible usage scenarios.
Effectiveness is one of the crucial criteria used to judge a product's usability. It relates to the ability of the user to achieve their specified goals when using the product.
Efficiency is one of the crucial criteria used to judge a product's usability. It relates to how well the user can achieve their specified goals, often implying minimal effort or time.
Satisfaction is one of the crucial criteria used to judge a product's usability. It refers to the user's positive feeling or contentment while interacting with the product in the specified context.

L24.subgoal: Define usability metrics and explain the principles of user-centered design

key_points.text: Usability is measured by three aspects: effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.
User-centered design involves involving users, either actively or passively, in the design lifecycle.
ISO prefers to use the term human-centered design rather than user-centered design.
Users are broadly categorized into novice, intermittent, and expert users.

key_terms.definition: Usability is a measure of how good a system is from the perspective of the user. Usability encompasses the metrics used to determine how well a system performs for the user.
User-centered design is the process where users are involved, either actively or passively, in the design lifecycle of a product. This design process aims to create products that increase usability.
Effectiveness refers to whether the user is able to successfully complete whatever they want to do with the product. This measure determines the product's overall ability to meet user goals.
Efficiency refers to how quickly the user can perform the tasks they want to accomplish using the system. This measure focuses on the speed and resource usage of user interaction.
Satisfaction refers to the degree to which the user feels content while using the system. This measure assesses the user's overall positive or negative emotional state during interaction.

L24.subgoal: Describe the architecture and human factors required for interactive XR systems

key_points.text: The core concern of extended reality systems is creating a relationship between the user and the virtual environment.
XR systems function through a data flow involving user input devices, a processing system (hardware, middleware, application layer), and output devices.
Input design must follow a user-centered approach to ensure that the user can provide input seamlessly and easily.
Perceptual design and modeling are necessary to ensure that the output stimuli are generated and perceived appropriately by the user.

key_terms.definition: Extended reality systems are the subject of discussion, focusing on creating a relationship between the user and the virtual environment. This relationship is built using both software and hardware components.

User-centered design requires considering the user's perspective when dealing with extended reality systems to ensure seamless and effective interaction. This philosophy applies to both how input is provided and how output is perceived.

Interaction design is the process of modeling how to provide input from the user's point of view, focusing on how easily the user can provide that input. This is a key part of the user-centered design approach.

Perceptual design and modeling is crucial for determining how well the output is generated, ensuring that the generated stimuli are appropriately perceived by the user. This is important because generating and perceiving stimuli are both vital for the system's effectiveness.
The XR engine is the middleware component within the system that utilizes hardware resources to generate output data. It processes the input data received from the user and system components.

L24.subgoal: Summarize interactive systems and introduce human factors relevant to XR

key_points.text: The lecture covered the basic idea, design concerns, and XR relevance of interactive systems.
Detailed interactive system design and development is outside the scope of this lecture.
Students can refer to specific books and MOOCs for further details on interactive system design.
The next lecture will focus on human factors relevant to extended reality systems.

key_terms.definition: Extended reality (XR) refers to systems that allow users to perceive or interact with environments that blend the real and digital worlds. This concept is central to the discussion of how humans interact with advanced systems.

Human factors refers to the study of how humans interact with technology, specifically focusing on factors relevant to extended reality systems. These factors are crucial for designing effective and usable XR experiences.
Interactive systems are a type of system characterized by a basic idea that differentiates it from other systems. These systems require specific design concerns to ensure effective user engagement.

Human-computer interaction (HCI) is a field of study that focuses on the design and implementation of how humans interact with computers. This field provides foundational knowledge for designing effective interfaces.

L25.subgoal: Explain the core components and design principles required for effective XR systems

key_points.text: The XR system is composed of hardware, middleware (the XR engine), and application software.
Two critical design aspects are interaction design, which ensures ease of use, and perceptual design, which ensures appropriate sensing of output.
The primary objective of designing interaction and perceptual stimuli is to create the best possible illusion of reality.
VR systems require total immersion, whereas AR or MR systems involve partial immersion.

key_terms.definition: Extended Reality is the broad domain of systems where emphasis is placed on the interaction between the user and the digital content. XR broadly belongs to the domain of interactive systems.

Human Factors refers to the knowledge that helps a developer build better Extended Reality systems by understanding the factors relevant to the user experience. This knowledge is crucial for designing effective XR systems.
Interaction design is important for providing the user with the ease of interacting with the system. It is a key component in building a usable system that the user can interact with easily.

Perceptual design is related to ensuring that the output generated for the user is appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived. It is one of the two critical design elements alongside interaction design.

Presence is the sense of reality that a system gives the user, making them feel as if they are actually in the real world. The interaction and perceptual stimuli must be designed to create this best possible illusion of reality.

L25.subgoal: Explain how the human perceptual system interacts with and is challenged by virtual reality

key_points.text: Virtual reality systems attempt to fool the user's perception system into believing they are in a familiar, real-world environment.
Human bodies are biologically designed to perceive the real world, not artificial or virtual worlds.
When virtual reality inputs are inconsistent with real-life behavior, the body may either adapt or fail to adapt.
Failure to adapt to virtual stimuli can result in adverse effects, such as cyber sickness (dizziness or nausea).

key_terms.definition: Perceptual system is the mechanism that dictates how our senses and perception function, driven by underlying physiology. Understanding this system is necessary to understand how we experience interactive and extended reality systems.

Immersion is the feeling that a user is immersed in the virtual environment, which is achieved through interactions designed into the VR system. This feeling is essentially the perception that the user is immersed.

Presence is the state of being fully present in the virtual world, which is the ultimate objective of designing a good VR system. Complete presence will not occur unless complete immersion is achieved.
Cyber sickness is a set of adverse physical symptoms that can occur while experiencing virtual reality systems. These symptoms include dizziness, nausea, or other related physical discomforts.

L25.subgoal: Explain the role and scope of perceptual psychology in designing extended reality systems

key_points.text: Perceptual psychology is the science that studies how the brain converts sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena.
Understanding human perception is crucial for designing better interactive and extended reality systems.
Perceptual psychology provides guidelines for addressing issues like virtual object distance, required video resolution, and the feeling of presence.
The lecture will cover basic physiology and the process of perception, while the topic of system interference will be addressed in subsequent lectures.

key_terms.definition: Perceptual psychology is the scientific study of how the brain transforms sensory input into experiences that are perceived. This science helps understand the relationship between external signals and the phenomena we consciously experience.

L25.subgoal: Identify the components, stimuli, and organs of various human senses

key_points.text: A device sensor converts an energy source into electrical signals, while a human bodily sensor converts a stimulus into neural impulses.
Vision uses electromagnetic energy as the stimulus, detected by photoreceptors in the eye.
Touch sense uses tissue distortion as the stimulus, detected by mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors in the skin and muscles.
The sense of balance uses gravity or acceleration as the stimulus, detected by mechanoreceptors in the vestibular organs.

key_terms.definition: Sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals within a circuit. This term is used when discussing a technological system or device.
Human bodily sensor is a body organ that converts a stimulus into neural impulses. This term refers to the sensory organs found within the human body.
Mechanoreceptor is a receptor that detects physical stimuli, such as air pressure waves, tissue distortion, or acceleration. These receptors are involved in senses like touch, auditory, and balance.
Chemoreceptor is a receptor that detects chemical composition. These receptors are responsible for the senses of taste and smell.
Vestibular organ is the sense organ that detects gravity or acceleration. It is specifically responsible for the sense of balance.

L25.subgoal: Identify the types of human receptors and the corresponding sensory systems

key_points.text: Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon where receptors are designed to activate only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.
The six senses used to perceive the world are vision, auditory, balance, taste, smell, and touch.
Receptors are categorized into different types, including photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, and mechanoreceptors.
The next part of the lecture will focus on how the sensing process works.

key_terms.definition: A receptor is a sensor that is part of a sensory organ. It is designed to target particular stimuli.
Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon where a receptor is designed to be activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives. This ensures the receptor targets particular stimuli.
A photoreceptor is a receptor found in the eyes. It targets electromagnetic energy, specifically in the frequency range of visible light.
A mechanoreceptor is a receptor that senses motion, vibration, or gravitational force. These receptors are involved in the auditory, touch, and balance senses.
A chemoreceptor is a receptor that provides signals based on the chemical composition of matter. These receptors are used for the senses of taste and smell.

L26.subgoal: Explain the biological and computational mechanism of perception using neural network analogies

key_points.text: Perception is a higher-level activity that only occurs after sense organs convert stimuli into neural impulses.
The cerebral cortex, which handles perception, contains roughly 20 billion neurons.
The interconnection of neurons can be modeled as a directed graph or network, similar to machine learning approaches.
Communication between neurons occurs across a gap called the synapse, transmitting electrical or chemical signals.

key_terms.definition: Perception is an abstract, higher-level activity that occurs after sense organs convert stimuli into neural impulses. This process is responsible for how we perceive things.
Sensing is the lowest level of the process, where sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimuli. These organs then convert that input stimuli into neural impulses.
Neuron is a basic unit of the brain that contains a nucleus, dendrites, and an axon. These parts allow the neuron to receive and transmit impulses.
Synapse is a gap between the axon of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron. Communication occurs across this gap via electrical or chemical signals.
Cerebral cortex is the part of the brain that handles perception and other functions like attention, memory, and language. Roughly 20 billion neurons are devoted to this task.

L26.subgoal: Illustrate how hierarchical processing detects increasingly complex patterns in stimuli

key_points.text: Initial receptor inputs are selective, responding only to a narrow range of stimuli across time, space, or frequency.
Hierarchical processing allows the detection of increasingly complex patterns in a stimulus.
Processing occurs in stages, moving from one level of aggregation to a higher level until it reaches the cerebral cortex.
When lower-level receptor information is aggregated by neurons, it results in slightly higher-level information.

key_terms.definition: Hierarchical processing is a type of neural processing that occurs in stages, where signals move from initial receptor inputs through successive levels of aggregation until they reach the cerebral cortex. This staged approach allows the detection of increasingly complex patterns within a stimulus.
Selectivity is the characteristic of a receptor where it responds only to a narrow range of stimuli. This narrow range can be defined across various dimensions, including time, space, or frequency.

The cerebral cortex is the specific part of the human brain that signals eventually reach after propagating through the neural network. It serves as the final destination for the processed information.

L26.subgoal: Explain how long-term knowledge combines with sensory input to create perception

key_points.text: Sensory signals are interpreted in the cerebral cortex by combining real-time stimuli with knowledge stored in long-term memory.
Stimuli interpretation depends not only on sensory inputs but also on the kind of real-life experience or knowledge an individual possesses.
The combination of sensory input and knowledge results in perceptual phenomena, such as face recognition or identifying a song.
Overall perceptual processing is the outcome of combining hierarchical processing with long-term knowledge and real-time sensory input.

key_terms.definition: Stimuli interpretation is the process where the meaning of a stimulus is determined, and it is not based solely on the sensory inputs received. It also depends heavily on the real-life experience and knowledge a person possesses.
Perceptual phenomena are the results of combining sensory input with existing knowledge, and they include abilities such as face recognition or identifying a song.
Perception is the ability to process raw stimuli into meaningful information, which occurs when knowledge and experience are combined with the raw signals received through sensory organs.
Perceptual processing is the overall outcome of combining real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge or experience. This process is also described as hierarchical processing.
Long-term memory is where knowledge and life experience are stored, representing information that has been gained or learned over an extended period of time.

L26.subgoal: Define proprioception and explain how the brain processes body position and movement

key_points.text: Proprioception is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them.
Proprioception is a form of perception that does not rely on a dedicated sensory organ or receptor.
The motor cortex sends signals, known as efference copies, to communicate executed motions to other parts of the brain.
Because it lacks a specific sensory organ, proprioception is often referred to as the sixth sense.

key_terms.definition: Proprioception is a form of perception that allows the body to sense the relative positions of its parts and the muscular effort used during movement. This sense is unique because it does not rely on a dedicated sensory organ or receptor.
Efference copies are signals sent by the motor cortex to other parts of the brain. These signals communicate the specific motions that have been executed by the body.

Sixth sense refers to a type of perception that functions without a dedicated sensory organ or receptor. This sense is derived from processing information sent by the motor cortex to understand body position and effort.

L26.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of sensory mismatch and its resulting effects in immersive XR systems

key_points.text: The brain processes information by combining signals from multiple senses and long-term learned experiences.
Immersive systems create a sensory mismatch because the brain does not have the long period of time required to adapt to the new input.
Sensory mismatch can lead to cyber sickness symptoms (like fatigue, dizziness, or nausea) or compromise the user's sense of presence.
Vection is an example of sensory conflict where visual input suggests motion while proprioception indicates stillness.
XR design must balance experiences across various senses to ensure the brain processes the information in the desired way.

key_terms.definition: Vection is an illusion of self-motion that occurs when a person is stationary but the visual input from a virtual environment suggests that they are moving or accelerating.

Cyber sickness is a significant issue or effect, such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, or nausea, that results from the inability of the brain to correctly process sensory information within a virtual reality context.
Presence is compromised when the brain becomes consciously aware of the conflict between sensory inputs, causing the user to immediately understand that the experience is artificial.
Sensory conflict is a situation where different sensory inputs, such as vision and proprioception, report contradictory information to the brain.
Brain development is essentially the process of learning, which involves the brain learning the processes of perception and cognition over a long period of time.

L26.subgoal: Summarize the lecture's scope and outline future topics in XR design

key_points.text: Designing XR systems requires significant effort in understanding users, choosing appropriate hardware, and addressing challenges like cyber sickness.
The lecture provided an overview of human physiology and the process of perception relevant to designing VR systems.
Future lectures will cover various sensory organs, their workings, and their implications for detailed XR system design.
The material for this lecture is primarily taken from the book *Virtual Reality* by LaValle.

key_terms.definition: Human physiology is a basic concept studied in the context of designing Virtual Reality (VR) systems. It provides foundational knowledge about the body's functions relevant to XR design.
Process of perception is a fundamental concept covered in this lecture regarding the design of VR systems. It describes how humans interpret sensory information.

Sensory organ is a biological component whose workings and implications are relevant for building Extended Reality (XR) systems. The lecture plans to cover these organs in detail in subsequent lectures.

L27.subgoal: Justify the study of visual perception and light propagation in XR systems

key_points.text: The lecture will cover how our visual senses function and how this knowledge informs the design of visual experiences in extended reality systems.
Visual perception in VR headsets is achieved through the combined action of engineered lenses (in the headset) and natural lenses (in the eyes).
Understanding light propagation allows developers to model physics accurately within virtual worlds and determine what should be rendered.
Knowledge of camera and visual sense working is crucial for building effective tracking hardware and software.

key_terms.definition: Visual perception is the process where light arrives on the retina, which is part of the eye, leading to the perception of the scene. This process is guided by both engineered and natural lenses.
Natural lens is the part of the eyes that is used in the combined lens system. Our eyes naturally contain lenses that contribute to visual perception.
Light propagation is the movement of light through the combination of lenses. This process eventually leads to the perception of the scene.
Combined system is the combination of engineered and natural lenses. This dual system essentially helps the user perceive the immersive visual content.

L27.subgoal: Compare the particle, wave, and ray descriptions of light and their applications

key_points.text: Light can be described as photons, tiny particles of energy, which is helpful for understanding light received by a sensor or receptor.
Light can be described as waves, which are ripples through space, and this description is helpful in understanding the spectrum of color.
Light can be described as rays, which are trajectories assumed to be created by a single hypothetical photon, and this view helps explain how lenses work.

key_terms.definition: A photon is a tiny particle of energy that moves through space at high speeds. These energy particles are often referred to as light particles.
A wave is a ripple that travels through space. This description of light as a wave is helpful for understanding the spectrum of color.
A ray is a trajectory or path assumed to be created by a single hypothetical photon. This concept of light as a ray is helpful in explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

L27.subgoal: Describe the three ways light interacts with material surfaces

key_points.text: Transmission occurs when light passes through the material and exits the surface.,,
Absorption occurs when light rays terminate within the material, meaning there is no further propagation outside the object.,,
Reflection happens when a ray falls on the surface and bounces off without penetrating the object.
Light rays can be reflected, absorbed, or transmitted, and all three processes can happen simultaneously.,,

key_terms.definition: Transmission is the process where a part of a light ray passes through a material and exits the material. This allows the object to allow light to pass through it.
Absorption occurs when a portion of a light ray is absorbed within the material, causing the ray to terminate inside the object. There is no further propagation of the ray outside the material.
Reflection is the phenomenon where a light ray falls on a surface and bounces off without entering or penetrating the object. The ray gets reflected from the surface.

L27.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of color perception using direct and ambient light sources

key_points.text: Color perception occurs when light reflects from a surface point and reaches the viewer's eye.
The perceived color is determined by the intensity of the light that reaches the viewer's eye.
Ambient light is light reflected from surrounding objects in the environment, mixing with direct light.
The final color is determined by the intensity of the combined light from both the direct source and the ambient light.

key_terms.definition: Color perception is the process where a viewer perceives a color based on the intensity of light that reaches their eye. This light is determined by how light rays interact with the surface of an object.
Ambient light is the light present in the environment that reaches the eye. This light is reflected from the object surface and combines with light coming from a direct source.

L27.subgoal: Trace the path of light and explain how the eye focuses images onto the retina

key_points.text: Light rays reach the eye after getting reflected from surfaces.
Light passes through the cornea, pupil, lens, and finally the retina.
The cornea and lens refract light to focus images onto the retina.
Light propagation through the eye can be understood in terms of light as ray and transmission of light rays.

key_terms.definition: Cornea is an outer surface component of the eye that refracts light rays as they pass through it.
Pupil is a component of the eye that is located between the cornea and the lens.
Lens is a component of the eye that refracts light rays, working in sequence with the cornea to focus images.
Retina is a component located at the back side of the eye where the light rays are focused to form images.
Transmission is the process where light falls through a surface, passes through the medium, and then emerges from the surface.

L27.subgoal: Describe the structure and function of the eye's visual components

key_points.text: The iris controls the amount of light entering the eye by dilating or constricting the pupil size.
Light travels through the cornea and lens before reaching the retina.
The retina contains photoreceptors and optic nerve fibers that transmit visual signals to the brain.
The retina contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, which are distributed differently (rods in periphery, cones in fovea).

key_terms.definition: Retina is the part of the eye located on the back side, which is composed of optic nerve fibers and photoreceptors.
Photoreceptor is a bodily sensor required for visual perception.
Iris is the structure that controls the amount of light entering the eye by dilating or constricting the pupil size.
Rods are a type of photoreceptor that are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina.
Cones are a type of photoreceptor that are mainly located in a small central region of the retina, which is called the fovea.

L27.subgoal: Compare how rods and cones contribute to different types of vision

key_points.text: Light passes through several semi-liquid materials, such as aqueous and vitreous humor, when propagating through the eye.
Rods can share an optic nerve to aid sensitivity in low light, whereas cones generally have one optic nerve fiber each to aid image resolution.
Photopic vision, accomplished with cones, allows for color perception and is related to central vision.
Scotopic vision, accomplished with rods, is related to peripheral vision and results in weak lights being visible as grays.

key_terms.definition: Photopic vision is the type of vision accomplished only with cones, which allows for the perception of colors and is associated with central vision.
Scotopic vision is the type of vision accomplished only with rods, which is related to peripheral vision and allows weak lights to be visible as a series of grays.
Image acuity is the ability to perceive fine detail, which is aided by having one optic nerve fiber for each cone.

L27.subgoal: Explain how the range of visible light frequencies leads to color perception

key_points.text: Visible light is defined as a spectrum of electromagnetic light waves within a specific frequency range.
The visible spectrum ranges from red light (4.3 x 10^14 Hz, 700 nm) to violet light (7.5 x 10^14 Hz, 400 nm).
Color perception, known as photopic vision, occurs when light waves within the visible range excite the cones in the eye.
Light outside the visible range cannot excite the photoreceptors (cones), meaning no color perception occurs.

key_terms.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves. This range encompasses the light waves that fall between the red and violet ends of the spectrum.
Photopic vision is the perception of color that occurs when light waves within the visible range excite the cones in the eye. This process is how we are able to perceive color.
Cones are photoreceptors in the eye that are excited by light waves within the visible range. Excitation of these cones is what gives us the perception of color.

L27.subgoal: Compare and contrast central and peripheral vision based on photoreceptor density

key_points.text: The two types of vision (central and peripheral) are determined by the density of photoreceptors across the retina.
Central vision is supported by the fovea, a central retinal region with the greatest concentration of cones.
To perceive a sharp color image, the eyes must be focused and pointed straight at the target due to the nature of central vision.
Peripheral vision occurs in regions of the retina with low rod and cone density, making it better for detecting movement but poor for color perception.

key_terms.definition: Fovea is the central region of the retina that possesses the greatest concentration of photoreceptors, specifically cones. This region is responsible for contributing to the perception of central vision.

Central vision is one of the two types of vision supported by human eyes, which is enabled by the high concentration of cones found in the fovea. This type of vision allows the perception of a sharp color image when the eyes are pointed straight at a target.

Peripheral vision is the other type of vision supported by human eyes, which relies on the peripheral region of the retina. This region has a lower density of photoreceptors and is better at detecting movement than central vision.
Cones are photoreceptors that are highly concentrated in the innermost part of the fovea. These cones are responsible for contributing to the idea of central vision and perceiving sharp color images.
Rods are photoreceptors found in the peripheral region of the retina, mixed with a lesser amount of cones. This region is particularly effective at detecting movement.

L27.subgoal: Explain the physiological cause and function of the blind spot

key_points.text: The blind spot is a region of the retina that lacks photoreceptors, meaning light falling there does not lead to perception.
The blind spot exists because the density of the optic nerve prevents photoreceptors from being placed in that specific region of the retina.
The previous discussion covered the nature of light, how it propagates, and how the eye processes light.
The next part of the lecture will apply this knowledge to understanding the working of immersive headsets and displays.

key_terms.definition: Blind spot is a region in the eye where the individual cannot perceive light or visual stimuli. This area is blind because it lacks photoreceptors.
Photoreceptor is a cell located in the retina that is responsible for detecting light. These cells are necessary for the eye to perceive visual stimuli.
Retina is the light-sensitive tissue located inside the eye. This tissue contains photoreceptors and is crucial for visual perception.

L28.subgoal: Identify and describe the key anatomical components of the human eye

key_points.text: The lecture aims to apply knowledge of vision physiology to understand the working principles of head-mounted displays.
The cornea functions as a powerful lens but possesses a fixed focal depth.
The human lens is a natural lens that provides variable focal depth.
The retina serves as the image surface where light rays fall and are transmitted to the brain.

key_terms.definition: Cornea is a powerful lens structure of the eye that possesses a fixed focal depth. It is the first structure through which light rays enter the eye.
Human lens is a natural lens within the eye that has the ability to adjust its focal depth. This variable focal depth allows the eye to focus on objects at different distances.
Retina is the portion of the eye where light rays fall and are subsequently transmitted to the brain via optical nerves. It functions as the image surface of the eye.
Image surface is the area of the eye where light rays fall, which is characterized as a non-planar surface. This surface is where the light is received before being transmitted to the brain.

L28.subgoal: Compare the optical mechanisms and media of the human eye and engineered lenses

key_points.text: An engineered lens setup uses parallel lights converging to a focal point, which defines the focal depth.
In the human eye, a non-planar retina replaces the concept of a focal plane.
Light travels through five different media before hitting the retina in the human eye.
The five media and their refractive indices are air (1.009), cornea (1.376), aqueous fluid (1.336), natural lens (1.413), and vitreous fluid (1.337) [32-35].

key_terms.definition: Engineered lens is an artificially created lens used in setups to model optical concepts for comparison with biological systems. It is designed to converge parallel lights to a specific focal point.
Focal plane is the specific plane where parallel lights converge when passing through an engineered lens. The distance between the lens and this focal point is known as the focal depth.
Retina is a non-planar, spherically curved surface in the human eye that functions as the light-receiving surface. This structure replaces the concept of a flat focal plane in the natural human eye.

Photoreceptor is a component contained within the retina that performs the function of converting light energy into neural pulses. This conversion process is essential for the human eye to perceive light.
Refractive index is a property of a medium that quantifies the amount of light that passes through it. This index is unique to each medium and affects how light travels through it.

L28.subgoal: Explain the mechanism by which the human eye focuses light onto the retina

key_points.text: A minimum lens power of 40 diopters is required to converge parallel light rays onto the retina center.
The eye utilizes two convex lenses for focusing: the cornea and the natural lens.
The cornea has an optical power of approximately 40 D, and the eye lens has an approximate power of 20 D.
The combined optical power of the cornea and natural lens is 60 diopters, which is sufficient for normal vision.

key_terms.definition: Focal point is the specific point on the retina center where light rays are converged after passing through the eye's lenses. This point is where the image of the object is formed.
Cornea is a convex lens that functions as one of the two primary focusing elements in the eye. It is considered a type of lens that contributes significantly to the eye's overall optical power.

Combined power is the total optical strength achieved when multiple lenses, such as the cornea and the natural lens, are used together. This combined power determines whether faraway objects are focused correctly onto the retina.
Diopter is a unit of measurement used to quantify the optical power of a lens. This measurement is necessary to determine if the eye has sufficient power to focus light correctly.
Retina is the center of the eyeball where light rays are focused to form an image. It is the surface that receives the focused light from faraway objects.

L28.subgoal: Explain the optical mechanism of a VR headset using convex lenses

key_points.text: A convex lens is used in a VR headset to increase optical power and focus the image onto the user's retina.
For the best VR experience, the engineered lens must be placed at the distance of its focal length.
The screen appears as an enormous virtual image that is infinitely far away, even though a real image is projected onto the retina.
The objective of the artificial display system is to convert light into normal light that falls on the eye, supplementing normal eye operation.

key_terms.definition: Convex lens is an optical component that increases optical power, functioning similarly to reading glasses. It is used inside the VR headset to help focus light onto the retina.
Virtual image is the appearance of the screen as an enormous image that is perceived as being infinitely far away.
Real image is an image that is nevertheless projected onto the retina. Perception of the world requires that real images are formed on the retina.
Focal distance is the specific distance between the screen and the engineered lens that must be maintained for the best user experience. The engineered lens is usually placed at this distance.

L28.subgoal: Explain the mechanisms of depth perception using field of view, binocular vision, and stereoscopy

key_points.text: The human eye has an approximate 180-degree horizontal and 150-degree vertical field of view.
Binocular vision uses the common region seen by both eyes to enhance depth perception and the understanding of 3D space.
Stereoscopic vision generates a 3D view by simultaneously processing two 2D images, one captured by each eye.

key_terms.definition: Binocular vision is the process of looking at something using both eyes. It involves both eyes seeing the same image within a common region.

L28.subgoal: Define the types and components of degrees of freedom in 3D space

key_points.text: Virtual worlds support two main types of movement: translational (for navigation) and rotational (for changing angles).
There are a total of 6 degrees of freedom in 3D space, which indicate the different ways an object can move.
The 6 degrees of freedom consist of 3 rotational degrees (yaw, roll, and pitch) and 3 translational degrees.
The 3 translational degrees of freedom correspond to movement along the x, y, and z axes.

key_terms.definition: Degrees of freedom is a concept that indicates the different ways an object can move in space. There can be a total of six degrees of freedom in three-dimensional space.
Translational movement is a type of movement used for navigating within a three-dimensional space. This movement is used for navigating in the 3D space.
Rotational movement is a type of movement primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis. Broadly, these two types of motions can be found in any virtual world.
Yaw is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom. Yaw is one of the specific rotational movements that can be observed.
Roll is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom. Roll is one of the specific rotational movements that can be observed.

L28.subgoal: Identify the key perceptual factors influencing VR display hardware design

key_points.text: Physiological properties, such as photoreceptor density, directly impact the engineering requirements for visual display hardware.
VR displays should ideally be designed to perfectly match the performance of the visual sense they are trying to fool.
Spatial resolution, defined as pixels per square area, is one important consideration for display design.
Intensity resolution and range must be determined based on how many values the human system can process without compromising perceptual quality.
Temporal resolution, or frame rate, is a very important consideration, especially in the context of motion perception.

key_terms.definition: Photoreceptor density refers to basic physiological properties that directly impact the engineering requirements for visual display hardware. This knowledge determines how display hardware is designed.
Spatial resolution is a consideration that determines how many pixels are needed within a specific square area. This metric is crucial for designing effective displays.

Intensity resolution and range define how many intensity values a display can produce, along with the minimum and maximum values. These values must be determined based on how many values can be processed without compromising perceptual quality.
Temporal resolution is a consideration that dictates how fast displays need to change their pixels. This is also referred to as the refreshing or frame rate.

VR displays are engineered systems that should ideally be designed to perfectly match the performance of the visual sense they are trying to fool. This design goal requires understanding the limits of human perception.

L28.subgoal: Compare resolution requirements for distant and close-proximity displays

key_points.text: Aliasing is the jagged appearance of lines (staircases) that occurs when spatial resolution is insufficient.
The screen door effect is a visual artifact commonly observed in images produced by LCD projectors.
A retina display is defined as a display supporting a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi).
For close-proximity displays like VR headsets, the required PPI must be 7 to 8 times higher than the traditional retina display resolution.

key_terms.definition: Aliasing is the visual effect where a sharp diagonal line appears jagged or stair-stepped when the image is zoomed out. This effect occurs when the display cannot accurately represent fine details.
Screen door effect is an image artifact commonly seen in LCD projectors that makes it appear as if there is a physical screen overlaying the image. This happens due to the way the image is displayed.
Spatial resolution is a concept that describes the level of detail a display supports. This resolution is crucial for preventing visual artifacts like aliasing or the screen door effect.

Retina display is a type of display that requires a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi) to achieve a high level of visual clarity. This concept is suitable for displays viewed from a distance.
Pixel density is the required measure of how many pixels a display needs to have. This density ensures that individual pixels or aliasing effects are not perceived by the viewer.

L28.subgoal: Summarize the key concepts of visual perception and their application in XR system design

key_points.text: Higher frame rates are necessary for perceiving motion in immersive VR environments compared to standard media.
The lecture covered the physiology of human vision, including how we perceive color, depth, and scenes.
Visual perception knowledge helps in designing XR systems by informing decisions about resolutions and frame rates.
The next lecture will cover auditory systems and their relevance to building better XR experiences.

key_terms.definition: Temporal resolution is a concern related to the speed at which motion is perceived in an immersive environment. It requires much higher frame rates compared to the standards used by ordinary television or movies.
Frame rates measure the number of images displayed per second, and for immersive environments, they must be significantly higher than those typically seen on standard desktop or television displays.
Physiology of human vision refers to the biological makeup of our eyes. This knowledge helps explain how we perceive various elements such as color, depth, and scenes.

Visual perception is the process of understanding how our eyes process visual information. This understanding is crucial for relating human perception to the design of Extended Reality (XR) systems and experiences.

XR systems are the technological frameworks that utilize principles of visual perception. These systems are designed to create Extended Reality experiences, and they require careful management of factors like resolutions and frame rates.

L29.subgoal: Introduce the role of auditory senses and hearing physiology in extended reality

key_points.text: Human factors influence the design and overall experience of interactive systems.
The previous lecture discussed the physiology of the visual senses.
This lecture will cover the human auditory system and its relevance for extended reality experiences.
The focus will be on VR because it is more relevant for immersive experiences.

key_terms.definition: Auditory sense is the human ability to perceive sound, and the lecture will cover its physiology and relevance to extended reality experiences. This sense is the primary focus of the current lecture.
Immersive experience refers to the overall feeling or quality of an experience that is enhanced by technology. This experience is highly relevant to extended reality (XR) applications.
Extended reality systems are the technological environments that incorporate human factors into their design. These systems encompass various forms of reality interaction.
Human factors are the elements that influence the design and overall experience of interactive systems. These factors are crucial for creating usable and effective interactive systems.

L29.subgoal: Explain how auditory input enhances immersion and presence in VR systems

key_points.text: Visual sense alone cannot provide the full picture of a virtual environment, affecting the immersive experience.
Auditory effects reinforce the perception of object properties such as size, volume, distance, and material when combined with vision.
Combining vision and audio enhances the emotional connection and believability of the virtual environment.
Auditory experience plays a critical role in maintaining presence within a virtual environment.

key_terms.definition: Immersive experience is the overall feeling derived from extended reality systems, which is significantly enhanced when multiple senses are included. This experience is affected by how well the virtual environment is perceived through combined sensory input.

Auditory sense is one of the non-visual senses that contributes powerfully to providing an immersive experience in virtual reality. This sense involves the recording and reproduction of sound, which can enhance the believability of the virtual environment.

Presence is a state achieved in a virtual environment that requires two things: the reinforcement of the virtual experience as believable, and the development of an emotional attachment to that experience. Auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing this presence.

Proprioception is identified as one of the six senses, alongside the five standard senses, that influences our experience with extended reality systems. This sense is one of the other senses besides vision and audio that contributes to the overall experience.

L29.subgoal: Define sound, explain its propagation mechanism, and identify its wave properties

key_points.text: Sound is vibration in a medium (such as air, water, or solids) and requires a medium to propagate, unlike light.
Sound propagates through a medium by creating pressure differences, ranging from compression (high pressure) to rarefaction (low pressure).
Sound is represented as a sound wave, which is a plot showing pressure variation against time.
The three primary properties used to characterize sound waves are frequency, amplitude, and phase.
The human ear is physiologically limited to hearing frequencies between 20 Hertz and 20,000 Hertz.

key_terms.definition: Sound is a vibration that occurs within a medium, which can be air, water, or other gases, liquids, and solids.
Frequency is the number of alterations between one maximum to another maximum per second, which is measured in Hertz.

L29.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of sound transmission through the outer, middle, and inner ear

key_points.text: The human hearing system is composed of three parts: the outer ear, middle ear, and inner ear.
The outer ear canal amplifies sound pressure but attenuates high frequencies due to its design.
The middle ear uses three bones (ossicles: malleus, incus, and stapes) to transfer vibrations from the tympanic membrane.
The inner ear contains the cochlea, which converts sound energy into neural impulses transmitted to the brain.

key_terms.definition: The outer ear is the initial part of the human hearing system that receives sound waves. It contains components like the canal, which amplifies sound pressure for a range of frequencies.
The middle ear is the section of the hearing system located after the outer ear. It houses the three bones, known as ossicles, which transfer vibrations.
The inner ear is the final part of the human hearing system, which is roughly the size of a marble. It contains the cochlea, the organ responsible for hearing.
The tympanic membrane is a structure in the middle ear that vibrates when a sound wave passes through the outer ear canal. This vibration initiates the transfer of sound energy.
The cochlea is the sense organ housed within the inner ear. It converts incoming sound energy, which is a wave, into neural impulses for transmission to the brain.

L29.subgoal: Explain the importance of sound in immersive experiences and describe the basic mechanism of hearing

key_points.text: Vision combined with sound is preferable for achieving a better perception and higher presence in a virtual world.
Sound is fundamentally defined as a wave.
The human ear is composed of three parts: the outer ear, middle ear, and inner ear.
Sound waves are converted into neural impulses within the ear and transmitted to the brain for perception.
Future lectures will cover how sound is perceived and how it is rendered to achieve the best immersive experience.

key_terms.definition: Sound is defined as a wave. This wave is the physical phenomenon that is converted into neural impulses by the ear.
Auditory system is the mechanism that excites the hearing system. It converts sound waves into neural impulses which are then transmitted to the brain for perception.

L30.subgoal: Identify and describe the three levels of sound perception

key_points.text: Sound is perceived at three distinct levels: social, warning, and primitive.
The social level of sound perception helps individuals carry out social interactions.
The warning level of sound perception provides alerts or warnings about potential events.
The primitive level involves the intuitive understanding of background noises that are often ignored.

key_terms.definition: Auditory perception is the process of understanding how we perceive sound, which is crucial for creating immersive experiences in extended reality systems.
Sound perception is the way we perceive sound, which is structured into three distinct levels of understanding.
Social level perception is the type of perception that helps individuals carry out social interactions with others.
Warning level perception provides an alert or warning about a specific event or situation.
Primitive level perception is generally the intuitive understanding of sound, often relating to background noises that individuals tend to ignore.

L30.subgoal: Define psychophysics, psychoacoustics, and the laws governing perceived sound

key_points.text: Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena produced by physical stimuli, while psychoacoustics is the specific study of phenomena produced by acoustic stimuli.
Stevens' power law characterizes the relationship between the actual magnitude of a physical stimulus (M) and its perceived magnitude (P) using the formula P = C * M^x.
The Just Noticeable Difference (JND) is the minimum change in a stimulus required for subjects to perceive a change in at least 50% of trials, which is captured by Weber's law ($\Delta M / M = C$).

key_terms.definition: Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that result from physical stimuli. It is defined as a broader field of study.
Psychoacoustics is a specific area of psychophysics that focuses on sound. It is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena produced by acoustic stimuli.

Stevens' power law is a well-known result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude. This relationship is mathematically represented as P equals Cm to the power x.
Just noticeable difference (JND) is a well-known result from psychophysics that refers to the minimum amount a stimulus must change for subjects to perceive the change in at least 50% of trials.
Weber's law is a law used to capture the Just noticeable difference (JND). It is represented by the formula delta M by M equals C, where C is a constant.

used_concepts: Identification of the suitable perception level

L30.subgoal: Apply psychophysical laws to predict auditory perception in VR systems

key_points.text: Psychophysical laws, such as Weber's and Stevens', are applicable to both physical and acoustic stimuli (psychoacoustics).
Stevens' Power Law describes how perception (P) relates to the physical stimulus (m) using an exponent (x).
If the exponent (x) is less than 1, a large increase in physical stimulus results in only a moderate increase in perception.
The Just Noticeable Difference (JND) defines the threshold for whether a change in stimulus is perceived or not.

key_terms.definition: Psychophysics is the field of study that examines the relationship between physical stimuli and the resulting sensory experiences. This discipline provides the foundational laws, such as Weber's law, that govern how we perceive external inputs.

Psychoacoustics is the application of psychophysical principles specifically to the study of auditory perception. This field investigates how humans perceive sound and how acoustic stimuli affect our hearing.

Stevens' Power Law is a psychophysical law that describes the relationship between physical stimuli and perceived sensation. This law states that the perception of a stimulus, such as loudness, is related to the physical stimulus by a power function.
Just Noticeable Difference is the minimum change in a stimulus that a person can detect 50% of the time. Changes must be above this threshold to be perceived, or within it to remain unnoticed.

L30.subgoal: Explain the principles of pitch perception and the importance of sound localization in VR systems

key_points.text: The ability to discriminate changes in pitch decreases as the frequency of the sound wave increases.
Localization is the psychoacoustic process of estimating the location of a sound source by hearing it.
Localization is crucial in VR experiences to give the user a better idea of the orientation and position of objects.
Matching auditory and visual cues is required in immersive environments to prevent problems like a break in presence or cyber sickness.

key_terms.definition: Pitch perception is the ability to perceive the pitch of a sound, which is defined by the frequency of the sound wave. This perception is better at low frequencies, allowing for the detection of very small frequency differences.

Localization is a main area of psychoacoustics that involves estimating the physical location of a sound source solely through auditory input. This ability is crucial for providing users with a better sense of orientation and position within a virtual environment.

Loudness perception is the ability to perceive the volume of a sound, which can be analyzed using established psychophysical or psychoacoustic theories. These theories are used to design effective auditory systems.
Psychoacoustics is a main area of study that deals with how humans perceive sound. This field focuses on estimating the location of a sound source by hearing it.

L30.subgoal: Define the parameters and cues used for auditory localization

key_points.text: Localization is represented using spherical coordinates: azimuth (horizontal angle), elevation (vertical angle), and radius (distance).
The Minimum Audible Angle (MAA) is the smallest angular variation a human listener can detect, which depends on frequency and direction.
Interaural Level Difference (ILD) is a binaural cue based on the difference in sound magnitude received by each ear, often caused by acoustic shadows.
Interaural Time Difference (ITD) is a binaural cue based on the difference in sound arrival time at each ear, which is utilized for localization.

key_terms.definition: Minimum Audible Angle is the smallest angular variation that a human listener can detect. This value is dependent on both the frequency and the direction of the sound source.
Azimuth is the angle measured in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the sound source. This angle represents the vector projected onto the horizontal plane.
Elevation is the angle that corresponds to the deviation of the sound source from the horizontal plane. This angle is measured between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane.

Interaural Level Difference (ILD) is the difference in sound magnitude as perceived by each ear. This difference can occur when one ear is facing the sound source while the other is in an acoustic shadow.
Interaural Time Difference (ITD) is the difference in the arrival time of a sound source to each ear. This difference is caused by the physical distance between the two ears.

L30.subgoal: Explain the role of HRTF in synthesizing and localizing sound within XR systems

key_points.text: Sound perception is primarily determined by four factors: sound perception levels, loudness, pitch, and localization.
For immersive experience, the auditory component of an XR system must be non-stationary and interactive.
HRTF (Head-Related Transfer Functions) models how sound is received from a specific location in space.
Due to the unique HRTF of every individual, system development typically relies on an average listener HRTF.,

key_terms.definition: Head-related transfer function (HRTF) models how a person receives sound originating from a specific location in space. This model is relevant for dealing with sound in any system, including Extended Reality (XR) systems.
Binaural sound is synthesized using a pair of Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTF) for both ears. This synthesis allows for the accurate implementation of localization effects.

Localization is one of the important considerations in sound perception, referring to the ability to determine the spatial location of a sound source. It is a key perception that must be implemented within an XR system.
Immersive experience is the context in which sound perception is relevant, requiring consideration of factors such as loudness, pitch, and localization.

L30.subgoal: Summarize the key concepts of sound and its role in immersive XR experiences

key_points.text: HRTF (Head-Related Transfer Functions) must be implemented to achieve ideal sound localization in XR experiences.
Sound perception is categorized into different levels, including social, individual, warning, and primitive.
The lecture covered the importance of sound in XR, the physiology of the auditory system, and sound perception.
Future lectures will cover other sensory systems, including taste, smell, and touch, and their role in XR.

key_terms.definition: Localization is a kind of perception that involves determining the source of a sound. This perception is a key element that must be implemented for the best immersive experience.

Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) are necessary to implement localization in sound systems. Generally, these functions are implemented for the average human user, although individual variations exist.

Loudness perception is one of the specific levels of sound perception that must be accounted for when generating sound in an embedded system. It is one of the factors contributing to the overall immersive experience.

Pitch perception is one of the specific levels of sound perception that must be accounted for when generating sound in an embedded system. It is a factor that contributes to the overall quality of the immersive experience.

L31.subgoal: Identify the remaining senses and their relevance to building immersive XR systems

key_points.text: The human senses include visual, auditory, touch, smell, taste, and proprioception (the sixth sense).
Previous lectures covered the relation between human physiology and AR-VR systems, focusing on the visual and auditory perceptual systems.
This lecture will cover the remaining senses (touch, taste, smell, and proprioception) and their connection to XR.
The lecture will explore the physiology of these senses and how that knowledge can be used to build better XR systems.

key_terms.definition: Proprioceptive sense is the sixth sense, which is discussed in relation to the standard five senses. This sense is also referred to as proprioception.
Full immersive experience is the topic of discussion that involves the role of senses beyond the visual and auditory senses.
Human visual perceptual system is the system whose knowledge assists in the construction of better Extended Reality (XR) systems. This system is one of the senses discussed in detail.
Human auditory system is a sensory system that helps create an immersive experience within Extended Reality (XR). It works in addition to the visual perceptual system.

L31.subgoal: Describe the somatosensory system and the six types of haptic exploration

key_points.text: The human somatosensory system is responsible for handling touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.
Proprioception is the conscious awareness of the pose of movable body parts, while kinesthesis provides information on movement parameters like velocity and acceleration.
Haptic perception, a major part of touch, involves object handling to infer the overall geometric shape of objects.
Haptic exploration involves six types of manipulations—such as lateral motion, enclosure, and unsupported holding—to perceive properties like texture, shape, and weight.

key_terms.definition: Proprioception is the conscious awareness of the pose of movable human body parts. This awareness allows us to know what we are doing when moving these parts.
Kinesthesis provides information regarding velocities, acceleration, and forces while moving body parts. It is the awareness of various parameters associated with movement.
Haptic perception is the perception of the overall geometric shape of objects. This shape is inferred through the process of haptic exploration, which involves object handling.
Muscle spindle is a receptor embedded inside each muscle. It reports to the brain about changes in the length of the muscle whenever movement occurs.
Golgi tendon organ is a receptor embedded in tendons, which are tough bands connecting muscles to bones. It reports changes in muscle tension associated with muscle movement.

L31.subgoal: Explain the role of haptic perception and its various implementation methods in XR systems

key_points.text: Haptic exploration is essential for creating mental models and improving the immersive experience in VR.
Touch sensation in XR systems is often provided through engineered devices like force feedback, smart gloves, or body suits.
Tangible user interfaces use real-world objects to provide touch feedback, serving as an alternative to computer-controlled haptic devices.
Mixed reality displays align real and virtual worlds, allowing users to interact with physical objects while receiving virtual enhancements.

key_terms.definition: Haptic exploration is the process of performing touch-based investigation to aid in the creation of a mental model of the surrounding world. Haptic exploration offers an extra dimension to a virtual reality world, allowing users to perceive the environment better through touch.

Immersive experience is the feeling of being truly present within an artificial or real world. Allowing haptic exploration in a virtual world increases the immersive experience by helping the user feel more deeply engaged in the environment.

Force feedback is a method of providing touch sensation stimuli, typically delivered through vibrations from XR applications. Force feedback devices are commonly used in VR systems, such as smart gloves or body suits, to allow users to experience physical forces.

Haptic pin array is a device containing a matrix of pins that is controlled by a computer system. The pins are forced upward as the user's fingertip scans the surface, simulating various textures of an object.

Tangible user interface is a method where real-world objects are used to provide feedback to the somatosensory system. This approach replaces computer-controlled haptic devices by allowing users to interact with physical objects whose virtual avatars exist in the world.

L31.subgoal: Analyze the principles and current state of smell and taste interfaces in XR systems

key_points.text: Taste and smell are classified as chemical senses, relying on chemoreceptors that interact chemically with arriving molecules.
Smell interfaces, or olfactory displays, typically use air pumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose for personal or room-scale experiences.
Integrating pleasant odors into immersive experiences has been shown to potentially reduce visually induced motion sickness (cyber sickness).
Developing taste interfaces is generally difficult because it often requires the user to consume food during the experience.

key_terms.definition: Chemoreceptor is a type of receptor that functions by interacting chemically with molecules. Chemoreceptors are designed to respond to specific chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations.
Smell interface is a device intended to provide chemical stimuli to the nose. It typically utilizes air pumps to spray chemical compounds into the air.
Olfactory display is a generic term used to refer to systems that function as smell interfaces. These displays are designed to generate and deliver odor stimuli to the user.
Taste interface is a device used to simulate the sensation of taste electronically. This simulation often requires placing electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation.
Cyber sickness is a type of motion sickness that can be induced by visual stimuli. Pleasant odors have been shown to potentially reduce the effect of this sickness.

L31.subgoal: Summarize the discussion on human senses and preview interactive system development

key_points.text: The discussion covered remaining human senses, including touch, proprioception, taste, and smell.
Haptic exploration helps perceive the geometric properties of objects and increases immersion and presence in XR settings.
Research into generating the effects of smell and taste is complex and currently limited.
The next lecture will focus on how to build interactive XR systems and the systematic process for development.

key_terms.definition: Human somatosensory system is the biological mechanism related to the perception of touch and proprioception. This system utilizes several receptors dedicated to sensing different aspects of the body and environment.
Haptic explorations are methods of perceiving the world through touch. These explorations allow us to perceive the geometric properties of objects around us.

Immersion is a quality that can be increased when support is provided in a Virtual Reality or Extended Reality setting. This support helps the user feel more deeply involved in the virtual environment.

Presence is a feeling that can be increased when support is provided in a Virtual Reality or Extended Reality setting. This feeling contributes to the user's sense of being physically present in the virtual environment.

L32.subgoal: Define user-centric design and explain its role in building acceptable interactive systems

key_points.text: XR systems are fundamentally a class of interactive systems because their users are laypersons.
The design and development of interactive systems must account for human factors, leading to the concept of user-centric design.
User-centric design involves incorporating users into the design process to understand their needs, expectations, and goals.
The goal of any interactive system is to make it usable for a specific group of users within a specified context of use.

L32.subgoal: Define user-centered design and explain its role in creating usable systems

key_points.text: Usability is always defined relative to a specific group of users, a specified context, and specific tasks.
The objective of user-centered design is to design application software that increases usability.
User-centric approaches emphasize the active or passive involvement of users in the overall design lifecycle.
The core concern of user-centric software is building usable, interactive systems for laypersons.

key_terms.definition: Usability refers to the quality of a system when considering a specific group of users, a defined context of use, and particular tasks. Usability is not a universal quality that applies to every user, context, or task.

User-centered design is an objective aimed at creating products that increase usability. This design philosophy emphasizes the active or passive involvement of users throughout the entire design and implementation lifecycle.

Layman user is a person who is expected to use interactive software without needing specialized knowledge of how the hardware or software functions. These users are the target audience for the application software.

Interactive system is a type of application software that is designed to be used by individuals who may not possess technical knowledge of the underlying hardware or software. This design ensures the software is accessible to non-experts.

L32.subgoal: Explain the necessity and function of the Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)

key_points.text: A systematic, step-by-step approach is required to ensure the successful creation of usable software applications.,
The Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) provides a systematic and structured way to manage the entire software development process.,
SDLCs capture and represent all the design and development activities necessary for building software.
The practice of following a software development lifecycle is synonymous with software engineering.,

key_terms.definition: Software development life cycle is a process followed to develop and deploy software. This cycle comprehensively captures and represents the design and development activities required for building the software.
Software engineering is the single term used to represent the idea of software development life cycle. It involves the structured process of engineering a software.

Stages are the components that capture or structure the whole development process. Through their connection, they represent how the development process should take place to achieve the desired outcome.
Usable software is the desired output of the development process. It is the functional software application that the systematic process aims to produce.

L32.subgoal: Analyze the design space and selection challenge using a calendar application example

key_points.text: A structured development lifecycle is necessary when engineering software to achieve defined goals.
The design space is defined as the set of all possible designs for a system.
The theoretical size of a design space with N distinct objects is N factorial.
Practical considerations, such as required ordering, invalidate many theoretical designs, but a manageable number of choices often remain.

key_terms.definition: Development lifecycle is a structured way of achieving a goal when engineering software. It provides a systematic framework for building a software product.
Design space is the set of all possible designs for a given problem. The size of this space is determined by the number of elements that must be placed on a screen.
Usability is the criterion used to determine which design is the best or the right one. It refers to how effective and practical a design is for the user.

L32.subgoal: Describe the highly iterative lifecycle required for building usable interactive systems

key_points.text: A systematic approach, provided by the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), is necessary to identify the best design solution, as intuition is insufficient.
Building usable interactive systems requires involving users as active or passive participants in every stage of the design process.
Incorporating users necessitates a highly iterative lifecycle, where stages loop back to previous steps to account for user feedback.
The iterative lifecycle for interactive systems includes stages such as Feasibility Study, Requirement Gathering, Design/Prototyping/Evaluation, Coding, Testing, and Deployment.

key_terms.definition: Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a set of stages that must be followed in a particular sequence to help identify the best possible design choices among all valid options. This systematic approach ensures a structured path toward a solution.

Interactive systems are systems that require users to be taken into account in every stage of the design process. These systems necessitate involving users as active or passive participants in the design.

A highly iterative lifecycle is a software development lifecycle that requires frequent looping between stages. This structure is necessary to account for user feedback and implement a user-centric design approach.
The Design prototype evaluate cycle is a specific phase within the development process. This cycle comprises the design stage, prototyping stage, and early evaluation stage.

L32.subgoal: Describe the stages of interactive system development, focusing on user involvement

key_points.text: Interactive systems require considering the requirements of end users, in addition to client requirements.
Methods for gathering end user requirements include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes.
The design-prototype-evaluate loop is used to refine early designs based on user feedback through multiple iterations.
The design-prototype-evaluate cycle primarily addresses interface and interaction design, which is separate from code design.

key_terms.definition: Requirement gathering stage is the initial phase where the project's needs are identified, focusing specifically on gathering requirements from end users in addition to the client. This stage involves methods like contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes to understand user needs

Design prototype evaluate loop is an iterative process required for refining early designs based on feedback provided by users. This loop involves creating a prototype, evaluating it, identifying problems, and then modifying the design repeatedly until significant problems cease to be identified

Interface design is one of the two activities included in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle. Interface design focuses on the visual and functional aspects of the system from the user's point of view

Interaction design is the second activity included in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle. Interaction design focuses on how the user interacts with the system based on the requirements gathered from the user

Code design is a separate design part that is distinct from the design activities within the design-prototype-evaluate cycle. Code design deals with the implementation of the system and can be performed using traditional software engineering methods

L32.subgoal: Compare the purpose and scope of different evaluation stages in interactive system development

key_points.text: Minimizing iterations is crucial because code design is a highly skilled and costly process.
The iterative software development life cycle includes three types of evaluation: early evaluation, code testing, and empirical study.
Code testing verifies that the code is executable and bug-free, but empirical study ensures product usability from the end user's perspective.
Empirical study is a unique stage in interactive system development because it involves systematic testing with end users.

key_terms.definition: Usability is the quality metric that ensures a product conforms to the needs and expectations of the end user. Usability is what is assessed during empirical studies.
Empirical study is a unique stage in interactive system development that involves systematic testing with end users. This stage is required to ensure the product conforms to usability.
Evaluation is a process that occurs at multiple stages of the iterative software development life cycle. Evaluation includes early evaluation, code testing, and empirical study.

Code design is a highly skilled and costly process that requires skilled manpower and is the initial stage of the development life cycle. Code design is often revisited if issues are found during testing.
Interactive system is a type of software system that requires an empirical study stage to ensure it conforms to usability. This requirement differentiates it from other software systems.

L32.subgoal: Explain the principles of managing iterative loops within the Interactive System Development Lifecycle

key_points.text: Frequent use of certain development loops (e.g., code testing) significantly increases project cost and risk of abandonment. (Subject)
The Interactive System Development Lifecycle (ISDLC) includes requirement analysis, design prototype evaluation, coding, and empirical testing stages. (Subject)
Subsequent lectures will focus on requirement gathering, interaction design, and evaluation using a case study related to extended reality systems. (Course)

key_terms.definition: Interactive systems are systems that are designed to be usable, and in this course, the focus is on developing extended reality systems.
Extended reality systems are a specific type of interactive system that the course focuses on developing.
Usability is a basic concern when building interactive systems, meaning the system must be designed to be effective and easy to use.
Interactive System Development Lifecycle is the overall idea or process used to build interactive systems.
