key_terms.definition: Cyber sickness is a condition that researchers aim to minimize while a user is experiencing an immersive system. Minimizing this sickness is a primary goal when framing the VR optimization problem.

Psychophysiological optimization is a type of optimization in VR that is essentially equated with the overall VR experience optimization. This focus relates to the user's physical and mental state during the experience.
VR experience optimization is the process of improving the quality of the virtual reality experience. This concept is essentially equated with psychophysiological optimization.
Presence is a very important factor when trying to optimize cyber sickness. If presence is compromised, the overall quality of the experience will deteriorate regardless of optimization efforts.
Natural walking experience is the desired outcome of the optimization effort. It involves creating a realistic walking experience within the VR world, particularly in a system-controlled tour.

L50.subgoal: Outline the steps used to develop a realistic walking behavior model

key_points.text: Realistic VR navigation requires displaying optic flow that matches the user's instantaneous walking speed.
The lecture will discuss a model of natural walking behavior for system-controlled VR navigation.
Model development is a process comprising several stages.
The four stages of model development are empirical research, data analysis, model creation, and validation.

key_terms.definition: Optic flow is a visual speed that is displayed to the user and must match the user's instantaneous walking speed. This matching is necessary for a realistic walking experience.

Realistic walking behavior model is a model of natural walking behavior that can be utilized to address concerns regarding VR navigation. This model is specifically designed for system-controlled VR navigation.
VR navigation experience is the process of moving within a Virtual Reality environment that requires optimization. The goal of optimization is to ensure a realistic walking experience for the user.

L50.subgoal: Outline the experimental setup and participant requirements for the speed estimation study

key_points.text: The overall purpose of the empirical study was to gather real-life data to propose a speed estimation model.
The study involved 40 participants, consisting of 26 males and 14 females, aged 19 to 42 years.
The experiment was conducted in a physical corridor and utilized seven paintings as points of interest.
The task assigned to each user was to start walking and stop at each painting to click a photo.
Height is an important variable in the study because it affects walking behavior.

key_terms.definition: Empirical research is a process used to collect real-life working data from participants. This process involves gathering data to support or build a specific model.
Speed estimation model is a proposed model designed to gather real-life working data when a user moves from one point to another.
Walking behavior is the manner in which a user moves, which is affected by factors such as height.
System-controlled tour is a scenario where a user moves through an environment and must stop and pause at specific points of interest.
Photograph-clicking task is an assigned activity where the user stops at a painting to click a photo, ensuring they stop after walking a predefined distance.

L50.subgoal: Describe the methodology and observed walking patterns from the study

key_points.text: Footstep data was collected using a fixed smartphone camera recording the user's legs at 30 frames per second.
A step was defined as the interval between one foot strike and the next foot strike on the ground.
Participants did not maintain a constant speed during the walking task.
The walking velocity generally increased, reached a maximum, and then slowed down before the target was reached.

key_terms.definition: Instantaneous step frequency is the number of steps per second that a participant is taking at a specific moment. This metric is calculated by observing the number of steps recorded in the video.
A step is defined as the interval between one foot strike and the next foot strike on the ground. This interval signifies the occurrence of a step.

Velocity is the speed of the user, which the study tracked to observe how it changes over time during walking. The user's velocity was observed to increase gradually, reach a maximum, and then decrease before stopping.

L50.subgoal: Explain the difference between actual and perceived speed when modeling movement in virtual reality

key_points.text: The observed CISO pattern is similar to the Fourier series approximation of a square pulse wave.
There is a difference between the actual speed of movement and the speed the user perceives.
Generally, an individual perceives visual or optic flow slower than the actual movement.
Virtual tours should not exactly replicate actual walking behavior but must account for perceived speed.

key_terms.definition: Slow in slow out pattern is a specific pattern observed in the study, characterized by a change in speed that starts slowly, accelerates, remains constant, and then slows down.
Fourier series is a mathematical series that approximates any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision by using weighted terms.
Optic flow is the apparent motion of the visual scene that an individual perceives when they or the objects around them are moving.
Perceived speed is the rate of movement that an individual experiences visually, which may not be the same as the actual physical speed of movement.
Virtual tour is a simulated environment where a user can experience movement, and its design must account for the difference between actual and perceived speed.

L50.subgoal: Model the relationship between actual movement and perceived visual speed using visual gain

key_points.text: The desired perceived visual speed is obtained by multiplying the actual speed by a factor known as visual gain.
The relationship between perceived speed (v_perceived), visual gain (g), and actual speed (v_actual) is represented by the equation v_perceived = g * v_actual.
The visual gain (g) is typically considered to be 2.10, which provides a good visual gain for natural walking behavior.
Actual walking speed (V_actual) is modeled as a function of the instantaneous step frequency (f(x)) and the user's height (h).

key_terms.definition: Visual gain is a factor multiplied by the actual speed to compute the desired visual speed. This factor is used to obtain a different speed that is perceived as natural.
Actual visual speed is the speed obtained by multiplying the instantaneous speed by the visual gain. This resulting speed is what is perceived as natural.
Actual speed is the speed at which the user is physically moving, which is related to the instantaneous step frequency. This speed is represented by a specific mathematical formulation.
Instantaneous step frequency is the rate of steps taken by the user, which is represented as a function of distance. This frequency is similar or related to the actual speed.
CISO pattern is a specific pattern revealed by studies that is similar to the Fourier transform of sinusoidal waveforms. This pattern allows for the computation of the actual speed.

used_concepts: Distance between the source and destination

L50.subgoal: Evaluate the effectiveness of natural walking speed models versus constant speed in VR

key_points.text: The empirical study compared constant speed navigation against a natural walking speed model to enhance perceived realism in VR.
The experiment involved 34 participants in a virtual art exhibition environment using Oculus Rift.
User perception was measured using two 1-10 rating scales: level of realism and user preference.
The instantaneous (natural) speed model resulted in statistically significant higher perceived realism and user preference compared to constant speed.

key_terms.definition: Natural walking behavior is the desired perception that the user experiences when moving through the virtual environment. This behavior is achieved by computing natural walking behavior and multiplying it by a visual gain factor.

Empirical study is a stage of the model evaluation process used to confirm whether a model enhances perceived realism compared to a constant average speed. The purpose of this study was to confirm the model's effectiveness.
Perceived realism is the measure of how real the user experiences the virtual environment to be. The study aimed to confirm whether the usage of the model enhances this perceived realism.
Practice effect is a confounding variable that may affect the results of an experiment. Researchers must take care of this effect to ensure the data is not biased.
Instantaneous speed is the natural walking speed model utilized in the experiment. This speed model is contrasted with a constant speed experience.

L50.subgoal: Summarize the model's limitations and outline the next steps for optimizing the VR experience

key_points.text: The current realistic walking speed model does not adequately address the concern of cyber sickness.
The primary objective of the model was to provide a realistic walking experience without compromising presence.
The next lecture segment will focus on minimizing cyber sickness while maximizing presence using the existing model.
Students are strongly encouraged to review the provided references to gain a better understanding of how the models were developed.

key_terms.definition: Presence is a state that is likely to increase when certain factors are introduced into the experience. It is a factor that must be maximized when designing virtual reality experiences.
Cyber sickness is a concern that researchers aim to optimize and minimize within virtual reality experiences. It is a key issue that the system must address.
Realistic walking speed model is a model designed for system-controlled virtual reality tools. Its primary purpose is to maximize the presence of the user.
Level of realism refers to the quality of the experience that is judged by the user. This level is one of the requirements that the developed model must meet.
Preference for such a model refers to the user's specific desires regarding the design of the model. The developed model must satisfy this user preference.

L51.subgoal: Explain the approach of optimizing VR experience by controlling exposure duration

key_points.text: The previous model used to enhance presence does not provide solutions for experience optimization.,
Cyber sickness symptoms rise proportionally with the duration of VR exposure.,
A key optimization approach is controlling exposure duration to minimize cyber sickness.,
The lecture will discuss one specific approach to optimizing VR experience for cyber sickness.

key_terms.definition: Optic flow is the rate at which the scenes change in the virtual world. This rate allows the user to perceive movement, which is necessary for a natural walking experience.

Cyber sickness is a condition correlated with the duration of exposure in a VR environment. The severity of symptoms associated with cyber sickness rises proportionally with the length of the VR session.
Presence in the virtual world is a quality that can be enhanced by models. It refers to the user's perception of being immersed within the virtual environment.
VR navigation experience refers to the specific topic of optimizing how a user moves and navigates within a virtual reality environment. This optimization is a focus of the course discussion.
Exposure duration is the length of time a user spends in the virtual world. This duration is a key factor that contributes to the onset and severity of cyber sickness.

L51.subgoal: Analyze methods for controlling VR exposure duration and their limitations

key_points.text: The duration of cyber sickness depends on factors such as virtual world size, travel speed, and interaction time.
Higher travel speed reduces the overall duration of exposure in the virtual world.
Teleportation reduces exposure duration by allowing instantaneous movement, but it lacks naturalness.
Arbitrarily changing the terrain shape prevents users from building a mental map, which hampers wayfinding.

key_terms.definition: Cyber sickness is a condition whose duration depends on several factors, including the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, and the interaction time. These factors include inspection, selection, and manipulation of objects.
A virtual environment is a digital space that can range from very small, such as a room, to very large, like a city. It can also be extremely large, such as a specific island.
Teleportation-type movement is a method of navigation where the speed is at its maximum. This results in instantaneous movement occurring between two specific points.
A mental map is a concept that users build in the virtual world. This map is essential for the user's ability to perform wayfinding activities.
Wayfinding is the ability to navigate in the virtual world. This ability is supported by the user's capacity to build a mental map.

L51.subgoal: Explain the characteristics and purpose of semi-interactive VR tours

key_points.text: A semi-interactive tour is defined as interaction with Points of Interest (POIs) combined with navigation controlled by the system.
In a semi-interactive tour, travel is automatic and system-controlled, but user interactions are limited to specific objects or POIs.
The primary objective of studying semi-interactive system control tools is to reduce the duration of exposure to the virtual world.

key_terms.definition: A semi-interactive tour is a virtual tour where the travel between locations is managed automatically by the system, but users are allowed to interact with specific objects at designated points of interest. This type of tour does not totally disregard user interactions.
Points of interest are specific, chosen locations within the virtual environment where users are permitted to interact with objects. These are the limited areas where user interaction is allowed.
Interaction time is the specific duration of time required for a user to interact with the virtual objects. This time can be ignored in entirely system-controlled VR tools.

A system-controlled VR tool is a virtual reality application where the movement or travel between points is managed automatically by the system. In this scenario, the interaction time can be disregarded.

L51.subgoal: Define the two optimization problems for creating an efficient VR tour

key_points.text: Interaction time at points of interest can be limited based on an a priori estimate of the average user's required time.
One optimization approach seeks an optimum path that allows users to experience all points of interest in minimum time.
The second optimization approach seeks an optimum path that maximizes the number of points of interest within a fixed time limit.
These two approaches provide methods for optimizing the duration of exposure in a virtual tour.

key_terms.definition: Points of interest are specific locations within the virtual environment that users are intended to interact with or explore during a tour. These locations are the focus of the time optimization process.

A semi-interactive tour is a virtual tour design that imposes a limit on the amount of time a user can spend interacting at any single point of interest. This time limit is used to optimize the overall duration of the experience.
Duration of exposure refers to the total time a user spends experiencing a virtual tour. This duration is the primary variable that the optimization process seeks to improve.

Optimum path is the most efficient route designed to meet a specific goal within the virtual tour. This path either ensures all points of interest are visited in minimum time or maximizes the number of points visited within a fixed time.

L51.subgoal: Formulate the optimal POI travel problem using graph theory

key_points.text: The virtual world is modeled as a weighted graph G, where V is the set of vertices and E is the set of edges.
Vertices (V) represent all the Points of Interest (POIs) in the virtual world.
Edge weights are determined by the Euclidean distance between two connected POIs.
The graph does not need to be complete because direct paths between all POIs are not guaranteed in realistic environments.
The objective is to find a path that covers all vertices while minimizing the time required and maintaining a realistic speed.

key_terms.definition: Weighted graph is a representation of the virtual world where the connections between points of interest are assigned numerical values. These weights typically denote the distance between the connected points.
Vertex is a node in the graph that represents a specific point of interest within the virtual world. Each point of interest is assumed to be a vertex in the graph structure.

Edge weight is the value assigned to a connection between two vertices, representing the cost or distance of traveling between them. This weight is calculated using the Euclidean distance if a direct path exists, or a very large number if no direct path is available.

Points of interest are specific locations or objects within the virtual world that are designated as nodes in the graph. A single point of interest corresponds to a single node in the graph structure.

Cyber sickness is a prevalence of sickness that may be optimized by controlling the duration of exposure to the virtual experience. The onset of this sickness is directly related to how long a user is exposed to the virtual environment.

L51.subgoal: Derive the formula for computing travel time between connected nodes using a natural walking model

key_points.text: The initial stage of the algorithm requires computing the time needed to travel between two directly connected nodes at natural walking speed.
Total travel time is calculated by integrating the instantaneous time (dt) over the total distance (D).
The travel time estimate (tau_D) between directly connected vertices simplifies to the form tau_D = D / V_0.
The calculated travel time assumes the user is moving at a natural walking speed.

key_terms.definition: Natural walking speed is the foundational model used to calculate the time required to travel between connected points. This model assumes a realistic human gait for the movement.

Perceived instantaneous walking speed is the walking speed as experienced by the user, which is represented by the visual gain into the actual instantaneous speed. This speed is represented in a specific mathematical form.
Actual instantaneous walking speed is the realistic speed of the user at any given moment, represented by the variable V act. This speed is derived from the user's step frequency and height.

Total travel time is the cumulative time required to traverse a distance, which is found by taking an integral of the instantaneous time element over the total distance. This calculation determines the time between two connected nodes.

Travel time estimate tau D is the final computed value for the time between two directly connected vertices. This estimate is derived after applying various mathematical simplifications and Fourier series expansions.

L51.subgoal: Transform the path optimization problem into a solvable Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) instance

key_points.text: The objective is to find a path that minimizes total travel time while ensuring all vertices of the graph are included (153-156).
The problem discussed is a variation of the classical Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) (157).
Since the initial graph may not be complete, hypothetical edges are introduced between unconnected vertices (161-164).
The weight of a hypothetical edge is defined as the shortest path length between the two vertices (165-171).

key_terms.definition: The Travelling salesman problem is a problem that seeks the shortest possible path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node within a complete graph.
A complete graph is a type of graph where every node is directly connected to every other node.
A Hamiltonian path is a path within a graph that covers all nodes, where each node is visited exactly once.
A hypothetical edge is an introduced edge used for computation when two vertices lack a direct connection in the original graph.
The modified edge weight is the weight between two nodes, defined as the Euclidean distance if they are directly connected, or the shortest path length if they are not.

L51.subgoal: Apply the two-phase algorithm to find the optimal path in a non-complete graph

key_points.text: To use a standard TSP solver, the original graph must be converted into a complete graph by computing hypothetical edge lengths (shortest paths) between all vertices.
The edge weights in the modified complete graph must be replaced with the travel time between vertices, rather than Euclidean distance.
The path output by the TSP solver ($P_{opt}$) may contain hypothetical edges that do not exist in the original graph G.
The final step requires replacing any hypothetical edges in the optimal path with the shortest path found in the original graph G.

key_terms.definition: Hypothetical edge is an edge that is introduced into the modified graph but does not exist in the original graph. These edges are used to convert the original graph into a complete graph for the TSP solver.
Complete graph is a graph structure where every vertex is directly connected to every other vertex. This structure is created by adding hypothetical edges to the original graph.
Shortest path is the optimal route between two vertices in the original graph. This path is used to replace any hypothetical edges found in the TSP solver's output.
Travel time is the specific weight assigned to an edge in the modified graph. This weight represents the actual time taken to travel from one vertex to another.

L51.subgoal: Summarize the procedure for minimizing travel time to cover all points of interest

key_points.text: The problem is converted into a graph where nodes are points of interest and edges are weighted by Euclidean distance.
Finding the minimum duration path covering all points of interest is mapped to the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP).
Travel time between vertices is computed using the natural walking speed model, even if a hypothetical edge is introduced.
The next lecture will cover the alternative optimization approach: maximizing points covered within a given time limit.

key_terms.definition: Travelling salesman problem is a standard classical problem that the task of finding an optimal path covering all points of interest is mapped to. This problem seeks the shortest possible route that visits a set of locations and returns to the origin.

Graph theoretic problem is the method of converting the virtual world into a graph structure. This structure uses points of interest as nodes and weighted edges representing the distance between them.
Complete graph is a modified graph where hypothetical edges are introduced between every pair of vertices. This modification allows the calculation of travel time between any two points of interest.

Cybersickness time threshold is the maximum time limit that, if exceeded, increases the possibility of cybersickness. The algorithm must ensure the calculated minimum time remains below this threshold.
Points of interest are the nodes in the graph that represent specific locations within the virtual world. These are the locations that the optimized path must cover.

L52.subgoal: Define the problem of maximizing points of interest covered within a time threshold

key_points.text: The new optimization goal is to maximize the number of points of interest covered, given a time constraint.
A Time Threshold (TTH) is defined to restrict the user's VR exposure time and prevent cyber sickness.
The TTH can be determined using empirical studies or by referencing pre-existing research.
The new approach does not require visiting every single point of interest, unlike the previous method.

key_terms.definition: Cyber sickness is a possibility of sickness that can be induced when the user's VR exposure time exceeds a specific time threshold. This sickness is a problem that the optimization process aims to minimize.
Time threshold is a defined limit on the user's movement or VR exposure time. This threshold must not be crossed because crossing it increases the possibility of cyber sickness.
Points of interest are specific locations or vertices within the virtual world. The objective of the second optimization approach is to cover the maximum number of these points.
Optimal path is a specific route within the virtual world designed to meet a defined objective. This objective may be traversing in minimum time or covering the maximum number of points of interest.

L52.subgoal: Define node importance and formulate the path optimization problem

key_points.text: The importance of every node (vertex or point of interest) is defined using a function, f_v, that maps to a positive real number.
The total importance of a given path is calculated by summing the individual importance of each node within that path.
The objective of the problem is to maximize the total importance (Fp) for paths that can be completed within a specified time threshold (TH).

key_terms.definition: Importance function is a function (f, v) that assigns a positive real number to every vertex or point of interest. This number indicates the importance of that specific vertex.
Node importance is the measure of how important a specific node is, captured as a positive real number. A higher value of this number signifies a higher importance.
Total importance is the aggregated measure of a given path. This value is calculated by summing the individual importance of every node within that path.
Path is a sequence of nodes, denoted as P, that contains nodes from V1 to Vn. This path is the route being evaluated for optimization.
Time threshold is the maximum allowed time limit within which a path must be completed. This constraint dictates which paths are viable for the problem statement.

L52.subgoal: Define the waiting time function and calculate total waiting time for a path

key_points.text: Path optimization aims to maximize total importance while keeping the total time less than or equal to a defined threshold.
Waiting time is defined as the time required for a user to inspect or interact with a specific point of interest (node).
The waiting time function (W) maps each node to a real positive number indicating the maximum time required for interaction at that node.
Total waiting time for a path is calculated by summing the individual waiting times of all nodes within that path.

key_terms.definition: Waiting time is the time required by a user to inspect or interact with a particular object located at a node. This value represents the maximum time a user needs to spend at that point of interest.

The waiting time function is a defined function that maps every node to a real positive number. This number indicates the maximum time required for a user to inspect or interact with the object at that node.

Total waiting time is calculated by summing the individual waiting times for all nodes that constitute a specific path. This calculation is performed in a manner similar to calculating total importance.
A point of interest is a specific node where the user is expected to spend time to inspect or perform an action with an object. These points are critical locations when determining an optimal path.

L52.subgoal: Explain how the VR path optimization problem relates to VRP with Profit

key_points.text: The goal is to maximize the total importance (profit) of paths that complete within a specified time threshold (TP + WP <= T threshold).
The problem is identified as a generalization of the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP), specifically VRP with Profit (VRPP).
The optimization requires maximizing importance within the time constraint without necessarily visiting all nodes.
Existing VRPP solvers can be utilized to find the optimal path that maximizes profit within the given time constraint.

key_terms.definition: Vehicle routing problem (VRP) is a well-known problem in operations research that serves as the basis for the problem being solved in this lecture.
VRP with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP) where the goal is to maximize profit within given time constraints.
Traveling salesman problem is an existing problem whose solvers can be utilized, similar to VRPP solvers, to find optimal paths.
Cybersickness is a condition that may occur when a user's exposure time exceeds a specific time threshold.

L52.subgoal: Outline the algorithm for optimizing VR paths considering importance and wait time

key_points.text: The goal is to find an optimal path that maximizes importance (F) while keeping the total exposure time (travel time plus wait time) below a specified threshold.
The initial graph is converted into a complete graph, and the edge weights are replaced with travel time calculated using the natural walking model.
The VRPP solver is used on the modified graph, providing node importance (F) and waiting time (W) as inputs to determine the optimal path.
The final optimal path must be modified to reflect the original graph structure by replacing the hypothetical edges with the shortest paths.

key_terms.definition: Optimal path P is the desired output of the algorithm, representing a route that maximizes the importance (F) of visited nodes while ensuring the total exposure time remains below a specified threshold.
Complete graph is a modified graph structure where every vertex is connected to every other vertex, replacing non-directly connected edges with the shortest path between those vertices.
Total exposure time is a metric that represents the overall time spent in the environment, calculated by summing the time spent traveling and the time spent waiting at each node.
VRPP solver is a specialized computational tool used to determine the optimal path by taking the final modified graph, node importance values, and waiting times as input.
Natural walking model is a method used to compute the travel time between nodes, ensuring that the resulting travel duration provides a realistic experience.

L52.subgoal: Explain the refined optimal path formulation for VR experience optimization

key_points.text: The initial minimum time path approach may not address cyber sickness if the time required is still large.
A refined optimal path formulation is used, incorporating node weights, importance, and waiting times.
This optimal path aims to cover the maximum number of the most important Points of Interest (POIs) within a given time threshold.

key_terms.definition: Experience optimization is the process of improving the quality of the user's experience within a virtual reality environment. This involves addressing various issues to ensure a better user interaction.

Cyber sickness issues are concerns related to virtual reality that may be induced if the time spent in the environment is too large. These issues are a primary concern that optimization strategies must address.

Optimal path is a specific path formulation designed to maximize the number of most important Points of Interest (POIs) covered by the user. This path must be covered within a given time threshold, while accounting for node importance and waiting times.
Time threshold is a specific time limit that the user must be able to cover the optimal path within. This limit is used to ensure the user can complete the experience within a manageable timeframe.

Point of interest (POI) is a specific location within the virtual environment that is important for the user. Users must spend time at these points to inspect or interact with the objects present there.

used_concepts: Graph representation of a virtual environment

L53.subgoal: Compare navigation optimization approaches and plan the practical application of time-constrained routing

key_points.text: If the virtual world is very large, the minimum time required to cover all points of interest may still be too long, potentially inducing cyber sickness.
The optimal path under time constraint approach limits user exposure to a time threshold and aims to cover the maximum number of important points within that duration.
The lecture will apply the optimization theory by modeling a practical problem using the Majuli River Island case study.

key_terms.definition: Cyber sickness is a related issue in VR experience optimization that measures the possibility of discomfort or illness experienced by the user during virtual exposure. Measures are taken to avoid or minimize the onset of this sickness.

Optimal path approach is a method for identifying a route in a virtual world that allows the user to explore every point of interest in the shortest possible time. This approach seeks to cover all points of interest in minimum duration.

Optimal path under time constraint is a method where the user must cover a path that maximizes the number of important points of interest within a predefined time threshold. This constraint sets an upper limit on the duration of the virtual tour.

Points of interest are specific locations within a virtual world that the user is expected to explore, interact with, or inspect during a virtual tour. These locations are critical for the user's experience.

Graph theoretic form is the mathematical structure used to model a practical problem so that optimization approaches can be applied to it. This form allows the theoretical concepts to be put into practice.

L53.subgoal: Determine optimal paths for VR exploration based on time and experience constraints

key_points.text: Majuli is a large river island in Assam, India, which hosts various cultural sites called Satras.
The target Satra campus covers approximately 1200 square meters and contains at least 25 points of interest.
Full physical exploration of the site is too time-consuming (up to a day) and is not recommended for VR due to cyber sickness.
The goal is to propose an optimal path to maximize user experience by either minimizing duration or maximizing POI coverage within a time threshold.

key_terms.definition: Points of interest are specific locations within a site that are estimated to be significant enough to be included in a virtual tour. These points are used to guide the user's exploration and provide specific experiences.

Cyber sickness is a negative physical reaction that can be induced in a user when they are exposed to a virtual world for an extended period. This discomfort is a reason why long virtual tours are not recommended.

Walking-based exploration is a method of virtual tour where the user navigates the virtual environment by simulating natural walking movements. This method is used to achieve a realistic experience within the virtual world.

Optimum path is a calculated route designed to achieve a specific goal, such as minimizing the total duration of a tour. This path ensures the user can explore the most important points within a given time limit.

L53.subgoal: Describe the methodology for converting a physical site into a weighted graph for VR navigation

key_points.text: A physical site must be mapped to a graph where points of interest (POIs) serve as nodes and Euclidean distance is used for edge weights.
Converting a site to a graph is an iterative process that requires detailed field study and patience.
The data required for the graph model is gathered through contextual inquiry, observing travel behavior, and interviewing local residents.
The final graph model uses filled circles to denote points of interest and rectangular forms to represent artifacts or places.

key_terms.definition: Graph is a representation where points of interest are defined as nodes, and connections between these nodes are represented by edges. This structure allows for the mapping of a site, such as a campus, into a navigable model.

Points of interest are specific locations or objects within a site that are designated as nodes in the graph model. These points are the locations that users are expected to visit or interact with during navigation.

Contextual inquiry is a field study method used to observe people's travel behavior and gather information about places of importance in their natural environment. This method involves observing users in situ and talking to local people for clarity.
Euclidean distance is a method used to calculate the straight-line distance between two points. This calculated distance is then used as the weight for the edges connecting those points in the graph.
Edge weights are numerical values assigned to the edges connecting nodes in a graph. These weights typically represent the calculated distance between the connected points of interest.

L53.subgoal: Apply optimization algorithms (TSP/VRPP) to find optimal paths in a weighted graph

key_points.text: The distance between points of interest (POIs) is used as the weight for the edges in the graph.
Algorithms can find an optimal path that covers all nodes in minimum time using a TSP solver.
Algorithms can find an optimal path within a given time threshold using a VRPP solver.
Path optimization can also consider relative importance and wait time at each POI.

key_terms.definition: Points of interest are specific locations that are identified and used as nodes in the graph formulation for pathfinding. These locations are critical for determining the optimal route.
Graph is a structure formulated to represent connections between nodes, where the distance between nodes is measured. This structure allows algorithms to determine optimal paths.

Weight is the value assigned to an edge or between nodes, which represents either the measured distance or the relative importance of the connection. This value is used by algorithms to calculate the most efficient path.

Optimal path is a route determined by algorithms that either covers all nodes in minimum time or is traversed within a specific time threshold. The goal is to find the most efficient route based on defined criteria.
Time threshold is a specific time constant set by the user that an optimal path must be traversed within. This constraint allows the algorithm to find a path that meets a predefined time limit.

L53.subgoal: Summarize the key concepts and outline the focus of the next lecture

key_points.text: VR experience optimization emphasizes psychophysiological optimization to address issues like cybersickness.
There are two types of optimization important to XR: psychophysiological/experience optimization and resource optimization.
The next lecture will focus specifically on resource optimization for immersive experiences.
Six references (1 through 6) are provided to help students gain more clarity on the topics discussed.

key_terms.definition: Psychophysiological optimization is a type of optimization in VR experience that is primarily aimed at addressing cybersickness issues. This optimization focuses on the physical and psychological aspects of the user's experience.

Experience optimization is one of the two types of optimizations important to XR, specifically referring to psychophysiological optimization. This type of optimization focuses on improving the quality of the user's experience.
Resource optimization is the second type of optimization discussed in XR. It focuses on managing the necessary resources for an immersive experience.

Cybersickness issues are problems encountered in VR experience that psychophysiological optimization is primarily aimed at taking care of. These issues relate to the physical and psychological discomfort of the user.

L54.subgoal: Define the objectives and challenges of optimizing VR resource requirements

key_points.text: Extended reality (XR) and virtual reality (VR) systems are resource hungry, meaning they require a large amount of resources.
Optimization in the extended reality domain includes experience optimization, psychophysiological optimization, and resource optimization.
The primary objective is to minimize resource requirements while simultaneously maximizing the user experience.
This lecture focuses specifically on learning ways to optimize the VR resource requirements, moving beyond previous discussions on optimizing VR experience.

key_terms.definition: Resource optimization is an objective in extended reality that involves building systems to minimize the requirement of resources. This is done without compromising the user experience, which means maximizing the experience.

Experience optimization is a technique used in the context of VR or immersive experience to reduce or minimize the onset of cyber sickness. This is one of the major types of optimization discussed in the extended reality domain.
Extended reality (XR) is a domain, such as Virtual Reality (VR), that is characterized as being resource hungry. This means that extended reality requires a large amount of resources to function.

Resource requirements are the necessary resources that extended reality (XR), particularly virtual reality (VR), needs to operate. Systems must be built to minimize these requirements while simultaneously optimizing the experience.

L54.subgoal: Identify and categorize the various types of resources relevant to VR systems

key_points.text: Resources in a broad sense encompass hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure. [19-23]
In the context of VR, hardware resources include input, processing, and output devices.
VR software includes developmental tools, SDKs, and application packages, while manpower covers staff for development and maintenance.
Supporting infrastructure includes physical elements (like rooms and furniture) and digital elements (like network gears and servers).

key_terms.definition: Resource, in the context of Virtual Reality, refers to the hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure required for the system. This includes specific components like input devices, processing devices, output devices, and various types of infrastructure.
Digital infrastructure refers to the network-related components necessary for a setup. This includes network gears, switches, routers, wires, and servers.
Physical infrastructure refers to the tangible elements supporting a setup. This includes rooms, furniture, and the supply of electricity.

L54.subgoal: Define the scope and necessity of optimizing client-side hardware for VR

key_points.text: Optimizing all resource types (including money, policy, and geopolitical issues) is generally too complex and impractical.
VR resource optimization primarily focuses on the hardware requirements available at the client or user end.
The objective of client-side optimization is to allow the end user to have a good experience with affordable hardware.
Specialized hardware is required in VR to manage issues arising from rendering and computer graphics.

key_terms.definition: Resource optimization is the process of making strategic choices about which resources to optimize, often by assuming that certain external factors are already fixed. This strategy allows the focus to be narrowed down to a manageable set of variables.

Client end refers to the location where the user has direct access to the hardware, making it the primary focus for resource optimization. This is the physical point where the user experiences the virtual reality system.
Computer graphics is the field that deals with generating visual content and images using computers. This field requires specialized hardware management to support a good immersive experience.

Immersive experience is the quality of the user's interaction with the system that requires specific hardware to manage rendering and computer graphics issues. The goal of optimization is to ensure the client has a good experience.
Hardware resources are the physical components available to the user that must be optimized to ensure a good experience. These resources are specifically located at the client or user end.

L54.subgoal: Define computer graphics and identify the fundamental challenges of image rendering

key_points.text: An image in computer graphics is constructed from geometric objects, each assigned a specific color.
The fundamental challenge of computer graphics is translating binary computer data into a realistic representation that humans can perceive.
The process of creating realistic imagery is broken down into four basic questions: representation, synthesis, manipulation, and motion.

key_terms.definition: Computer graphics is the field that discusses the basic idea of how images are rendered onto a computer screen or any display. This field aims to understand how images are created and displayed on a computer.
An interface is what a user gets to see on a computer screen. This display is the visual output presented to the user.
An object is a geometric shape that can be part of a specific item or part of the overall interface. Objects include the main item and interface elements like menus or icons.
An image is the entire thing displayed on the screen, which is not limited to just the main object. This whole display is comprised of geometric shapes, and each shape has an attached color.
Synthesis is the process of combining individual parts to form a complete and realistic image. This process addresses how parts are put together to create a full scene.

L54.subgoal: Identify the major components and data flow of a generic graphics system

key_points.text: The goal is to understand how a static image is rendered, including how components are represented and synthesized.
A generic graphics system includes a host computer, a display, and three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.
The host computer communicates with the display controller, which sends data to video memory for the video controller to render the image on screen.

key_terms.definition: Rendering is the process that determines how components are represented, synthesized, and finally displayed on the screen. This process is fundamental to understanding how images are created.

Generic graphics system is a framework that outlines the major components and basic terms needed to understand the process of rendering. This system provides the overall structure for image generation.
Display controller is a major component that receives display commands from the host computer and sends data to video memory for storage. It facilitates two-way communication with the CPU.
Video memory is a major component used for storing data that is sent by the display controller. This stored data is subsequently utilized by the video controller.
Video controller is a major component that utilizes data stored in video memory to render an image onto the screen. It is responsible for the final visual output.

L54.subgoal: Explain the function and necessity of the display controller and GPU

key_points.text: Image generation is a multi-stage process that requires significant computation.
If the CPU handles all rendering computations, its time will be consumed, preventing it from performing other tasks.
To increase system efficiency, rendering is typically carried out by a dedicated component called the graphics card, which contains a GPU.
The CPU delegates graphics rendering tasks to the display controller (GPU), which performs the computation without the CPU's involvement.

key_terms.definition: Display controller is a generic component responsible for creating a representation of an image that can be displayed on a screen. This component receives graphics rendering tasks from the CPU and manages the necessary actions for image creation.

Graphics card is a dedicated component of a computer designed to handle rendering-related computations. It typically comprises a Graphics processing unit (GPU) and is responsible for processing visual data.
Graphics processing unit (GPU) is a specialized processing unit found within the graphics card. This unit performs the complex computations related to rendering tasks assigned by the CPU.
Rendering is the multi-stage process of generating a 2D image when a scene is displayed on a screen. This process involves numerous computations to create the final visual output.

L54.subgoal: Trace the process from digital image generation to pixel activation

key_points.text: The display controller generates the image in a digital format (zeros and ones) which is stored in the video memory (VRAM).
A graphic display screen is composed of a grid of pixels that emit light when activated, creating a colored image.
The video controller converts the digital image stored in video memory into analog voltages needed to activate the pixels.

key_terms.definition: Display controller generates the image in a digital format, which consists of strings of zeros and ones. Display controller outputs this representation of the image in binary form.

Video memory is a dedicated part of the computer's memory hierarchy, typically residing within a separate graphics unit. Video memory stores the digital image representation generated by the display controller.
Video controller converts the digital image stored in the video memory into analog voltages. Video controller controls the mechanism that activates the pixels on the display screen.
Pixel is a picture element that is arranged in a grid on a graphic display screen. Pixels are activated to emit light, which allows the viewer to perceive a colored image.

L54.subgoal: Compare the mechanisms and characteristics of vector scan and raster scan rendering

key_points.text: Vector scan devices render images by activating only selective pixels that represent continuous geometric primitives like lines or curves.
Vector scan systems require high precision to target specific pixels, which makes them costly and typically unaffordable for mass consumption.
Raster scan devices view the image as represented by the whole pixel grid, meaning all pixels are considered for rendering.
Raster scanning is achieved by considering all pixels in a specific sequence, typically from left to right, top to bottom.

key_terms.definition: Rendering is the process of creating an image, which can be thought of in two fundamentally different ways based on how the pixels are excited.

A vector scan device is a graphic device that renders an image by activating only selective pixels that represent continuous geometric primitives, such as lines or curves. This method assumes that focusing on the rendering of these primitives allows the whole image to be perceived.

A raster scan device is a graphic device that renders an image by viewing it as represented by the whole pixel grid. In this method, all pixels are considered for rendering, not just the selected pixels.

L54.subgoal: Describe the raster scan mechanism and define the frame buffer structure

key_points.text: Raster scan displays use a left-to-right, top-to-bottom scanning sequence to activate all pixels [186-190].
Raster scan rendering is much cheaper than the selective rendering required by vector scan devices.
The frame buffer is the generally accepted term for the video memory component of a raster scan system [198-199].
The frame buffer stores intensity for each pixel, with one memory location per pixel, and its size equals the screen resolution [200-203].

key_terms.definition: Raster scan displays are the type of display typically found in commercial products such as smartphones or televisions. These displays utilize a specific scanning method to render images.
The frame buffer is the video memory component of a raster scan system. It contains one memory location corresponding to each pixel, storing the intensity value for that pixel.

L54.subgoal: Explain how pixel decay necessitates refreshing and why high refresh rates are vital for VR

key_points.text: Light emitted from pixel elements decays over time, which can lead to scene fading and image distortion during raster scanning.
Refreshing, which involves periodically re-exciting pixels, is used to maintain uniformity in the rendered image.
The refresh rate is the number of times a scene is refreshed per second and is typically measured in hertz (Hz).
A higher refresh rate is always preferable for VR experiences because the screen is much closer to the eyes than in typical computer usage.

key_terms.definition: Screen refreshing is the periodic re-excitation of pixels to counteract the natural decay of emitted light. This process ensures that the image remains uniform and stable even when the scene itself is not changing.
Refresh rate is the number of times a scene is refreshed per second on the screen. It is typically measured in hertz.

Raster scan device is a display mechanism that renders images by following a left-to-right, top-to-bottom scanning manner. This sequential scanning causes the excitation of pixels to occur at different times across the screen.

L54.subgoal: Explain color perception and introduce the concept of the 3D graphics pipeline

key_points.text: Color displays use pixels containing multiple elements (typically three) that emit light at different intensities (R, G, B).
Color is perceived when red, green, and blue light emissions mix in the eye.
The current focus of resource optimization is on hardware resources at the client end.
The 3D graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process that computes rendering from object representation to the pixel grid.

key_terms.definition: Color display is a specific type of screen where each pixel contains more than one type of element. These elements are capable of emitting light with different intensities.

Primary color refers to the three fundamental colors—red, green, and blue—that are typically used by elements in a pixel. These colors are emitted with different intensities to represent a combination of colors.

Resource optimization is the process of finding ways to optimize various resources within Extended Reality (XR) and Virtual Reality (VR). This process is necessary because of the need to manage different resources effectively.
Hardware resource refers to the physical components that are being focused on for optimization at the client end. Understanding these resources is necessary to understand the 'why' of optimization.
3D graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process that describes the computation flow. This process starts from the object representation and concludes with the rendering onto the pixel grid.

L55.subgoal: Define the 3D graphics pipeline and explain its function in computing frame buffer values

key_points.text: The graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process used to compute values stored in the frame buffer.
The display processor, which is part of the display controller, computes these values in distinct stages.
When dealing with 3D scenes, the process of computing frame buffer values is specifically called the 3D graphics pipeline.
The lecture will introduce the 3D graphics pipeline and discuss its various parts.

key_terms.definition: Graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process used to compute the values that are stored in the frame buffer. This process ultimately drives the display mechanism via the video controller.

Display processor is the component, which is part of the display controller, that is responsible for computing the necessary values in distinct stages. These values are real numbers stored in the framebuffer.
Frame buffer is the memory location that stores color values. The video controller uses these values to control the pixels, allowing a colored image to be perceived on the screen.

L55.subgoal: Describe the five stages and coordinate transformations within the 3D graphics pipeline

key_points.text: The 3D graphics pipeline consists of five main stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, viewing transformation, and scan conversion.
Modeling transformation places individual objects, defined in local coordinate systems, into a common world coordinate system.
The lighting stage assigns color to the 3D scene, which is essential for improving visual perception.
Scan conversion transforms the continuous device coordinate space into a discrete pixel grid description.
The overall process involves transforming data across multiple coordinate systems, including local, world, view, device, and pixel grid.

key_terms.definition: Object representation is the initial stage of the pipeline where objects that will be part of the image on display are defined. This definition establishes the fundamental components that together constitute the image to be rendered on a screen.

Modeling transformation is the second stage that moves objects from their individual local coordinate system definitions into a common world coordinate system. This process allows multiple objects of different shapes and sizes to be assembled into a single scene.

The lighting stage is the third stage where color is assigned to the constructed 3D scene. Assigning color is crucial because it makes the 3D nature of the scene more prominent and improves visual perception.

Viewing transformation is the fourth stage that simulates taking a snapshot by mapping the colored 3D scene from the world coordinate system to a 2D device coordinate system. This transformation moves the scene from a 3D world view to a 2D plane equivalent to the screen.

Scan conversion is the fifth stage that transforms the continuous device coordinate space description into a discrete pixel grid description. This process maps the real-valued coordinates of the image points to the integer coordinates of the pixels.

L55.subgoal: Identify the two fundamental challenges in object representation for realistic rendering

key_points.text: Objects must be represented with intricate details and characteristics to ensure a realistic viewing experience, as simplistic approximations lose realism.
The first fundamental question is how to represent objects with characteristic complexities so they can be rendered realistically.
The second fundamental question is how to create a representation that makes the rendering process efficient by optimizing space and time complexities.
The objective is to maintain a balance between capturing all intricate details (realism) and performing subsequent computations efficiently (performance).

key_terms.definition: Object representation is the method used to structure computer-generated scenes, allowing for the depiction of objects that possess varying shapes, sizes, and characteristics.
The 3D graphics pipeline is the sequence of stages through which computations are performed to determine the intensities at individual pixel levels.
Balance is the necessary equilibrium between having a representation that captures all intricate details and ensuring that subsequent rendering computations are performed efficiently.

L55.subgoal: Classify and describe the major techniques for 3D object representation in VR systems

key_points.text: 3D object representation techniques are broadly categorized into point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning (153).
Boundary representation often uses mesh representation, which defines objects using polygons and vertex lists (177, 178).
Parametric representation, such as splines, uses several lower-degree polynomials to represent complex curved surfaces (203, 210).
Space partitioning representation divides the 3D space into disjoint regions using a hierarchical structure called a space partitioning tree (219, 222).
Specialized techniques, such as fractal representation or skeletal models, are used for complex or photorealistic objects (228, 234).

key_terms.definition: Point sample rendering is a method where information is captured in the form of points on the scene, with each point carrying specific attributes. This process relies on real-world input sensors to generate a synthetic image of the scene.
Boundary representation is a technique where objects are defined by the surfaces that delineate the object's boundary. These surfaces can be either polygonal or curved.

Mesh representation is a boundary representation technique that uses polygons to define the surfaces of an object. The object is represented by a list of vertices and edges that define these connected polygons.

Spline representation is a higher-level method used to represent curved surfaces or curves, typically preferred by designers creating artificial environments. This representation uses several lower-degree polynomials to construct the complete curve.

L55.subgoal: Summarize the stages of the 3D graphics pipeline and its implementation flexibility

key_points.text: The 3D graphics pipeline consists of five broad stages: object representation, modeling transformation, viewing transformation, and scan conversion.
The pipeline involves transformations between a total of six coordinate systems.
The stages of the pipeline are important, but their specific sequence may not be followed exactly during implementation.
The course provides a brief overview, as a detailed discussion of computer graphics is not within its scope.

key_terms.definition: 3D graphics pipeline is a process that involves several stages, such as object representation and scan conversion, which transforms data from one coordinate system to another. The pipeline describes how computations take place in a stage-wise manner.
Object representation is the initial technique in the pipeline that defines how objects are represented for discussion. This stage is one of the broadly five stages of the 3D graphics pipeline.
Modeling transformation is one of the stages in the graphics pipeline that involves transforming data from one coordinate system to another. This stage is part of the overall process of 3D graphics.
Viewing transformation is a stage within the 3D graphics pipeline that involves transforming data from one coordinate system to another. This transformation is necessary for the rendering process.

L56.subgoal: Recap computer graphics fundamentals and outline the scope of the current lecture

key_points.text: The rendering process, which is central to immersive experiences, is studied within computer graphics.
Object representation is considered the first stage of the graphics pipeline.
The object representation stage does not involve computation related to pixel intensity calculation.
This lecture will cover the second and third stages of the graphics pipeline.

key_terms.definition: Computer graphics is the discipline that covers the idea of rendering and the complexities involved in rendering a scene. This discipline is essential because the rendering part is the key component of any immersive experience.
Rendering is the process of how a scene is rendered in front of the eyes of the user on a display device. The idea of rendering is covered within the discipline of computer graphics.
The 3D graphics pipeline is a structured process that consists of various stages used to process graphics. This pipeline includes stages such as object representation.
Object representation is the first stage of the graphics pipeline. This stage involves representing the objects in the scene, though it does not involve intensity calculation.

L56.subgoal: Describe the five stages and transformations of the 3D graphics pipeline

key_points.text: The 3D graphics pipeline is composed of five distinct stages.
Modeling transformation converts the local coordinate description to a world coordinate description.
The viewing pipeline involves several sub-stages, including viewing transformation, clipping, and projection transformation.,,
The lecture will cover the modeling transformation and lighting stages in the current part of the lecture.

key_terms.definition: Modeling transformation is the second stage of the graphics pipeline where the object's description is converted from a local coordinate system to a world coordinate system.
Lighting stage is the third stage of the pipeline that takes place within the world coordinate reference frame.
Viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the graphics pipeline, which contains several sub-stages starting with viewing transformation.
Clipping is an operation that takes place in the 3D view coordinate system.
Scan conversion is the fifth and final stage of the pipeline, transforming the scene description from a device coordinate into a screen coordinate or pixel grid description.

L56.subgoal: Apply basic and composite transformations using matrices to position objects in a world coordinate system

key_points.text: Objects are defined in local coordinate systems and must be transformed into a common world or scene coordinate system to construct a scene.
The four basic geometric transformations are translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing.
Transformations are typically represented by matrices, utilizing a homogeneous coordinate system (e.g., 4x4 for 3D).
When multiple basic operations are required, a composite transformation matrix is obtained by multiplying the individual transformation matrices.
Matrix multiplication is not commutative, meaning the sequence (order) of transformations is critical for obtaining the correct result.

key_terms.definition: Geometric transformation is the process of applying operations on an object's definition in local coordinates to transform it into the world or scene coordinate system. This stage is necessary to assemble multiple individually defined objects into a cohesive scene.

Local coordinate system is a definition where an object is represented individually, allowing its position, dimension, and other properties to be defined relative to itself. Essentially, each object is thought of as having its own coordinate reference frame.

World coordinate system is a common coordinate system where multiple objects are assembled and defined together to construct a scene. This system allows objects, which are individually defined in their own local systems, to be placed together in a shared setting.

Basic transformation refers to the fundamental operations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing, that constitute the building blocks of all geometric transformations. Combinations of these basic operations can be used to create any required transformation for scene construction.

Composite transformation matrix is a single matrix obtained by combining multiple basic transformations into one. This matrix is used when an object requires several operations, such as scaling and translation, to be moved from its local to the world coordinate system.

L56.subgoal: Explain how lighting models simulate color computation in computer graphics

key_points.text: Proper color assignment is essential for achieving a realistic perception of the 3D scene.
Lighting models are more computationally intensive than shading models, which are used as approximations to reduce computation.
Lighting models compute colors using continuous intensity values, which are typically normalized real numbers between 0 and 1.
Color perception is determined by the intensity of light that is reflected from a surface point to the viewer's eye.

key_terms.definition: Lighting model is a method used in computer graphics to simulate the process of light reflection and compute the color of a surface point. Lighting models involve a higher degree of computation compared to shading models.

Shading model is an approximation of color assignment that relies on lighting models. Shading models are designed to reduce computational requirements without significantly compromising the quality of the visual experience.
Color computation is the process of assigning colors to objects within a scene. If colors are not assigned properly, the ability to perceive depth in the 3D scene will be negatively affected.
Continuous intensity value is a real number, typically normalized, that lighting models use to compute colors. These values usually fall within the range of 0 to 1.

L56.subgoal: Analyze the components and formulas of simple lighting models

key_points.text: The total light intensity reaching the viewer is modeled as the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities.,
Reflection coefficients (Ka, Kd, Ks) range from 0.0 to 1.0, controlling whether a surface appears dull or shiny.
The diffuse reflection component is calculated using the surface normal (N) and the light source direction (L) via the dot product N dot L.
The specular component calculation uses the Phong model and requires the viewer direction (V) and the ideal specular reflection direction (R).,

key_terms.definition: Simple lighting model is a method for calculating the intensity of light reaching the viewer's eye by summing the contributions from ambient, diffuse, and specular components. This model provides a simplistic way of looking at how light interacts with a surface.

Reflection coefficient or reflectivity is a surface property that determines the fraction of incident light that gets reflected and comes to the viewer's eye. This coefficient varies between 0.0 and 1.0, where 0 represents a dull surface and 1 represents a shiny, mirror-like surface.
Ambient light is the light that falls on a surface after it has been reflected from surrounding surfaces. This component contributes to the overall light intensity reaching the viewer.
Diffuse light component is the light that is reflected in a diffuse manner when coming directly from the light source. This component accounts for the general, non-shiny reflection of light.

Specular reflection component is the light that is reflected with a specular effect, which appears as a shiny bright spot. This component is calculated using an approximate model, such as the Phong model.

L56.subgoal: Explain the methods for accounting for light intensity attenuation in rendering systems

key_points.text: Light intensity typically diminishes over distance, a factor known as intensity attenuation.
Radial intensity attenuation is calculated using an inverse quadratic function based on the distance between the light source and the surface point.
Angular intensity attenuation is used to create spotlight effects and is determined by a function such as cos(A1 phi).
When attenuation factors are applied, the simple lighting model is modified by multiplying the diffuse and specular components by the attenuation factor.

key_terms.definition: Intensity attenuation over distance is the phenomenon where the intensity of light diminishes as the distance between the light source and the surface point increases. This factor must be accounted for in realistic rendering.

Radial intensity attenuation is a factor that accounts for the effect of diminishing light intensity based on the distance from the light source. This factor is typically computed using an inverse quadratic function.

Inverse quadratic function is a mathematical expression used to compute the attenuation factor for radial attenuation. This function uses the distance between the source and the surface point as a primary variable.

Angular intensity attenuation is a factor used to control light visibility and brightness within a specific region. This factor is primarily considered when generating focused effects like spotlights.
Spotlight effect is a visual outcome where only elements within a defined region are visible or brightly visible. Areas outside this specific zone are rendered darker.

L56.subgoal: Model light intensity using colored light sources and multiple sources

key_points.text: In a colored light model, emitted light intensity is represented by a three-element vector corresponding to red, green, and blue primary colors.
Reflection coefficients (k, kd, ks) must also be specified as three-element vectors for red, green, and blue.
When there are multiple light sources (n), the total intensity (IP) is calculated as the ambient intensity plus a summation over all light sources.
If multiple colored light sources are used, the color computation must be performed for each individual color component.

key_terms.definition: Colored light model is a method for assigning colors where emitted light intensity is broken down into three components corresponding to the primary colors. These three intensities combine together to give the perception of any color.

Source intensity is a three-element vector (Is) that represents the light emitted by a colored light source. This vector consists of three components corresponding to the primary colors: red (Isr), green (Isg), and blue (Isb).

Reflection coefficients are three-element vectors (k, kd, ks) that must be specified for surfaces when computing color. These vectors individually specify the reflection properties for the red, green, and blue primary colors.

L56.subgoal: Explain the process of mapping continuous intensity values to finite device levels

key_points.text: Lighting models compute continuous intensity values (0 to 1), but display devices only support a finite, discrete range of values (e.g., 256 colors).
The mapping process requires determining a factor R, which is based on the psychophysiological property that humans perceive relative change rather than absolute change in intensity.
A lookup table is created that stores device-supported intensities (I0, I1, etc.) and their corresponding bit patterns.
The rendering pipeline involves transforming points, calculating intensity using a lighting model, and then mapping the computed intensity to a device-supported color.

key_terms.definition: Intensity mapping is the process of converting a continuous, infinite range of computed intensity values into a finite set of values supported by a display device. This process involves finding the nearest device-supported intensity value for any computed pixel intensity.

Lighting model is a mechanism used to compute the intensity of light that reflects from a point in a 3D scene and reaches the user's eye. This computation determines the color assigned to a point in the scene.

Transformation matrix is a mathematical matrix used to transform a point from its local coordinate system into the world coordinate system. This matrix can be either an individual basic matrix or a composite matrix.
Composite matrix is a type of transformation matrix that is commonly used in rendering pipelines. It is formed by combining multiple basic matrices.

L57.subgoal: Review the 3D graphics pipeline stages and understand the need for VR resource optimization

key_points.text: VR resource optimization is particularly emphasized because realistic scene generation requires more resources than AR experiences.
Computer graphics involves the rendering process onto display devices, such as HMDs.
The 3D graphics pipeline includes stages such as object representation, modeling transformation, and lighting calculation.
The current lecture segment will focus on the fourth stage of the pipeline, which is view transformation.

key_terms.definition: Computer graphics deals with the rendering process, which is the generation of images on a computer screen or any display device. This field is a foundational component in extended reality applications.

Rendering is a very important component in extended reality applications, specifically dealing with the process of generating images on a display device. It is the core process that computer graphics deals with.
Object representation is the first stage of the 3D graphics pipeline, which takes place within the local coordinate reference frame. This stage defines the object itself.

Modeling transformation is the second stage of the graphics pipeline, which transfers the object's definition from its local coordinates to the definition within a world coordinate scene. This process is also known as geometric transformation.
View transformation is the fourth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline. This stage is the focus of the current lecture segment.

L57.subgoal: Explain how 3D scenes are projected onto 2D screens using the viewing pipeline

key_points.text: Rendering involves selecting a portion of a 3D scene and projecting it onto a 2D display plane.
The viewing pipeline simulates the projection transformation from 3D space to a 2D screen.
The process of rendering is analogous to taking a photograph, where only the field of view is captured.
The lecture will focus on the basic idea of the viewing pipeline rather than going into intricate details.

key_terms.definition: Viewing pipeline is a set of stages used in computer graphics to simulate the process of rendering a three-dimensional scene onto a two-dimensional display.
View transformation is the process within the viewing pipeline that converts a portion of the three-dimensional scene into a two-dimensional screen representation.
Projection is the process of selecting a portion of a constructed three-dimensional scene and mapping it onto a two-dimensional display plane or view plane.

L57.subgoal: Describe the transformations and operations that constitute the 3D viewing pipeline

key_points.text: The viewing pipeline is composed of three transformations (viewing, projection, and window-to-viewport) and two operations (clipping and hidden surface removal).
The viewing transformation converts the 3D world coordinate description of the scene into a 3D view coordinate description.
The projection transformation converts the 3D view coordinate scene into a 2D view plane.
The sequence of stages within the viewing pipeline is not mandatory and can be altered depending on the implementation.

key_terms.definition: Viewing transformation transforms the 3D world coordinate description of the scene into a 3D view coordinate description. This process is akin to viewing the scene through a camera lens.
Projection transformation projects the 3D view coordinate scene onto a 2D view plane. This operation converts the scene from a 3D view coordinate system to a 2D view coordinate system.

Window-to-viewport transformation transforms the projected scene from a 2D view plane description into a 2D device coordinate space. This final transformation prepares the scene for display on the device.
Clipping is an operation that takes place within the 3D view coordinate system. It is one of the two operations that occur during the viewing pipeline.
Hidden surface removal is an operation that takes place within the 3D view coordinate system. This process determines which surfaces are visible and which are obscured by other objects in the scene.

L57.subgoal: Explain the process of 3D viewing transformation using camera parameters

key_points.text: The 3D viewing transformation converts coordinates from a world description to a view description.
The view coordinate system is defined by camera parameters, including the origin, look-at point, and view direction.
The three mutually orthogonal axes (N, V, U) of the view coordinate system are determined using vector operations like the cross product.
The transformation from world to view coordinates is achieved through two basic operations: translation and rotation.

key_terms.definition: 3D viewing transformation is the process of transforming a scene description from a 3D world coordinate description into a 3D view coordinate description. This transformation simulates the process of viewing a scene through a camera mechanism.

View coordinate system is a coordinate system that has its own axes (u, n, and v) and is used to represent the scene from the camera's perspective. This system is established based on the parameters of the camera.
